# Active Recovery & Stress-Recovery Balance Protocol — Managing Fatigue Across Domains

**Purpose:** Provide protocols for active recovery between training sessions and for managing the balance between training stress and total life stress. Recovery is not just "rest" — it is an active process that can be enhanced or impaired by your choices.

---

## The Stress-Recovery Equation

```
Recovery capacity = (Sleep quality × Duration × Consistency) 
                    + (Nutrition status) 
                    + (Active recovery methods)
                    + (Psychological detachment)

Total stress burden = Training stress + Work stress + Life stress 
                      + Sleep debt + Nutritional stress + Environmental stress

Recovery deficit = Total stress burden - Recovery capacity
```

**When recovery deficit is high:** Performance declines, injury risk rises, illness susceptibility increases, mood deteriorates.

**Goal:** Keep recovery deficit near zero. Short periods of deficit (intense training block) are OK if followed by deliberate recovery (deload).

---

## Active Recovery Modalities

### Low-Intensity Movement (Best All-Round)

| Activity | Duration | Intensity | Frequency |
|----------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| Walking | 20-60 min | Very light (2-4/10 effort) | Daily |
| Light cycling | 20-30 min | Light (3-4/10) | On rest days or post-training |
| Swimming | 20-30 min | Light (3-4/10) | 1-2×/week |
| Yoga / mobility flow | 15-30 min | Stretch (2-3/10) | 2-3×/week on rest days |
| Light hiking | 30-60 min | Light (3-5/10) | 1-2×/week |

**Rule:** You should be able to hold a conversation throughout. If you cannot, intensity is too high.

### Contrast Therapy

| Modality | Protocol | Frequency | Evidence |
|----------|----------|-----------|----------|
| Cold exposure (ice bath, cold shower) | 2-5 min at 10-15°C post-training | 2-4×/week | Reduces soreness. May blunt hypertrophy if used immediately after training (wait 4-6h if hypertrophy is primary goal) |
| Heat (sauna) | 10-20 min at 70-90°C post-training or evening | 2-4×/week | Increases blood flow, reduces cortisol, improves sleep. May improve endurance adaptations |
| Contrast (hot-cold) | 3-4 cycles: 3 min hot → 1 min cold | After intense training | Vasodilation/vasoconstriction cycling. Good for limb recovery |

### Stretching & Mobility

| Type | Best For | Protocol |
|------|----------|----------|
| Static stretching | Improving flexibility, reducing tension | Hold 30-60 sec per position. Total 5-10 min. Post-training or evening |
| Dynamic stretching | Pre-training activation | 5-10 min before training. Controlled, full ROM movements |
| Foam rolling / SMR | Reducing muscle tension, improving tissue quality | 30-60 sec per area. Pre-training or post-training. Avoid over bony prominences |
| PNF stretching | Range of motion gains (partner or band assisted) | Contract 20% → relax → stretch. 3 cycles per position |

### Massage & Soft Tissue

| Type | Frequency | Evidence |
|------|-----------|----------|
| Self-massage (foam roller, lacrosse ball, massage gun) | Daily as needed | Reduces perceived soreness. Temporary relief. Good adjunct |
| Professional sports massage | 1-2×/month during high volume | Reduces DOMS, improves recovery perception. Limited evidence for performance enhancement |
| Percussion therapy (Theragun, etc.) | 1-2 min per muscle group pre/post | Increases blood flow. Feel-good effect. Not a substitute for sleep or nutrition |

---

## Recovery by Domain

### Between Sessions (Intra-Week Recovery)

| Goal | Protocol |
|------|----------|
| Minimize DOMS between sessions | Post-training: light cool-down + protein timing. Next day: low-intensity movement (don't sit all day) |
| Maintain performance across week | Prioritize sleep + carb intake around training. Reduce life stress where possible |
| Prevent cumulative fatigue | One "easy" training day per week (reduce volume by 30-40%) or one full rest day |

### Between Training Blocks (Mesocycle Recovery)

| Goal | Protocol |
|------|----------|
| Reset accumulated fatigue | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Deload Protocol.md\|Deload Protocol]] — every 4-12 weeks depending on training age |
| Assess progress | Week 4-6 of block: review performance. Week 7-8: test maxes OR do deload |
| Plan next block | Use deload week to plan next mesocycle. Training should never be on autopilot |

### Life Stress Recovery

| Stressor | Protocol |
|----------|----------|
| High work stress | Reduce training volume by 10-20%. Do not reduce training entirely (exercise buffers stress) |
| Relationship stress | Increase sleep priority. Reduce alcohol. Maintain training as a non-negotiable anchor |
| Travel (time zone change) | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Shift Work & Circadian Rhythm Protocol.md\|Jet lag protocol]] |
| Illness (minor, no fever) | "Neck check": symptoms above neck (runny nose, sore throat) → light training OK. Below neck (fever, body aches, GI) → rest |
| Bereavement, major loss | 1-2 weeks minimal training. Walking only. Training can resume as emotional anchor after acute phase |

---

## Recovery Monitoring

| Tool | What It Tells You | Frequency | Action If Bad |
|------|-------------------|-----------|---------------|
| HRV (heart rate variability) | Parasympathetic vs sympathetic balance | Daily (morning, on waking) | Downward trend >5 days → reduce training load |
| Resting heart rate | Recovery status | Daily (morning) | Elevated >5 bpm from baseline → possible under-recovery or illness |
| Subjective readiness (1-10) | How you feel | Before each session | If <4/10 two sessions in a row → deload |
| Grip strength (hand dynamometer) | CNS recovery | Morning (optional) | Drop >5% from baseline → CNS fatigue |
| Sleep quality (self-report) | One of the best recovery proxies | Daily | Poor sleep >2 nights → deload |

**Minimal viable tracking:** Subjective readiness (1-10) + morning HRV. Everything else is supplementary.

---

## Psychological Recovery (The Overlooked Domain)

| Strategy | Protocol | Why It Works |
|----------|----------|--------------|
| Psychological detachment | No work emails/messages after 8 PM. No training thoughts outside training time | Mental fatigue accumulates just like physical fatigue |
| Digital boundaries | Phone-free hour before bed. No social media in the first hour after waking | Reduces cortisol, improves sleep onset, lowers baseline arousal |
| Nature exposure | 20+ min outdoors (nature, not city) daily | Reduces rumination, lowers stress markers |
| Social recovery | Quality time with friends/family without discussing training or work | Provides perspective, reduces fixation |
| Meditation / breathing | 5-10 min daily (box breathing, body scan, or guided meditation) | Reduces sympathetic tone, improves HRV, enhances sleep |

---

## Recovery Killers (Avoid These)

| Factor | Impact | Alternative |
|--------|--------|-------------|
| Alcohol >2 drinks | Impairs protein synthesis, fragments sleep, increases cortisol | Limit to 1-2 drinks, 3-4h before bed |
| Sleep <6h | Negates most recovery strategies | Prioritize sleep. Deload if sleep is uncontrollably poor |
| Chronic caloric deficit (4+ weeks) | Elevated cortisol, suppressed testosterone, poor recovery | Diet break at maintenance for 1-2 weeks |
| Mental rumination about training | Increases perceived fatigue, impairs sleep | Journal concerns. If you cannot stop thinking about training → you are likely overreaching |
| Overtraining despite recovery signals | Ignoring HRV, readiness, and performance data | Listen to your body. Data exists to inform decisions, not to be ignored |

---

# Beginner Progression System — Machine-to-Barbell Ramp + Volume Guide

**Purpose:** Provide a structured, graduated entry path from zero training experience to full free-weight competency. Prevents the two most common beginner failures: doing too much too soon (injury, overwhelm) and doing too little (no progress, dropout).

---

## Entry Point Determination

Use [[03_ASSESSMENTS/Beginner Technique Assessment.md\|Beginner Technique Assessment]] results:

| Assessment Score | Entry Tier | First Protocol |
|---|---|---|
| 6/6 Pass | Tier 3 — Free Weight Ready | [[04_TOOLS/Quick Start Protocol.md\|Quick Start]] with free-weight H-B or S-B |
| 3-5 Pass (rest Needs Correction) | Tier 2 — Machine Ramp | Machine-based protocol below (Weeks 1-2) |
| 2+ Cannot Perform | Tier 1 — Foundation Phase | Bodyweight-only protocol below |

---

## Tier 1 — Foundation Phase (Absolute Beginner, 2+ Cannot Perform)

**Duration:** 2-4 weeks (reassess weekly)

**Goal:** Build basic movement literacy and gym familiarity. No load, no complexity.

### Weekly Schedule
- 3 sessions/week, full body
- 20-30 min per session
- Every other day (Mon/Wed/Fri or Tue/Thu/Sat)

### Session Template
```
Warm-up (5 min):
  - Joint circles (ankles, knees, hips, shoulders)
  - Cat-cow (5 breaths)
  - Bodyweight squat (10 slow reps)

Workout (15-20 min) — 3 rounds:
  - Squat pattern: Box squat to chair (10 reps)
  - Push pattern: Wall push-up → incline push-up (8-12 reps)
  - Pull pattern: Band pull-apart (15 reps)
  - Core: Dead bug (5 reps per side)

Cool-down (5 min):
  - Child's pose (30 sec)
  - Standing hamstring stretch (30 sec per side)
```

### Progression Criteria
Move to Tier 2 when:
- All 6 movements rated at least "Needs Correction" (no "Cannot Perform")
- Completed 6+ sessions
- Can squat to parallel without support

---

## Tier 2 — Machine Ramp (Absolute Beginner / Needs Correction)

**Duration:** 4 weeks

**Goal:** Build strength and movement pattern confidence using fixed-path machines before introducing free-weight demands.

### Weekly Schedule
- 3 sessions/week, full body
- 30-40 min per session

### Session Template (Weeks 1-2: Full Machine)
```
Exercise                    Sets    Reps    Rest
Leg Press                   3       12-15   60s
Seated Cable Row            3       10-12   60s
Chest Machine               3       10-12   60s
Lat Pulldown                3       10-12   60s
Machine Shoulder Press      3       10-12   60s
Leg Curl                    3       12-15   60s
```

### Session Template (Weeks 3-4: Mixed Machine + Free Weight Intro)
```
Exercise                    Sets    Reps    Rest    Notes
Goblet Squat (DB)           3       10-12   60s     Introduce free-weight squat
Seated Cable Row            3       10-12   60s     Continue machine
DB Bench Press              3       10-12   60s     Introduce free-weight push
Lat Pulldown                3       10-12   60s     Continue machine
DB Overhead Press           3       10-12   60s     Introduce free-weight press
Leg Curl                    3       12-15   60s     Continue machine
```

### Progression Criteria
Move to Tier 3 when:
- All 6 movements rated "Pass" on technique reassessment
- Comfortable with gym environment and equipment
- Consistent 3 sessions/week for 2+ consecutive weeks

---

## Tier 3 — Free Weight Foundation (Novice, Technique Ready)

**Duration:** 8-12 weeks

**Goal:** Establish linear progression on compound lifts with proper form.

### Weekly Schedule
- 3 sessions/week, full body (A/B/A alternating)
- 40-50 min per session

### Session A
```
Exercise                    Sets    Reps    Progression
Goblet Squat → Barbell      3       8-12    +2.5 kg or +1 rep/session
DB Bench Press              3       8-12    +1 rep → +2.5 kg
Seated Cable Row            3       8-12    +1 rep → +2.5 kg
DB Overhead Press           3       8-12    +1 rep → +2.5 kg
Leg Curl                    3       10-15   +1 rep/session
Plank                       3       20-45s  +5s/session
```

### Session B
```
Exercise                    Sets    Reps    Progression
DB RDL → Barbell RDL        3       8-12    +1 rep → +2.5 kg
Lat Pulldown → Pull-up      3       6-10    +1 rep → add weight
DB Shoulder Press           3       8-12    +1 rep → +2.5 kg
Leg Press                   3       10-15   +2.5 kg or +1 rep/session
Face Pull                   3       15-20   +1 rep/session
Dead Bug                    3       5/side  +1 rep/side/session
```

### Linear Progression Rule
- Add 1 rep per session until you reach the top of the rep range
- Then add weight (smallest increment available — 1.25 kg / 2.5 lb plates)
- If you cannot add weight or reps for 3 consecutive sessions → deload (reduce load 10%, build back up)
- If you stall again after deload → you have graduated from linear progression (see below)

---

## Graduation Criteria — Beginner to Intermediate

A user is ready to graduate from Beginner Pathway to the full Intermediate system when:

| Criterion | Measure | How to Verify |
|-----------|---------|---------------|
| 1. Technique competence | All 6 movements scored "Pass" on assessment | [[03_ASSESSMENTS/Beginner Technique Assessment.md\|Technique Assessment]] |
| 2. Linear progression exhausted | Stalled 2+ times on main compounds after deload | Training log (3+ weeks of no progress) |
| 3. Training consistency | ≥80% session adherence for 8+ consecutive weeks | Attendance log |
| 4. Volume tolerance | Can recover from MAV-level volume (8-12 sets/muscle/wk) | No excessive soreness, sleep/HRV stable |
| 5. Body awareness | Can self-correct form, identify RIR within 1-2 reps | Coach observation or self-assessment accuracy |
| 6. Minimum strength landmarks | Can perform: bodyweight squat to parallel, 1 full push-up, 1 assisted pull-up (or 5s dead hang), 30s plank | Performance test |

**Graduation does not mean "leave the beginner system."** It means the user is ready for:
- Daily Undulating Periodization (DUP) instead of linear
- Full MAV volume targets (trained population table)
- Split routines (Upper/Lower or PPL) instead of full body
- Specialization blocks if desired

---

## Beginner Volume Landmarks Reference

| Muscle Group | MEV (sets/wk) | MAV (sets/wk) | MRV (sets/wk) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quads | 4-6 | 8-12 | 14-16 |
| Hamstrings | 3-4 | 6-10 | 12-14 |
| Chest | 4-6 | 8-14 | 16-18 |
| Back (lats) | 5-6 | 8-14 | 16-20 |
| Shoulders | 4-5 | 8-12 | 14-16 |
| Biceps | 3-4 | 6-10 | 12-14 |
| Triceps | 3-4 | 6-10 | 12-14 |
| Glutes | 3-4 | 6-10 | 12-14 |
| Calves | 4-6 | 8-12 | 14-16 |
| Abs/Core | 2-4 | 6-10 | 12-14 |

---

## Common Beginner Progress Patterns

| Week | Experience | Expected | Warning Sign |
|------|------------|----------|--------------|
| 1-2 | Soreness, awkward, unsure | High motivation, low competence | If no soreness at all → check intensity. If quitting → check enjoyment |
| 3-4 | Movement feels less foreign | Rapid strength gains (CNS adaptation) | If still struggling with form → need more machine time |
| 5-8 | Linear progression working | +2.5 kg or +1 rep per session on most lifts | If stalling already → check sleep + protein. Beginner should not stall before week 8 |
| 9-12 | First real plateau | Slower gains, first deload needed | If frustrated → explain accommodation. If still progressing → keep going |

# Cardio Programming Guidelines

## 1. Cardio Zones (5-zone model)

| Zone | Intensity (% HRmax) | Name | Purpose | RPE | Talk Test | Typical Session | Freq/Week | Adaptations |
|------|---------------------|------|---------|-----|-----------|-----------------|-----------|-------------|
| **Zone 1** | <65% | Recovery | Active recovery, blood flow, CNS reset | 2-3/10 | Full conversation | 20-40 min | 1-2 | Improves recovery capacity, increases blood volume |
| **Zone 2** | 65-75% | Aerobic base | Mitochondrial density, capillary network, fat oxidation | 3-4/10 | Nasal breathing only, can speak in full sentences | 30-60 min | 3-4 | ↑ Mitochondrial biogenesis, ↑ capillary density, ↑ fat oxidation enzymes, ↑ stroke volume |
| **Zone 3** | 75-85% | Tempo | Lactate clearance, muscular endurance, economy | 5-6/10 | Short sentences, labored | 20-40 min | 1-2 | ↑ Lactate threshold, ↑ running economy, ↑ buffering capacity |
| **Zone 4** | 85-92% | Threshold | Lactate threshold elevation, pace tolerance | 7-8/10 | 1-2 words only | 8-15 min total (e.g. 3x5 min, 2x8 min) | 1 | ↑ Maximal lactate steady state, ↑ tolerance to discomfort |
| **Zone 5** | 92-100% | VO2max | Maximal cardiac output, VO2max ceiling | 9-10/10 | Unable to speak | 2-5 min total (e.g. 4x3 min, 5x2 min) | 0.5-1 | ↑ VO2max, ↑ maximal cardiac output, ↑ oxidative capacity of Type II fibers |

**Notes:**
- HRmax estimate: 220 - age (or 207 - 0.7 × age for more accuracy per Kenney).
- Use perceived effort over HR when HR data is unreliable (e.g. caffeine, heat, fatigue).

## 2. Minimum Effective Dose

| Goal | Requirement | Reference |
|------|------------|-----------|
| General health | 150 min/week Zone 2 **or** 75 min/week Zone 3+ | WHO / ACSM |
| Cardio fitness improvement | 3 sessions/week, 20-40 min, mix Zone 2 + Zone 4 | Kenney *Physiology of Sport & Exercise* |
| Hypertrophy priority (interference avoidance) | Cap at 3h/week cardio | Fyfe 2014 |

### Key principles:
- Below these thresholds: health benefits still accrue but fitness gains plateau.
- Above 3h/week with hypertrophy focus: risk of attenuated resistance training adaptations (Fyfe 2014 meta-analysis).
- If goal is pure endurance: 6-10+ h/week warranted, with nutrition adjustments.

## 3. Cardio Periodization

### Base Building Phase
- **Duration:** 4-8 weeks
- **Zones:** 80-100% Zone 2, 0-20% Zone 1
- **Volume progression:** Start at 60-90 min/week, build to 3-4 h/week
- **Key focus:** Nasal breathing only, keep HR firmly in Zone 2. Do not creep into Zone 3.
- **Sign-off criteria:** Able to sustain 60 min Zone 2 without HR drift >5%

### Intensity Phase
- **Duration:** 4 weeks
- **Zones:** Introduce Zone 3-4 intervals, maintain ~70% volume in Zone 2
- **Sample week:** 2x Zone 2 (40 min), 1x Zone 4 intervals (e.g. 4x4 min @ 90-95% HRmax, 3 min rest), 1x Zone 3 tempo (25 min)
- **Key focus:** Quality over quantity — keep interval sessions crisp, stop when pace drops

### Peaking Phase
- **Duration:** 2-3 weeks
- **Zones:** Introduce Zone 5, drop total volume 20-30%
- **Sample week:** 1x Zone 2 (30 min), 1x Zone 5 intervals (4x3 min @ 95-100%), 1x Zone 3 (15 min)
- **Key focus:** Freshness + high-end power. Reduce junk miles.

### Maintenance Phase
- **Duration:** Ongoing
- **Volume:** 2 sessions/week, any zone mix
- **Goal:** Preserve ~80% of fitness gains with minimal time investment
- **Can sustain:** Indefinitely during hypertrophy blocks

## 4. Concurrent Training Guidelines

| Principle | Guideline | Source |
|-----------|-----------|--------|
| Separation | Separate cardio and resistance by **6h+ minimum** when possible | Fyfe 2014 |
| Order | If same session: **resistance first**, then cardio | Simultaneous training research |
| Hypertrophy priority | Limit cardio to **3h/week** max | Fyfe 2014 meta-analysis |
| Endurance priority | Limit resistance to **2-3 sessions/week maintenance** | Magness, *Science of Running* |
| Surface choice | Low-impact (bike, incline walk) preferred day before leg days | Practical recommendation |
| Interference mechanism | AMPK activation blunts mTOR pathway if proximal to resistance | Kenney, *Physiology of Sport & Exercise* |

### Practical application:
- **Same day (suboptimal):** Resistance → immediate light cardio (Zone 1-2, 15-20 min) for cooldown. Separate heavy intervals by 6h.
- **Different days:** Cardio on off-days from resistance, or at least AM/PM split.
- **Leg days:** Avoid Zone 4+ cardio within 24h before heavy lower-body resistance.

## 5. Protocol Presets

### Health Maintenance
| Session | Zone | Duration | Weekly Total |
|---------|------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | Zone 2 | 30 min | |
| 2 | Zone 2 | 30 min | |
| 3 | Zone 3 | 20 min | |
| | | **Total** | **80 min/week** |

Minimal dose to meet ACSM guidelines. Suitable for hypertrophy-focused lifters.

### Endurance Builder
| Session | Zone | Duration/Work | Weekly Total |
|---------|------|--------------|-------------|
| 1 | Zone 2 | 45 min | |
| 2 | Zone 4 | 4x4 min intervals (3 min rest) — ~30 min total w/ warmup/cooldown | |
| 3 | Zone 2 | Long slow: 60 min | |
| | | **Total** | ~135 min/week |

Designed to move Zone 2 pace and elevate lactate threshold. Can add a 4th session (tempo) at 6+ h/week.

### Interference-Minimal (Hypertrophy Focus)
| Session | Zone | Timing |
|---------|------|--------|
| 1 | Zone 2 (20 min) | Post-resistance, Zone 1-2 only |
| 2 | Zone 2 (20 min) | Post-resistance, Zone 1-2 only |

Cap here. 40 min/week keeps cardiovascular health markers positive without interfering with hypertrophy (per Fyfe 2014 threshold guidelines).

### Fat Loss Support
| Session | Zone | Duration | Notes |
|---------|------|----------|-------|
| 1 | Zone 2 (LISS) | 35 min | Morning fasted or post-resistance |
| 2 | Zone 2 (LISS) | 40 min | |
| 3 | Zone 2 (LISS) | 30 min | |
| 4 | Zone 5 (HIIT) | 15 min total (e.g. 8x30s all-out, 90s rest) | 1-2x/week max, monitor recovery |

LISS sessions drive total daily energy expenditure. HIIT sessions increase EPOC and improve insulin sensitivity. Do not exceed 1-2 HIIT sessions per week to avoid CNS burnout.

## 6. Assessment

### Talk Test (Zone 2 Confirmation)
- **Nasal only:** If you can breathe exclusively through your nose while moving, you are in Zone 2 (or below).
- **Full sentences:** If you can speak in complete sentences aloud, you are in Zone 2 or below.
- **If you need mouth breathing:** You have exceeded Zone 2.

### 3-Min Step Test (Baseline Estimate)
1. Use a 12-inch (30 cm) step.
2. Step up and down at 96 steps/min (24 cycles/min) for 3 minutes.
3. Sit and measure 60-sec HR immediately after.
4. Compare: <100 bpm = excellent, 100-120 = good, 120-140 = average, >140 = below average.

### 1-Mile Walk Test (VO2max Estimate)
1. Walk 1 mile (1.6 km) as fast as possible (consistent pace).
2. Record time (minutes) and post-walk HR (bpm).
3. Estimated VO2max = 132.853 − (0.0769 × weight in lb) − (0.3877 × age) + (6.3150 × gender: 1=male, 0=female) − (3.2649 × time in min) − (0.1565 × HR)
4. Useful for tracking changes over time without max effort testing.

### 12-Min Cooper Test (VO2max Estimate)
1. Run/walk as far as possible in 12 minutes.
2. Estimated VO2max = (distance in meters − 504.9) / 44.73
3. Requires maximal effort — use only after base-building phase.

### Heart Rate Drift Test (Aerobic Fitness Check)
1. Perform 60 min steady-state Zone 2 effort.
2. Record HR at 10 min and HR at 60 min at same pace.
3. Drift = (HR_60 − HR_10) / HR_10 × 100
4. <5% drift = well-conditioned aerobic system. >10% = detrained or pace too high.

---

**Sources:**
- Magness, Steve. *The Science of Running*
- Kenney, W. Larry, et al. *Physiology of Sport and Exercise*, 7th ed.
- Fyfe, J.J., et al. "Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference." *Sports Medicine*, 2014.

# Deload Protocol — When and How to Reduce Training Load

**Purpose:** Provide a structured decision framework for deloading — when to do it, how to structure it, and what to expect. Deloads are not a sign of weakness or failure. They are a strategic tool for long-term progress.

---

## What a Deload Is (and Isn't)

| Is | Is Not |
|----|--------|
| A planned reduction in training stress | A week of doing nothing |
| A strategy to manage accumulated fatigue | A punishment for poor performance |
| A tool for long-term progress | A sign that your program is broken |
| A reset for the nervous and muscular systems | A waste of time |

---

## When to Deload

### Scheduled Deload (Recommended for Most)

| Training Age | Deload Frequency |
|-------------|------------------|
| Beginner (<1 year) | Every 8-12 weeks |
| Intermediate (1-4 years) | Every 6-8 weeks |
| Advanced (4+ years) | Every 4-6 weeks |
| Masters (40+) | Every 4-6 weeks |
| High volume (20+ sets/week) | Every 4-6 weeks |

### Autoregulated Deload (When to Deload Early)

If 2+ of these are true, deload NOW regardless of schedule:

| Signal | Details |
|--------|---------|
| Performance drop | Key lifts down 5-10% for 2+ consecutive sessions with same effort |
| Chronic fatigue | Waking tired despite adequate sleep (7+ hours). Requiring stimulants to function |
| Mood changes | Irritability, low motivation, apathy toward training |
| Sleep disruption | Difficulty falling or staying asleep despite good sleep hygiene |
| HRV decline | 5+ day downward trend in HRV (requires consistent tracking) |
| Persistent soreness | DOMS that doesn't resolve within 72h of last session |
| Increased illness | Getting sick more often, slow recovery from minor illness |
| Joint pain | New or worsening joint pain that isn't acute injury |

### Seasonal Deload (Life-Based)

| Life Event | Action |
|------------|--------|
| Major stress (work, relationship, move) | Deload during the event. Training is not the priority |
| Illness (fever, infection) | Do not train. Full rest. Return with deload week |
| Vacation | Can be a deload naturally. If active, keep volume low. Enjoy it |
| Sleep debt (3+ nights <6h) | Deload until sleep normalizes. Training under extreme sleep debt increases injury risk |

---

## Deload Methods

### Method 1: Volume Reduction (Recommended for Most)

| Variable | Reduction | Notes |
|----------|-----------|-------|
| Sets per exercise | 40-50% (e.g., 4 sets → 2 sets) | Keep intensity (weight) the same |
| Reps per set | Keep same | Do not reduce reps |
| Exercises per muscle group | Reduce by 1 | Drop the least important accessory |
| Training frequency | Keep same | Do not skip entire sessions |
| RPE | Same or 1 lower | Do not push to failure |

**Example:**
- Normal: Squat 4×5 @ RPE 8 → Deload: Squat 2×5 @ RPE 7
- Normal: Bench 4×8 @ RPE 8 → Deload: Bench 2×8 @ RPE 7
- Normal: 3 exercises per muscle group → Deload: 2 exercises per muscle group

### Method 2: Intensity Reduction (Advanced)

| Variable | Change | Notes |
|----------|--------|-------|
| Weight | 60-70% of normal working weight | Lift explosively. Focus on technique |
| Sets | Keep same | Volume stays up, intensity drops |
| RPE | 4-5 | Weight should feel light |
| Reps per set | Keep same | No change |

**Best for:** Advanced lifters who need a neurological break, or during a technique-focused block.

### Method 3: Full Rest (Rarely Needed)

| Duration | Protocol |
|----------|----------|
| 3-5 days | Complete rest from training. Light walking OK |
| 5-7 days | Only if severe fatigue, illness recovery, or burnout |

**Best for:** Recovery from illness, extreme accumulated fatigue, or post-competition. Do not use as a regular deload — detraining begins at day 5-7.

---

## What to Expect During Deload

| Day | Feeling | Action |
|-----|---------|--------|
| 1-3 | Relief, less sore | Good. This is what you needed |
| 3-5 | Restlessness, wanting to train more | Stay disciplined. The urge to train is a sign you needed the deload |
| 5-7 | Fresh, motivated, eager | Perfect. You are ready for the next block |

**Warning:** If by day 5-7 you still feel flat, unmotivated, and fatigued → you may need a longer deload (add 3-5 days full rest) or medical checkup (ferritin, thyroid, vitamin D).

---

## Post-Deload Return

| Day | Protocol | Weight |
|-----|----------|--------|
| Week 1 (post-deload) | Normal volume. RPE 7-8 max | Same as last working weight OR 2.5-5 kg lighter |
| Week 2 | Normal loading. RPE 8-9 | Back to working weight. If it feels heavy, you were not recovered |
| Week 3 | Push for progress. RPE 9-10 | Attempt to exceed previous PR |

**If post-deload you cannot handle week 1 weights (RPE feels 9+ when it should be 7-8):**
- The deload was insufficient (wrong method or too short)
- Or accumulated fatigue was higher than estimated
- Solution: Take 3 more days full rest, then restart at 10% lower than expected

---

## Deload vs. Rest Week vs. Time Off

| Protocol | Length | When | Activity |
|----------|--------|------|----------|
| Deload | 5-7 days | Every 4-12 weeks | Reduced training volume (40-50%) |
| Rest week | 7 days | Severe fatigue, illness | Complete rest except walking |
| Time off | 1-4 weeks | Post-competition, burnout, injury recovery | Whatever feels good. Low-level activity OK |

---

## Common Deload Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's Wrong | Better |
|---------|---------------|--------|
| Training at normal intensity "just fewer sets" | RPE stays too high. Fatigue is not adequately reduced | Drop RPE to 7 or use 60-70% weight |
| Skipping deload entirely "because you feel fine" | Accumulated fatigue is insidious. By the time you feel it, you are overtrained | Schedule deloads proactively |
| Taking full week off when a reduction would work | >5 days of full rest causes measurable detraining (strength loss, glycogen depletion) | Use volume reduction method instead |
| Changing the program during deload | Deload is not the time to test new exercises or techniques | Keep exercises the same. Just do less |
| Deloading too frequently | Progress requires consistent overload. Deloading every 3 weeks prevents progress | Check training variables before deloading — is volume/RPE actually appropriate? |

---

# Exercise Selection & Rotation Protocol — Choosing the Right Movements

**Purpose:** Provide a framework for selecting, ordering, and rotating exercises to maximize results while minimizing injury risk and stagnation.

---

## Exercise Hierarchy

| Tier | Description | Examples | Frequency | How Many Per Muscle Group |
|------|-------------|----------|-----------|--------------------------|
| **Tier 1 — Main Lifts** | Compound, multi-joint, heavy, primary drivers of strength and mass | Squat, bench press, deadlift, overhead press, pull-up/row variants | Every mesocycle (6-12 weeks) | 1-2 |
| **Tier 2 — Supplemental** | Compound or semi-compound, targets weak points, supports main lifts | Front squat, incline bench, Romanian deadlift, chin-up, dip | Every mesocycle (rotate every 1-2 cycles) | 1-2 |
| **Tier 3 — Accessories** | Isolation, single-joint, targets specific muscles | Bicep curl, tricep extension, lateral raise, leg extension, calf raise | Rotate every 4-8 weeks | 2-4 |
| **Tier 4 — Correctives** | Prehab, mobility, injury prevention | Face pull, band pull-apart, tib raises, shoulder external rotation | Every session (or most sessions) | 1-3 |

---

## Exercise Selection Criteria (Priority Order)

| Criterion | What to Ask |
|-----------|-------------|
| 1. Goal alignment | Does this exercise directly contribute to my primary goal (strength, hypertrophy, muscle group)? |
| 2. Mechanical tension | Does this exercise load the target muscle through a meaningful range of motion? |
| 3. Progressive overload potential | Can I add weight or reps to this exercise reliably over time? |
| 4. Injury risk | Does this exercise place joints in vulnerable positions? Do I have the mobility to perform it safely? |
| 5. Fatigue-to-benefit ratio | Does the systemic fatigue cost justify the stimulus to the target muscle? |
| 6. Equipment availability | Do I consistently have access to the required equipment? |

---

## Rotation Frequency

| Exercise Type | Keep For | Rotate To |
|---------------|----------|-----------|
| Main lifts | 6-12 weeks | A variation of the same movement pattern (e.g., squat → front squat → safety bar squat) |
| Supplemental | 4-8 weeks | A different movement pattern for the same goal (e.g., pull-up → lat pulldown → chest-supported row) |
| Accessories | 4-8 weeks | Same muscle, different angle or implement (e.g., dumbbell curl → cable curl → barbell curl) |
| Correctives | Indefinitely | Ongoing. Swap if not addressing the issue |

**Do not rotate main lifts every mesocycle.** Strength is specific. If you squat for 12 weeks, you get better at squatting and stronger quads. If you swap to leg press every 4 weeks, you never accumulate enough skill and tension to drive meaningful adaptation.

---

## Exercise Order (Within a Session)

| Order | Purpose | Examples |
|-------|---------|----------|
| 1 | CNS activation / explosive movement | Box jump, medicine ball throw, clean pull |
| 2 | Main lift (technical, heavy, CNS-demanding) | Squat, bench, deadlift |
| 3 | Supplemental lift (slightly less CNS demand) | Front squat, incline press, RDL |
| 4 | Accessories (isolation) | Curls, extensions, lateral raises |
| 5 | Core / low CNS demand | Planks, ab wheel, pallof press |
| 6 | Correctives / prehab | Face pulls, band work, mobility |

**Rule:** Most CNS-demanding, most technical, and most important exercises go first. Do not fatigue a muscle before its main lift (e.g., don't do tricep extensions before bench press).

---

## Movement Pattern Coverage

Ensure your program covers all major movement patterns across the training week:

| Pattern | Main Exercise Examples | At Least |
|---------|----------------------|----------|
| **Squat** (knee dominant) | Barbell squat, front squat, leg press, Bulgarian split squat | 1 per week |
| **Hinge** (hip dominant) | Deadlift, RDL, hip thrust, good morning, kettlebell swing | 1 per week |
| **Horizontal push** | Bench press, incline press, push-up, dumbbell press | 1 per week |
| **Horizontal pull** | Row (barbell, dumbbell, cable, chest-supported) | 1 per week |
| **Vertical push** | Overhead press, seated dumbbell press, landmine press | 1 per 1-2 weeks |
| **Vertical pull** | Pull-up, chin-up, lat pulldown | 1 per week |
| **Carry / anti-rotation** | Farmer carry, suitcase carry, pallof press | 1 per week (optional but recommended) |

---

## Exercise Progression (Getting Harder Over Time)

| Level | Squat Pattern Example | Push Pattern Example | Pull Pattern Example |
|-------|----------------------|---------------------|---------------------|
| Beginner | Goblet squat | Push-up (eccentric) | Inverted row |
| Novice | Barbell back squat | Dumbbell bench press | Barbell row |
| Intermediate | Barbell back squat (heavier) | Barbell bench press | Weighted pull-up |
| Advanced | Low bar squat / front squat | Incline or close-grip bench | Chest-supported row |
| Elite | Safety bar squat, paused squat | Competition bench, slingshot | Weighted chin-up + row variation |

---

## Common Selection Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's a Problem | Fix |
|---------|-------------------|-----|
| Too many exercises per muscle group | Volume distributed too thinly. No exercise gets enough stimulus | Max 2-3 exercises per muscle group per session. Focus quality over variety |
| Always doing the same exercises | Specific adaptation leads to stagnation. Also increases overuse injury risk | Rotate tier 2-3 exercises every 4-8 weeks |
| Avoiding uncomfortable exercises | Missing entire movement patterns creates imbalances | Do the exercise you hate most first. That is likely the one you need |
| Picking exercises based on "feel" | Pump and feel does not equal stimulus. Some of the best exercises feel terrible | Use evidence (EMG, mechanical tension analysis) to guide choices, not just feel |
| Too many unstable exercises | Stability work has a place but does not replace loaded compound movements | 80%+ of volume should be stable, bilateral or split stance. Not on Swiss balls |

---

# Fiber Progression Protocol — The Gut-First Approach to Carbohydrates

**Purpose:** Provide a structured, gradual fiber introduction protocol for users transitioning from low-fiber diets (<15 g/day). Preventing digestive distress is the priority — fiber must increase slowly enough for the gut microbiome to adapt.

---

## Why Fiber Matters for Body Composition

| Benefit | Mechanism | Timeline |
|---------|-----------|----------|
| Satiety | Fiber increases gastric distension and slows gastric emptying | Immediate per meal |
| Glycemic control | Soluble fiber forms a viscous gel that reduces glucose absorption rate | Per meal, accumulates over 2-4 weeks |
| Microbiome diversity | Prebiotic fiber (inulin, GOS, FOS) feeds beneficial bacteria | 2-4 weeks for population shift |
| Caloric dilution | Fiber displaces more calorie-dense foods while maintaining volume | Immediate |
| Reduced inflammation | SCFAs (butyrate, propionate) from fiber fermentation reduce systemic inflammation | 4-8 weeks |
| Regularity | Insoluble fiber increases stool bulk and speeds transit | 3-7 days |

---

## Baseline Assessment

| Current Intake | Classification | Risk |
|----------------|---------------|------|
| <10 g/day | Very low | High risk of digestive distress if increased too quickly |
| 10-15 g/day | Low | Moderate risk. Start at Level 1 |
| 15-25 g/day | Moderate | Low risk. May start at Level 2 |
| 25-35 g/day | Adequate | No protocol needed — maintain current intake |
| 35+ g/day | High (uncommon without legumes + whole grains + vegetables) | Ensure adequate water intake (30 ml/kg + 500 ml per 10 g fiber above 30 g) |

**Target:** 25-35 g/day total fiber (mixed soluble + insoluble) from whole food sources.

---

## The Progression Protocol

### Level 1: Foundation (Weeks 1-2)

**Target:** Increase to 15 g/day

| Add These | Serving Size | Fiber per Serving | Total Contribution |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|-------------------|
| Oats OR cooked quinoa | 1 cup cooked | 4 g | +4 g/day |
| Apple with skin OR pear | 1 medium | 4-5 g | +4-5 g/day |
| Broccoli OR spinach with dinner | 1 cup cooked | 4 g | +4 g/day |

**Total added:** 12-13 g/day above baseline

**Rules:**
- Add one new fiber source every 2-3 days, not all on day 1
- Drink an extra 500 ml water per day when increasing fiber
- Do NOT use fiber supplements (psyllium, inulin powder) in Level 1 — whole food only

### Level 2: Expansion (Weeks 3-4)

**Target:** Increase to 20-25 g/day

Keep all Level 1 foods + add:

| Add These | Serving Size | Fiber per Serving |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|
| Legumes (lentils, chickpeas, black beans) | 1/2 cup cooked | 7-8 g |
| Nuts or seeds (almonds, chia, flax) | 30 g (small handful) | 3-4 g |
| Second vegetable serving (different colour) | 1 cup | 3-5 g |
| Berries (raspberries, blackberries) | 1 cup | 6-8 g |

**Pick 2-3** from this list, not all. Spread across the day.

**Rules:**
- Only 1 legume serving per day initially (high FODMAP, can cause gas if not habituated)
- Soak dry legumes overnight or rinse canned legumes thoroughly
- If bloating occurs: reduce legume serving by half, increase cooking time
- Continue extra water

### Level 3: Optimization (Week 5+)

**Target:** 25-35 g/day

Keep Level 1-2 foods + add for variety:

| Category | Options | Serving | Fiber |
|----------|---------|---------|-------|
| Additional legumes | Edamame, peas, kidney beans | 1/2 cup | 5-8 g |
| Whole grains | Barley, bulgar wheat, whole wheat pasta, brown rice | 1 cup cooked | 3-6 g |
| High-fiber fruit | Avocado (1/2), dried figs (2), orange | Per serving | 5-7 g |
| Additional vegetables | Sweet potato with skin, Brussels sprouts, carrots | 1 cup | 4-5 g |
| Seeds | Pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, sesame | 30 g | 3-5 g |

**By this stage, your total should come from a mix of:**
- Vegetables (8-10 g)
- Fruit (4-6 g)
- Legumes/grains (8-12 g)
- Nuts/seeds (3-5 g)

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Solution |
|---------|-------------|----------|
| Bloating, gas | Fiber increase too fast OR new high-FODMAP food | Drop back to previous level for 1 week. Re-introduce new foods one at a time |
| Constipation | Insufficient water OR too much insoluble fiber without soluble | Increase water by 500 ml/day. Add soluble fiber (oats, chia, psyllium) |
| Stomach pain after legumes | Not accustomed to legume fiber + oligosaccharides | Reduce legume to 1/4 cup. Rinse thoroughly. Try lentils instead of beans (lower FODMAP) |
| Feeling too full to eat enough protein | Fiber volume displacing calorie density | Prioritize protein at meals first, then add fiber. May need to eat more frequently |
| Diarrhoea | Fiber increase too rapid OR food intolerance | Drop to Level 1 for 2 weeks. Re-introduce at half speed |

## Water Intake Rule

**For every 10 g of fiber above 15 g/day, drink an additional 500 ml of water.**

- 15 g fiber/day: 2 L water minimum
- 25 g fiber/day: 2.5 L water minimum
- 35 g fiber/day: 3 L water minimum

---

## Fiber Sources Reference

### Soluble Fiber (viscous, gel-forming)
- Oats, oat bran
- Barley
- Psyllium husk
- Apples (with pectin), citrus fruits
- Carrots
- Chia seeds, flax seeds
- Legumes (lentils, chickpeas)

**Primary benefit:** Cholesterol reduction, glycemic control, satiety

### Insoluble Fiber (bulking, non-fermentable)
- Wheat bran, whole wheat
- Vegetables (broccoli, leafy greens, green beans)
- Nuts and seeds
- Potatoes with skin
- Brown rice

**Primary benefit:** Regularity, stool bulk, reduced transit time

### Prebiotic Fiber (fermentable, feeds microbiome)
- Inulin (chicory root, Jerusalem artichoke, onion, garlic, leek)
- GOS (legumes, chickpeas)
- FOS (banana, onion, garlic, asparagus)
- Resistant starch (cooked and cooled potatoes/rice, green banana flour)

**Primary benefit:** Microbiome diversity, SCFA production, immune modulation

---

## Who Needs This Protocol Most

| User Profile | Starting Level | Notes |
|-------------|---------------|-------|
| Standard Western diet (processed food, low veg) | Level 1 | Most common. Expect bloating Week 1 — normal |
| Vegan / plant-based with whole foods | Skip — already adequate | Ensure water intake matches fiber |
| Keto / carnivore returning to carbs | Level 1, double duration | Gut microbiome has shifted. 4 weeks minimum at Level 1 |
| Binge eating history | Level 1, no tracking | Add fiber but don't create rules about it. Gentle Entry approach |
| Cutting (caloric deficit) | Level 2 | Fiber helps satiety in deficit. Prioritize high-volume veg |
| Recomp | Level 2-3 | Fiber supports the energy flux model by allowing higher food volume |

protocols.Gentle Entry Protocol:
# Gentle Entry Protocol — For Users with Eating Disorder Risk or Severe Adherence Constraint

**Purpose:** Provide a safe, structured entry path for users who cannot safely use standard Muscle OS protocols due to eating disorder risk (current or past), severe adherence struggles, or a history of all-or-nothing behavior.

**Core principle: ADD, never subtract.** Do not remove foods. Do not restrict calories. Do not create rules that can be "broken." Every intervention adds something positive — a new food, a new habit, a new awareness.

---

## Who This Is For

| User Profile | Trigger | Entry Path |
|---|---|---|
| Current binge eating (≥1x/week) | Safety Triage B2 Red | [[05_SYSTEMS/Pre-Program Clearance Gate.md\|Clearance Gate]] → Professional clearance → Gentle Entry Level 1 |
| Occasional binge eating (<1x/month) | Safety Triage B2 Yellow | Gentle Entry Level 1 (no clearance needed, but monitor for escalation) |
| Past eating disorder, recovered | Safety Triage B1 Yellow | Gentle Entry Level 1-2 (professional clearance recommended) |
| Severe adherence struggles | Constraint Resolution — Adherence binding | Gentle Entry Level 1 (simplest possible entry) |
| All-or-nothing personality | Self-reported or coach observation | Gentle Entry Level 1 (prevent binge-restrict cycle) |

---

## The Three Levels

### Level 1 — Awareness Only (Minimum 4 weeks)

**Goal:** Build awareness without changing behavior. No tracking, no rules, no deficits.

**Training:**
- 2-3 sessions/week, full body
- No performance tracking. Session completion is the only metric
- Exercise selection: user's choice from pain-free options. "Do what feels good today"
- Duration: 20-40 min. User decides when to stop

**Nutrition:**
- **No tracking of any kind.** No calories, no protein, no macros, no food log
- No food rules. No banned foods. No "good" or "bad" foods
- **One addition per week** from the food hierarchy below
- Protein awareness encouraged but not required

**Metrics (Level 1 only):**
- Sessions completed per week (target: 2-3)
- Subjective energy/mood (1-10, optional)
- Binge frequency (if user is willing to track discreetly)
- **Bodyweight tracking: NOT permitted** for first 2 weeks. Optional after 2 weeks if user confirms it is not triggering

**Food Addition Hierarchy (Level 1):**
```
Week 1: Add 1 serving protein to any meal (any source, any amount)
Week 2: Add 1 serving vegetables (any vegetable, any preparation)
Week 3: Add 1 serving fruit (any fruit, any time)
Week 4: Add 1 glass of water with one meal per day
```

### Level 2 — Gentle Structure (Week 5-8)

**Goal:** Introduce minimal structure while maintaining the "add, never subtract" principle.

**Training:**
- 3 sessions/week, full body
- Track: exercises performed (not weight/reps — just which exercises)
- Gradual progression: "Can you do one more rep than last session?" (optional)
- If user wants to track weight: "Track only the weight, not how you feel about it"

**Nutrition:**
- Still no calorie counting, no deficits, no banned foods
- Add: "Three meals per day. Each meal includes a protein source." (guideline, not rule)
- Continue food additions from Level 1
- Optional: Add 1 structured snack between lunch and dinner
- **If binge episodes occur:** Do NOT restrict more. Add a pre-emptive eating window (eat every 3-4 hours)

**Metrics (add to Level 1):**
- Exercise completion (yes/no per planned session)
- Meal regularity (how many days had 3 meals)
- Continue binge frequency tracking

### Level 3 — Full Protocol Entry (Week 9-12, only if stable)

**Goal:** Transition toward standard Muscle OS protocols with significant modifications.

**Prerequisites:**
- 8+ consecutive weeks with no binge escalation (if binging was present, frequency reduced by ≥50%)
- User reports feeling stable and ready
- Professional clearance if applicable

**Training:**
- 3-4 sessions/week. Full body or Upper/Lower
- Full tracking: exercises, sets, reps, weight
- Standard linear progression (2.5 kg or 1 rep per session)
- **RIR: 4 (very conservative).** No training to failure

**Nutrition:**
- Protein target: 1.6 g/kg (guideline, not rule. "Aim for this, don't stress if you miss")
- Still NO calorie deficit. Eat at or above maintenance
- NO banned foods
- NO tracking required. User may optionally track protein if non-triggering
- **If any tracking triggers restriction thoughts → Stop tracking immediately, return to Level 2**

**Metrics:**
- Standard beginner KPIs: sessions completed, top set performance, protein intake awareness
- Monthly check-in: "How is your relationship with food/training?"

---

## Trigger Analysis Framework

Use discreetly and only with user consent. The purpose is to identify patterns, not to increase obsession with food.

| Trigger Category | Examples | Intervention |
|---|---|---|
| Stress | Work deadline, argument, financial pressure | Add breathing (2 min before eating). Add structured break between stress trigger and eating opportunity |
| Restriction | Skipped a meal, ate "too much" yesterday, diet started Monday | Add pre-emptive eating (scheduled meal/snack before hunger peaks). Add permission (no food is off-limits) |
| Boredom | Evening alone, no plans, scrolling phone | Add alternative activity list (walk, shower, tea, call someone). Add 10-min rule: "If I still want it in 10 minutes, I can have it" |
| Social | Party, dinner out, pressure to eat/not eat | Add anchoring: "I can eat what I want. I can also stop when I'm full." Add go-to phrase: "This looks great, I'll have some" |
| Emotional | Loneliness, sadness, shame, anxiety | Add referral to therapist. Add non-food comfort list. Add body check: "Am I hungry or am I feeling something?" |

---

## The 10-Minute Rule

When the urge to binge arises:

1. **Notice:** "I am having the urge to binge." (No judgment. No shame. Just noticing.)
2. **Wait:** Set a timer for 10 minutes. Do not eat during this time.
3. **Do something else:** Walk, text someone, shower, breathe (4-7-8 pattern), hold ice cube, brush teeth
4. **After 10 minutes:**
   - Urge passed? → Great. Continue.
   - Urge still present? → Eat what you want. No guilt. The 10 minutes built awareness, even if you ate.
5. **Record (optional):** "Before: ___ (trigger). After 10 min: ___ (result)."

---

## Professional Integration

### When to Refer

- Binge frequency does not reduce after 8 weeks of Gentle Entry Level 1
- Purging behavior emerges
- Bodyweight changes >5% in 4 weeks (especially loss, suggesting restriction)
- User expresses shame about eating >50% of the time
- User cannot maintain the 10-minute rule without extreme distress
- Any purging, restriction <1,200/1,500 kcal, or extreme exercise compensation

### How to Integrate Professional Advice

1. Export user's trigger log (if tracking) as structured data
2. Therapist/dietitian provides recommendations: "Gentle Entry is appropriate" or "Modify X"
3. Integrate recommendations as protocol overrides
4. Re-check monthly during Professional Input Mode

---

## Contraindications

**Do NOT use this protocol if:**
- User has current purging behavior (→ crisis referral first)
- User has severe underweight (BMI <16) or rapid weight loss
- User has active suicidal ideation
- User refuses professional referral despite Red flags on Safety Triage

**In all above cases:** Return to [[05_SYSTEMS/Pre-Program Clearance Gate.md\|Pre-Program Clearance Gate]]. Do not bypass.

---

protocols.Habit Building & Environment Design Prot:
# Habit Building & Environment Design Protocol — Making Consistency Automatic

**Purpose:** Provide evidence-based protocols for building lasting habits around nutrition, training, sleep, and recovery. Knowledge is useless without execution. This protocol bridges the gap.

---

## The Habit Loop

```
Cue → Craving → Response → Reward
```

Every habit follows this loop. To build a new habit, engineer each element. To break a bad habit, disrupt the loop at any point.

---

## Building New Habits: The Framework

### Step 1: Minimum Viable Habit (MVH)

Start so small that failure is impossible:

| Goal | MVH |
|------|-----|
| Eat more protein | Eat 1 serving of protein at 1 meal per day |
| Train consistently | Do 1 set of 1 exercise per session |
| Sleep better | Go to bed 5 min earlier |
| Drink more water | Drink 1 glass of water with 1 meal |
| Track food | Track 1 meal per day |

**Rule:** Do your MVH every single day for 2 weeks. If you miss a day, the habit is too big. Shrink it.

### Step 2: Implementation Intention

Format: **"I will [BEHAVIOR] at [TIME] in [LOCATION]."**

| Habit | Implementation Intention |
|-------|------------------------|
| Pre-training meal | "I will eat 30 g protein + 50 g carbs at 7 AM in the kitchen." |
| Evening routine | "I will start my wind-down at 9 PM in the bedroom with lights dimmed." |
| Training | "I will train at 6 AM in the gym, Monday/Wednesday/Friday." |
| Water intake | "I will drink 500 ml water at 8 AM at my desk." |

### Step 3: Habit Stacking

Attach the new habit to an existing one: **"After [EXISTING HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT]."**

| Existing Habit | Stack |
|----------------|-------|
| After I brush my teeth in the morning | I will drink 500 ml water |
| After I pour my morning coffee | I will prep my lunch protein |
| After I finish my last work email | I will change into training clothes |
| After I sit down for dinner | I will chew slowly and put my fork down between bites |

### Step 4: Environment Design

Make good habits easy and bad habits hard.

| Goal | Make It Easy | Make the Opposite Hard |
|------|-------------|----------------------|
| Train in the morning | Sleep in training clothes. Pack gym bag the night before | Put phone across the room (no snooze) |
| Eat protein with every meal | Pre-portion chicken/eggs in the fridge | Remove easy carb-only snacks from the kitchen |
| Drink more water | Keep a 1 L bottle on your desk at all times | Do not keep soda or juice in the house |
| Stop phone scrolling before bed | Charge phone in another room | Do not bring phone into the bedroom |
| Track food intake | Keep measuring cups on the counter. Use a tracking app with the fewest taps | Do not eat from the bag. Plate everything |

---

## Breaking Bad Habits

### Method 1: Disrupt the Cue

| Bad Habit | Cue | Disruption |
|-----------|-----|------------|
| Mindless snacking | Seeing the snack cabinet | Move snacks to a high shelf or opaque container. Better: do not buy them |
| Scrolling phone in bed | Phone on nightstand | Charge phone in the kitchen |
| Skipping meals | No prepped food available | Meal prep on Sunday. See [[04_PROTOCOLS/Meal Structure Library.md\|Meal Structure Library]] |
| Late-night eating | Being awake + bored | Go to bed earlier. Remove evening food triggers |

### Method 2: Increase Friction

| Bad Habit | Add Friction |
|-----------|-------------|
| Eating junk food | Make it require a 20-minute round trip to buy. Keep none at home |
| Scrolling social media | Log out after each use. Delete the app. Use website blockers after 9 PM |
| Skipping training | Set a financial penalty (e.g., $5 to a friend for every missed session) |

### Method 3: Replace, Don't Remove

| Bad Habit | Replacement |
|-----------|-------------|
| Evening beer | Sparkling water + lime or herbal tea |
| Phone scrolling in bed | Reading a physical book |
| Afternoon sugar crash snack | Greek yogurt + berries or a protein shake |
| Stress eating | 5 min box breathing or a short walk |

---

## Tracking Habits (Minimal)

| Tool | How | Why |
|------|-----|-----|
| Paper calendar | X mark for each day the habit is done | Visual streak. Satisfying. Cannot be ignored |
| Habit app | Simple check-in (e.g., Habitica, Streaks) | Digital convenience. Streak counting |
| Training log | Check if you trained and hit minimum volume | Combined with overall progress |

**Do NOT track more than 3 habits at once.** Adding 7 habits simultaneously is a recipe for failure. Add habits one at a time, 2-3 weeks apart.

---

## When You Miss a Day

| Rule | Why |
|------|-----|
| **Never miss twice in a row** | A single miss does not break a habit. Two misses in a row starts the decline |
| **Reduce scope, not frequency** | If you miss a training day → do 1 set of 1 exercise at home. Do not skip entirely |
| **Do not "make up" missed days** | Compensatory behavior burns out quickly. Just get back on schedule |
| **Forgive the miss. Analyze why it happened** | Was the habit too big? Was the cue missing? Was the environment stacked against you? |

---

## Accountability Structures

| Structure | How It Works | Best For |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| Training partner | Mutual commitment to show up | Consistency, especially early morning |
| Coach | Paid accountability + programming | Those who need both guidance and consequence |
| Public commitment | Post training logs publicly (social media, forum) | External validation + social pressure |
| Financial stake | Commit money to a cause you hate if you miss | High motivation. Use for high-priority habits |
| Automated check-in | App or calendar reminder + response required | Minimum viable accountability |

---

# Hydration Protocol — Water, Electrolytes, and Performance

**Purpose:** Provide clear, actionable hydration targets for daily life and training sessions. Hydration is the single most underrated performance variable — even 2% bodyweight fluid loss impairs performance, cognitive function, and recovery.

---

## Daily Hydration Targets

| Context | Minimum | Optimal | Maximum Useful |
|---------|---------|---------|----------------|
| Sedentary (<3,000 steps/day) | 1.5 L | 2 L | 3 L |
| Active (5,000-10,000 steps + training) | 2 L | 2.5-3 L | 4 L |
| Very active (10,000+ steps + training in heat) | 2.5 L | 3-4 L | 5 L |
| Per 10 g fiber above 15 g/day | +500 ml | +500 ml | — |
| Per 500 mg sodium above baseline | +500 ml | +500 ml | — |

**Rule of thumb:** Drink 30 ml per kg bodyweight as baseline. Add 500-1,000 ml per hour of training.

- 60 kg person: 1.8 L baseline + training = 2.3-2.8 L
- 80 kg person: 2.4 L baseline + training = 2.9-3.4 L
- 100 kg person: 3 L baseline + training = 3.5-4 L

**Source of fluid:** Water is best. Tea, coffee, and sparkling water count toward total (do NOT subtract caffeine's mild diuretic effect — it is negligible at habitual intake).

---

## Training Hydration

### Pre-Training (2-3 hours before)
- Drink 500-750 ml water
- Add pinch of salt (sodium) if training in heat or >60 min

### During Training

| Session Duration | Protocol |
|-----------------|----------|
| <45 min | Water as needed (thirst-guided) |
| 45-90 min | 500-750 ml water. If heavy sweater: add electrolyte tab or 1/4 tsp salt + squeeze lemon |
| 90+ min | 500-1,000 ml water + electrolytes (Na 500-700 mg, K 200-300 mg per hour). Sip every 10-15 min |

### Post-Training
- Rehydrate with 500-750 ml water per kg of bodyweight lost during session
- Weigh yourself before and after training for 1-2 weeks to learn your sweat rate
- If you lost 1 kg during training → drink 1 L post-training over the next 1-2 hours

---

## Hydration Status Check

| Signal | Status | Action |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Urine pale yellow (straw colour) | Well hydrated | Continue current intake |
| Urine dark yellow | Mildly dehydrated | Drink 500 ml water now, increase daily baseline |
| Urine amber or brown | Dehydrated | Drink 1 L water now. Investigate cause (illness, heat, caffeine overuse) |
| Thirst | Already 1-2% dehydrated | Drink water immediately. Thirst is a lagging indicator |
| Dry mouth, headache, fatigue | Dehydrated | Rehydrate over 2-3 hours. Do not chug — sip |
| Frequent urination (every 30-60 min) with clear urine | Overhydrated | Reduce intake slightly. May be flushing electrolytes |
| Muscle cramps during training | Possible electrolyte deficit | Increase sodium + magnesium intake. Add electrolytes to training water |

**Note:** Dark urine in the morning is normal (overnight concentration). If it clears within 1-2 glasses of water, you are fine.

---

## Electrolyte Additions

| Context | Sodium | Potassium | Magnesium |
|---------|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Standard day, normal diet | Diet covers needs | Diet covers needs | Diet covers needs |
| Training >60 min in heat | Add 1/4-1/2 tsp salt to pre-training meal | Banana or coconut water post-training | Get from diet (nuts, seeds, leafy greens) |
| Heavy sweater (salt stains on clothes) | Add 500-1,000 mg Na via salt or electrolyte tabs | Monitor | Monitor |
| Keto / low-carb (first 2-4 weeks) | Add 2-3 g extra Na (keto increases sodium excretion) | Add 1 g extra K | Add 100-200 mg extra Mg |
| Diuretic use (caffeine >400 mg/day, alcohol) | Add 1/4-1/2 tsp salt to meals | Eat potassium-rich foods | Magnesium glycinate pre-bed |

**See also:** [[03_SECTIONS/Pillar 1/Electrolyte & Hydration Pathway.md\|Electrolyte & Hydration Pathway]] for full mechanism detail.

---

## Special Populations

| Population | Adjustment | Why |
|------------|------------|-----|
| Shift workers | Drink 250 ml water every 2 hours during shift. Avoid large volumes before sleep window | Circadian disruption affects thirst signalling. Need structured schedule |
| Masters athletes (50+) | Increase baseline by 500 ml. Thirst sensitivity decreases with age | Older adults are at higher risk of dehydration without feeling thirsty |
| High-fiber diet | +500 ml per 10 g fiber above 15 g/day | Fiber absorbs water in the gut. Without adequate water, fiber causes constipation |
| High caffeine intake | Do NOT subtract caffeine from total. Add 250 ml per 200 mg caffeine | Caffeine's mild diuretic effect is offset by habitual adaptation, but adding water is safer |
| Hot climate / outdoor training | Add 500-1,000 ml to daily target. Increase electrolytes | Sweat losses are significantly higher in heat |

---

## Daily Hydration Schedule (Example)

| Time | Amount | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| Wake (6-7 AM) | 500 ml | Kick-start hydration after overnight fast |
| Morning (9-11 AM) | 250-500 ml | Sip throughout morning |
| Pre-lunch (12 PM) | 250 ml | |
| Afternoon (2-4 PM) | 250-500 ml | Can include tea or sparkling water |
| Pre-training (if training PM) | 500 ml | 2-3 hours before session |
| During training | 500-750 ml | Sip every 10-15 min |
| Post-training | 500-750 ml | Replace sweat losses |
| Evening (7-9 PM) | 250 ml | Stop 1-2 hours before bed to avoid nocturnal urination |

---

# Individualization Decision Protocol — Tailoring the System to You

**Purpose:** Help users identify their individual response patterns, preferences, and constraints, and adjust the system accordingly. Generic advice works for most people, but the best results come from personalization.

---

## Responder Analysis

### Volume Sensitivity

| Type | Description | Optimal Sets/Muscle Group/Week | Signs |
|------|-------------|-------------------------------|-------|
| **High responder** (low volume needs) | Makes good progress on low volume | 6-10 | Progress on 6-8 sets/week, stalls when volume increases, gets sore easily |
| **Average responder** | Moderate volume needs | 10-16 | Steady progress in the moderate range |
| **High volume need** | Needs more volume to grow | 16-24+ | Progress only when volume is high, rarely sore, recovers quickly between sessions |

**How to assess:** Start at 10 sets/muscle group/week. If you progress for 4 weeks → stay there. If you stall → add 2 sets. If you regress or get excessively sore → reduce by 2 sets.

### Intensity Sensitivity

| Type | Optimal RPE Range | Signs |
|------|-------------------|-------|
| **Low intensity tolerance** | RPE 6-8 (2-4 RIR) | Poor performance when training close to failure. Long recovery from hard sessions. CNS fatigue accumulates quickly |
| **Moderate tolerance** | RPE 7-9 (1-3 RIR) | Balanced. Can handle occasional RPE 10 sessions |
| **High intensity tolerance** | RPE 8-10 (0-2 RIR) | Thrives on hard training. Recovers quickly from failure. May struggle with low-intensity work |

**How to assess:** Train at RPE 8-9 for 2 weeks. If you feel destroyed → you prefer lower intensity. If you feel unchallenged → you tolerate high intensity well.

### Frequency Preference

| Frequency | Best For | Example Schedule |
|-----------|----------|------------------|
| **Low** (1×/muscle group/week) | Beginners (first 3-6 months), high-volume sessions, poor recovery | Push/Pull/Legs |
| **Moderate** (2×/muscle group/week) | Most intermediates, balanced recovery | Upper/Lower, PPL |
| **High** (3×/muscle group/week) | Advanced, enhanced recovery, small muscle groups | Full body, specialized programs |

---

## Limb Length & Anthropometric Adjustments

| Proportion | Movement Characteristics | Programming Adjustment |
|------------|------------------------|----------------------|
| **Long femurs** | Squat: more forward lean, hips rise first. Deadlift: advantage | Low bar squat. Spoto press. Deficit deadlift (variation, not main) |
| **Short femurs** | Squat: upright torso, more quad-dominant. Deadlift: disadvantage | High bar squat. Block pulls or rack pulls |
| **Long arms** | Bench: disadvantage (longer ROM). Deadlift: advantage | Close-grip bench. Floor press as accessory. Sumo or conventional both work |
| **Short arms** | Bench: advantage. Deadlift: disadvantage | Wide-grip bench. Conventional deadlift may feel better |
| **Long torso** | Squat: upright easier. Deadlift: long ROM | High bar squat. Sumo deadlift may fit better |

**Note:** These are tendencies, not rules. Technique adjustments often overcome anthropometric limitations. Do not use this as an excuse to avoid a lift.

---

## Lifestyle & Constraint Assessment

### Time Constraints

| Time Available | Optimal Setup |
|---------------|---------------|
| <30 min, 3×/week | Full body. 2-3 compound lifts. RPE 7-9. Minimal rest 60-90 sec |
| 45-60 min, 3-4×/week | Upper/Lower. Compounds + 1-2 accessories. Standard rest |
| 60-90 min, 4-5×/week | PPL or Bro split. Full accessories. Longer rest on compounds |
| 90+ min, 5-6×/week | Any split. High volume. Can include dedicated weak point training |

### Equipment Constraints

| Available Equipment | Program Options |
|--------------------|----------------|
| Full gym (barbell, rack, plates, dumbbells, cables) | Any program. No constraints |
| Home gym (barbell + rack) | Compounds + bodybuilding accessories. Swap cable work for dumbbell/barbell variations |
| Dumbbells only | DB-focused programs. Lunges, DB press, rows, goblet squats |
| Bodyweight only | Calisthenics progressions. High volume. Tempo work. Skill focus |
| Hotel / travel | Bodyweight circuits + bands. Minimal equipment protocols |

### Schedule Constraints

| Constraint | Strategy |
|------------|----------|
| Unpredictable work hours | Autoregulated training. RPE-based. Flexible weekly schedule (get 3 sessions in when possible) |
| Early morning training (before work) | Train fasted or light pre-session meal. Longer warm-up. Start at RPE 7, ramp to RPE 8-9 |
| Late evening training | Dinner-first schedule. Caffeine cut-off before session. Wind-down after training |
| Long breaks (vacation, business trip) | Maintenance protocol: 2×/week full body. 3-5 sets per muscle group. Prevent detraining |

---

## Psychological Profile

| Profile | Tendency | What to Watch |
|---------|----------|---------------|
| **Eager beaver** | Wants to train hard every session, add volume, go to failure | Overtraining. Injury. Ignoring recovery. Needs a program with strict caps |
| **Hesitant / fearful** | Holds back, avoids heavy weights, stays comfortable | Under-stimulation. Slow progress. Needs clear progression rules and a coach |
| **Program hopper** | Changes programs every 2-4 weeks out of boredom or perceived lack of progress | Never accumulates enough stimulus. Needs to commit to 12-week blocks |
| **Perfectionist** | Waits for perfect conditions, misses sessions if not "optimal" | Inconsistency. Needs to lower standards: "good enough" is better than nothing |
| **Data obsessed** | Tracks everything, makes decisions based on daily fluctuations | Paralysis by analysis. Needs to look at 4-week trends only |

---

## When to Individualize vs. When to Follow the Standard

| Factor | Follow Standard Protocol | Individualize |
|--------|------------------------|--------------|
| Training age | <6 months | 1+ years |
| Current progress | Progressing well | Stalled for 4+ weeks |
| Recovery | Full recovery between sessions | Persistent fatigue |
| Health | No limitations | Injury, condition, medication |
| Response | Average response | Clear low or high responder pattern |
| Goal | General | Very specific (competition, sport) |

**Default assumption:** Follow the standard protocol. Individualize only when you have data showing the standard does not work for you.

---

# Injury Management Protocol — Central Hub

First-stop reference for any injury. Use [[04_TOOLS/Decision Trees/Injury Diagnosis Tree.md|Injury Diagnosis Tree]] to route from symptoms to the correct protocol below.

---

## Acute Care: PEACE & LOVE (First 72 Hours)

Modern replacement for RICE. Apply to ANY acute injury before starting rehab.

| Letter | Meaning | Action |
|--------|---------|--------|
| **P** | Protection | Unload or restrict movement for 1-3 days. Pain is your guide — let it settle. |
| **E** | Elevation | Elevate the limb above heart level when possible to manage swelling. |
| **A** | Avoid anti-inflammatories | NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) may impair long-term tissue healing. Use paracetamol if needed for pain. **Source: E3 Rehab, current tendinopathy guidelines** |
| **C** | Compression | Wrap with elastic bandage to limit swelling and internal bleeding. |
| **E** | Education | Understand that pain ≠ damage. Recover actively, not passively. |
| **L** | Load | Gradually reintroduce mechanical load as pain allows. Movement heals. |
| **O** | Optimism | Expectation of recovery improves outcomes. Pain reprocessing matters. |
| **V** | Vascularisation | Pain-free movement increases blood flow to healing tissues. |
| **E** | Exercise | The primary rehab tool. Exercise restores capacity. |

**When to move past PEACE & LOVE:** When swelling has stabilized, pain is tolerable during daily activities (≤3/10), and you can begin progressive loading.

---

## Pain-Monitoring Framework

Use the **Traffic Light System** for ALL rehab exercises:

| Zone | Pain Level | Action |
|------|-----------|--------|
| Green | VAS 0-3/10, settles within 1 hour | Safe. Proceed with current load. |
| Yellow | VAS 3-5/10, resolves within 24 hours | Hold current load. Do NOT progress. |
| Red | VAS >5/10, or worsens next day | Regress — reduce load, volume, or range of motion. |

**Source:** E3 Rehab (next-day symptom response rule), validated across tendinopathy and muscle strain protocols

---

## RED FLAGS — Do NOT Self-Treat

These require **medical evaluation** (PT, sports medicine, or orthopedist):

| Red Flag | Urgency |
|----------|---------|
| Traumatic pop/tear sensation followed by inability to bear weight / use limb | Immediate |
| Joint swelling with redness, heat, and fever | Same day |
| Numbness, tingling, or weakness in a dermatomal pattern (nerve) | Within 1 week |
| Night pain that wakes you (not positional) | Within 1 week |
| Loss of bladder/bowel control + lower extremity weakness | Emergency (cauda equina) |
| Morning stiffness >45 minutes with improvement through the day | Suggests inflammatory arthritis → rheumatology |
| Unintentional weight loss + persistent pain | Rule out systemic disease |
| No improvement after 4-6 weeks of consistent rehab | Reassess diagnosis with professional |

---

## Understanding How Injuries Develop: Cumulative Injury Cycle

Injuries rarely happen from a single event. Most follow a predictable cycle described by NASM's Cumulative Injury Model:

```
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │         TISSUE TRAUMA           │
               │  (microtears, strain, overload) │
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │          INFLAMMATION           │
               │  (swelling, pain, heat, redness) │
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │         MUSCLE SPASM            │
               │  (protective guarding, tightness)│
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │           ADHESIONS             │
               │  (fascial restrictions, knots)   │
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │    ALTERED NEUROMUSCULAR         │
               │         CONTROL                 │
               │  (compensation patterns)         │
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
               │       MUSCLE IMBALANCES         │
               │  (overactive/underactive pairs)  │
               └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                              │
                              │  (cycle repeats)
                              │
                              ▼
                         TISSUE TRAUMA (worse)
```

**How to break the cycle:**
1. **Early stage** (trauma → inflammation): PEACE & LOVE protocol. Anti-inflammatory nutrition. Relative rest
2. **Middle stage** (spasm → adhesion): SMR (foam rolling), static stretching, soft tissue work
3. **Late stage** (altered control → imbalances): Corrective exercise (ILAI model — see [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]]), neuromuscular re-education

**Key insight:** Most chronic injuries are not caused by the acute incident — they are caused by the MUSCLE IMBALANCES that develop from poor posture and repetitive movement patterns. This is why rehab + posture correction must go together.

**Source:** NASM 7th Edition Ch.14, Cumulative Injury Cycle

### Pattern Overload

Pattern overload is excessive repetition of the same movement pattern, leading to tissue adaptation in one plane only and eventual injury. Common examples:

- **Only pressing, no pulling** → anterior shoulder tightness → impingement
- **Only quad-dominant work** → hamstring weakness → patellofemoral pain
- **Always the same squat depth/hand position** → repetitive joint stress in the same ROM

**How to prevent:** Regularly rotate exercise variations. Use the [[04_TOOLS/Default Exercise Pool.md|Default Exercise Pool]] to consciously choose different squat stances, press angles, and pull variations across mesocycles.

---

## Rehab Protocol Index

| Injury | Protocol | Key Principle |
|--------|----------|---------------|
| Shoulder impingement | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Shoulder Impingement.md\|Shoulder Impingement]] | Scapular control → rotator cuff loading |
| Patellofemoral pain | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Patellofemoral Pain.md\|Patellofemoral Pain]] | Hip + quad strengthening, load management |
| Hamstring strain | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Hamstring Strain.md\|Hamstring Strain]] | Progressive lengthened eccentrics |
| Low back pain (mechanical) | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Low Back Pain.md\|Low Back Pain]] | Movement variety, graded exposure |
| Achilles tendinopathy | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Achilles Tendinopathy.md\|Achilles Tendinopathy]] | Heavy slow resistance, isometric first |
| Elbow tendinopathy | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Elbow Tendinopathy.md\|Elbow Tendinopathy]] | Isometric → eccentric gripping |
| IT band syndrome | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/IT Band Syndrome.md\|IT Band Syndrome]] | Hip abductor loading, avoid compression |
| Plantar fasciitis | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Plantar Fasciitis.md\|Plantar Fasciitis]] | Calf stretch + foot intrinsic strengthening |
| Groin strain | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Groin Strain.md\|Groin Strain]] | Isometric adduction → progressive loading |
| Shin splints | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Shin Splints.md\|Shin Splints]] | Calf strengthening, tibialis posterior loading |
| Wrist overuse | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Wrist Overuse.md\|Wrist Overuse]] | Grip strengthening, relative rest |
| Calf strain | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Calf Strain.md\|Calf Strain]] | Isometric → heavy slow resistance |
| Hip flexor strain | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/Hip Flexor Strain.md\|Hip Flexor Strain]] | Hip flexor isometrics → eccentric loading |
| SI joint dysfunction | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Rehab/SI Joint Dysfunction.md\|SI Joint Dysfunction]] | Core + glute stabilization, mobility |

---

## Rehab Progression Principles

1. **Isometric first** — Pain-free isometrics maintain strength + reduce pain without irritating the joint
2. **Progress to isotonic** — Controlled concentric/eccentric through tolerable range
3. **Add energy storage** — Faster movements, plyometrics for tendon/muscle conditioning
4. **Return to sport** — Sport-specific drills, graded exposure
5. **Prehab** — Once recovered, continue maintenance exercises 2×/week

**Never progress if:** Pain exceeds VAS 5/10 during exercise, or next-day symptoms are worse than baseline.

---

*Links to: [[04_TOOLS/Decision Trees/Injury Diagnosis Tree.md\|Injury Diagnosis Tree]], [[05_SYSTEMS/Intervention Priority Engine.md\|Intervention Priority Engine]], [[04_TOOLS/Default Exercise Pool.md\|Default Exercise Pool]]*
