# Intermittent Fasting Decision Protocol — When It Works, When It Doesn't

**Purpose:** Provide a structured decision framework for users considering intermittent fasting. IF is neither good nor bad — it is a tool that works brilliantly for some users and poorly for others. This protocol helps determine which camp you are in.

---

## Who IF Is Appropriate For

### Likely to Work
- Busy professionals who skip breakfast anyway and feel fine
- Users who eat most calories in a 4-8 hour window naturally
- Users who struggle with evening snacking (time restriction reduces eating window)
- Users looking for maintenance or slow fat loss
- Users with good sleep, low stress, stable energy

### Likely to FAIL (Do Not Recommend)
| Profile | Reason | Alternative |
|---------|--------|-------------|
| Female with irregular cycles or history of amenorrhea | Caloric windowing can disrupt menstrual cycle. Women are more sensitive to energy restriction signals | 3 meals + snack. Do not restrict timing |
| History of eating disorder (B1/B2/B3/B6 flagged) | Any form of time restriction can trigger restriction-binge cycling | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Gentle Entry Protocol.md\|Gentle Entry Protocol]]. No eating windows |
| High stress + poor sleep (cortisol elevated) | IF increases cortisol. Adding to already elevated baseline is counterproductive | Short feeding window (10-12h), not 6-8h |
| Bulking / muscle gain | IF reduces the anabolic window. Harder to eat enough in restricted window | 3-4 meals spread across 12-14h |
| High training volume (4+ sessions/week) | Energy availability during training is lower. Performance can suffer | Periodize: eat around training. Don't IF on training days |
| Beginner (<1 year training) | Building habits matters more than optimizing timing. IF adds unnecessary complexity | [[04_TOOLS/Quick Start Protocol.md\|Quick Start]]. Just eat consistently |

---

## The IF Decision Tree

```
Q1: Do you have a current or past eating disorder?
  → Yes → DO NOT USE IF. Use Gentle Entry Protocol instead.
  → No → Q2

Q2: Are you female with irregular cycles, trying to conceive, or under 25?
  → Yes → STRONG CAUTION. Women are more sensitive to IF's effects
           on the HPA axis and menstrual cycle. Start with 12h fast max.
           If any cycle disruption → stop immediately.
  → No → Q3

Q3: Are you currently bulking or have high training volume (4+ sessions/wk)?
  → Yes → TRF only (10-12h eating window, not 6-8h).
           Ensure protein is distributed across the feeding window.
           Do NOT train fasted for key sessions.
  → No → Q4

Q4: Is your stress >6/10 or sleep <6.5h average?
  → Yes → STRONG CAUTION. IF adds physiological stress.
           Only try if you can keep eating window 10+ hours.
           If stress increases → stop.
  → No → Q5

Q5: Do you naturally skip breakfast and feel fine?
  → Yes → TRF (8-10h eating window) may work well for you.
           Run the 2-week trial below.
  → No → Standard 3-meal structure is likely better.
           Consider TRF only if you want to try it.

Decision Summary:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Most users → TRF (10-12h eating window)    │
  │  Stress >6 or female → 12h window minimum   │
  │  Eating disorder history → DO NOT USE        │
  │  Bulking/high volume → TRF 10-12h            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## IF Protocols

### Time-Restricted Feeding (TRF) — Most Common

| Protocol | Eating Window | Fasting Window | Best For |
|----------|--------------|----------------|----------|
| **16:8 (Standard)** | 8h (e.g. 12 PM - 8 PM) | 16h | Maintenance, slow fat loss, experienced fasters |
| **14:10 (Gentle)** | 10h (e.g. 10 AM - 8 PM) | 14h | Most users, women, beginners, high stress |
| **12:12 (Minimal)** | 12h (e.g. 8 AM - 8 PM) | 12h | Anyone. Essentially normal eating without late-night snacks |

**Recommendation for most users:** Start with 12:12. Only tighten to 14:10 or 16:8 if it feels natural. Do not force longer fasts.

### Meal Structure Within Eating Window

| Meal | Time (16:8 example) | Composition |
|------|--------------------|-------------|
| First meal (break fast) | 12 PM | Protein + veg + moderate carb. Do NOT skip protein. Even if "not hungry yet," eat 20-30 g protein |
| Second meal | 3-4 PM | Protein + carb + veg |
| Third meal (pre-fast) | 7-8 PM | Protein + carb + veg + fat. Largest meal. Slow-digesting protein (casein or cottage cheese) recommended to maintain anabolic signalling through the fast |

**Critical:** Protein must be adequate despite restricted window. If you cannot hit 1.6 g/kg in 8 hours → you need a longer eating window.

### Pre-Breakfast Training (Fasted Training)

| Condition | Recommendation |
|-----------|---------------|
| Training before first meal | OK for low-to-moderate intensity. Take BCAAs or EAA (5-10 g) before session to attenuate muscle breakdown |
| Strength training fasted | Not ideal. Performance will be suppressed. If you must, take caffeine + EAAs 15 min before |
| Cardio fasted | Well-tolerated. No special protocol needed |
| High-volume hypertrophy fasted | Not recommended. Insufficient energy for high-quality sets |

---

## 2-Week IF Trial Protocol

If you decide to try IF, run this trial before deciding whether to continue:

| Day | Protocol | Check-in |
|-----|----------|----------|
| 1-3 | 12:12 (12h eating window) | How is your energy? Hunger? Training performance? |
| 4-7 | 14:10 if 12:12 felt easy | Sleep quality? Mood? Cravings? |
| 8-14 | 16:8 only if 14:10 felt natural | Full assessment below |

**After 14 days, assess:**

| Signal | Continue IF | Stop IF |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| Energy | Stable or improved | Declining, especially mid-morning |
| Hunger | Manageable | Distracting, leading to cravings or binges |
| Training performance | Same or better | Down >5% on key lifts |
| Sleep | Same or better | Worse onset or quality |
| Mood | Same or better | More irritable, anxious, or low |
| Menstrual cycle (female) | Unchanged | Disrupted or irregular → STOP IMMEDIATELY |
| Relationship with food | Neutral or positive | Preoccupation with food, guilt about eating window |

---

## Contraindications (Do NOT Use IF)

| Condition | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| Current or past eating disorder | IF can trigger restriction-binge cycle |
| Underweight (BMI <18.5) | Energy restriction is harmful |
| Pregnancy / breastfeeding | Increased energy needs throughout the day |
| Type 1 diabetes | Hypoglycemia risk during fasting window |
| Adrenal insufficiency | Cannot handle additional cortisol stimulus |
| Current HA (hypothalamic amenorrhea) | Energy availability must be increased, not restricted |
| Active infection or illness | Immune system needs consistent nutrient supply |
| Children or adolescents (<18) | Growing bodies need consistent energy |

---

## Links

- [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 1 - Diet Maxing.md\|Pillar 1 — Diet Maxing]]
- [[04_PROTOCOLS/Meal Structure Library.md\|Meal Structure Library]] (non-IF meal structures for comparison)
- [[04_PROTOCOLS/Gentle Entry Protocol.md\|Gentle Entry Protocol]] (alternative for eating disorder risk)
- [[05_SYSTEMS/Muscle OS Safety Triage.md\|Safety Triage]] (B1-B6 eating disorder screening)

protocols.Master Integration Protocol:
# Master Integration Protocol — Full System Assembly

*The highest-tier protocol output from the [[Muscle OS Core Engine]] Phase 4. Only recommended when all constraint domains are optimal.*

**Philosophy:** The synergy of all pillars operating simultaneously. This is the master protocol for the lifter who has the resources, time, and commitment to run every variable at optimal levels.

## Daily Timeline

### Morning (06:00-08:00)
- Wake at same time (±15 min)
- Sunlight exposure 5-10 min
- 500ml water with electrolytes
- Morning HRV reading
- Pre-training meal: 40g protein, 50g carbs (if training) OR fasted with EAAs

### Training (08:00-10:00)
- 10g EAAs if fasted
- Intra: 30-60g cyclic dextrin + 5g creatine + 6-8g citrulline malate
- Post: 50g whey isolate + 60-80g high GI carbs
- Cold shower or brief cold exposure post-training

### Day (10:00-18:00)
- Meals every 3-4 hours, minimum 0.5g/kg protein per meal
- 4-6 total meals depending on caloric target
- 30-40 minute afternoon walk (NEAT optimisation)
- Optional: 20-30 min nap if sleep deficit

### Evening (18:00-22:00)
- Last meal: 50g casein + healthy fats (slow digestion)
- 5g glycine + 200-400mg magnesium glycinate
- No screens 30-60 min before bed
- 10 min box breathing or meditation
- Reading (blue light blocking glasses if using devices)

### Sleep (22:00-06:00)
- 8 hours minimum target
- Pitch black room (blackout curtains, no LEDs)
- 18-20°C room temperature
- Earplugs if noise

## Weekly Structure

| Day | Training | Focus | Nutrition |
|-----|----------|-------|-----------|
| Mon | Upper (heavy) | Strength focus | Surplus |
| Tue | Lower (hypertrophy) | Volume focus | Surplus |
| Wed | Active recovery | Mobility + cardio | Maintenance |
| Thu | Upper (hypertrophy) | Volume focus | Surplus |
| Fri | Lower (heavy) | Strength focus | Surplus |
| Sat | Weak point specialisation | High volume | Surplus |
| Sun | Complete rest | Stress management | Maintenance |

## Monthly Structure
- Week 1-3: Accumulation (increasing volume)
- Week 4: Deload (half volume, maintain intensity)
- Every 12 weeks: Full deload week (light activity only)

## Measurement & Adjustment
- Daily: HRV, sleep score, body weight
- Weekly: strength levels on main lifts, circumference measurements
- Monthly: progress photos, DEXA or impedance if accessible
- Every 8-12 weeks: full protocol review and adjustment
protocols.MDE Protocols:
# Minimum Effective Dose (MED) Protocols

*Selected during [[Muscle OS Core Engine]] Phase 4 (Protocol Selection) when the constraint analysis points to MED tier.*

**Philosophy:** The smallest intervention that produces a meaningful result. For the time-poor lifter who wants 80% of results for 20% of the effort.

## Diet MED
- Protein: 1.6g/kg/day, evenly distributed across 3-4 meals (minimum 0.4g/kg per meal)
- Calories: maintenance or slight surplus (+200kcal)
- Leucine: minimum 2.5g per meal (approx 25-30g protein from quality sources)
- Supplements: creatine 5g/day

## Training MED
- Volume: 10-15 hard sets per muscle group per week
- Frequency: 2x per muscle group per week
- Progression: double progression in 5-8 rep range
- Exercise selection: compound-dominant, 5-8 rep range

## Sleep MED
- Duration: minimum 7 hours
- Consistency: same bedtime/wake time ±1 hour
- Environment: pitch black, cool (18-20°C), no screens 30 min before bed

## Recovery MED
- Deload: one week per 8-12 weeks, halve volume, maintain intensity
- Stress: 10 min mindfulness or box breathing daily

## Strength MED
- Heavy singles/doubles: 1 session per week per main lift
- Submaximal work: 70-80% of 1RM, technical focus
protocols.Meal Structure Library:
# Meal Structure Library — What to Eat, When, and How to Prepare It

**Purpose:** Provide concrete meal templates, grocery lists, batch cooking protocols, and daily eating structures for users who know "eat protein and vegetables" but don't know what that actually looks like on a plate.

---

## Daily Meal Structures

### 3-Meal Template (Standard)

| Meal | Composition | Example |
|------|------------|---------|
| **Breakfast** | Protein + complex carb + fruit/veg | 3 eggs + oats/berries OR Greek yogurt + granola + fruit OR protein shake + banana |
| **Lunch** | Protein + carb + vegetables | Chicken breast + rice + broccoli OR tuna wrap + salad OR leftovers from dinner |
| **Dinner** | Protein + carb + vegetables + fat | Salmon + sweet potato + asparagus with olive oil OR beef stir-fry + noodles + mixed veg |
| **Optional snack** | Protein or fruit | Whey shake, apple + peanut butter, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese |

**Target:** Every meal has a protein source. At least 2 meals include vegetables. At least 1 meal includes fruit.

### 4-Meal Template (Higher Volume / Recomp)

| Meal | Time | Composition |
|------|------|-------------|
| Breakfast | Wake + 1h | Protein + carb |
| Lunch | Midday | Protein + carb + veg |
| Afternoon snack | 3-4 PM | Protein + fruit or veg |
| Dinner | Evening | Protein + carb + veg + fat |

### 2-Meal Template (Time-Constrained / Intermittent Fasting)

| Meal | Time | Composition |
|------|------|-------------|
| First meal | 12-2 PM | Protein + carb + veg + fat (larger meal, ~50% daily calories) |
| Second meal | 6-8 PM | Protein + carb + veg + fat (balance of daily calories) |

**Constraint:** Harder to hit protein target (need 40g+ per meal). Not recommended for users <60 kg or with high protein needs (>2.0 g/kg).

---

## Meal Templates by Cuisine

### Template A: Chicken + Rice + Vegetable (Universal)
- **Protein:** 150-200 g chicken breast (cooked weight)
- **Carb:** 150-200 g rice (cooked) or 200-300 g potato
- **Vegetable:** 200 g broccoli, asparagus, green beans, or mixed stir-fry veg
- **Fat:** 1 tbsp olive oil or 1/2 avocado
- **Prep time:** 25 min
- **Calories:** ~500-650

### Template B: Eggs + Oats (Breakfast / Anytime)
- **Protein:** 3-4 eggs + 1 scoop whey (optional in oats)
- **Carb:** 50-80 g oats (dry weight) or 1-2 slices whole grain bread
- **Fruit:** 1 banana or 100 g berries
- **Fat:** From eggs + 1 tbsp peanut butter
- **Prep time:** 10 min
- **Calories:** ~450-600

### Template C: Salmon + Sweet Potato + Greens
- **Protein:** 150-200 g salmon fillet
- **Carb:** 200-300 g sweet potato (baked or roasted)
- **Vegetable:** 150 g spinach, kale, or rocket + lemon
- **Fat:** From salmon + 1 tbsp olive oil on veg
- **Prep time:** 30 min
- **Calories:** ~550-700

### Template D: Beef Stir-Fry
- **Protein:** 150-200 g beef strips (sirloin or mince)
- **Carb:** 200 g noodles (cooked) or 150 g rice
- **Vegetable:** 200 g mixed stir-fry veg (bell pepper, broccoli, carrot, onion)
- **Fat:** 1 tbsp sesame oil + soy sauce
- **Prep time:** 15 min
- **Calories:** ~500-650

### Template E: Vegetarian Bowl
- **Protein:** 150-200 g firm tofu OR 200 g cooked lentils/chickpeas OR 2 eggs + 100 g Greek yogurt
- **Carb:** 150-200 g quinoa or brown rice
- **Vegetable:** 200 g roasted veg (sweet potato, cauliflower, bell pepper)
- **Fat:** 1/2 avocado + tahini dressing or olive oil
- **Prep time:** 20 min (tofu) / 30 min (lentils)
- **Calories:** ~450-600

---

## Batch Cooking Protocols

### Sunday Prep (60 min, covers 4-5 days)

| Step | Task | Time |
|------|------|------|
| 1 | Cook 2 cups dry rice or quinoa | 20 min (passive) |
| 2 | Roast 2 trays vegetables (broccoli + sweet potato + bell pepper) | 25 min (passive) |
| 3 | Cook protein: grill 6 chicken thighs + hard boil 6 eggs OR cook 500 g mince + lentils | 20 min (active) |
| 4 | Portion into containers: protein + carb + veg per meal | 10 min |
| 5 | Wash + cut fresh veggies for salads / snacks | 5 min |

**Result:** 10-12 meals ready. Reheat + eat.

### Express Prep (20 min, covers 3 days)

| Step | Task | Time |
|------|------|------|
| 1 | Cook 1 cup dry rice in rice cooker | Passive |
| 2 | Open + drain 2 cans chickpeas or lentils. Toss with olive oil + salt | 2 min |
| 3 | Cut 1 kg chicken breast into pieces. Season. Pan-fry 6 min total | 10 min |
| 4 | Wash salad greens + cherry tomatoes. Portion into bags | 5 min |
| 5 | Portion rice + chicken + chickpeas into containers | 3 min |

**Result:** 6 meals ready.

---

## Grocery Shopping List (Weekly, Standard)

### Protein
- [ ] Chicken breast or thighs (1-1.5 kg)
- [ ] Eggs (12-18)
- [ ] Greek yogurt (500 g-1 kg)
- [ ] Canned tuna or salmon (3-4 cans)
- [ ] Whey protein (optional)
- [ ] Lentils / chickpeas / tofu (if plant-based)

### Carbohydrates
- [ ] Rice or quinoa (1 bag)
- [ ] Oats (1 bag)
- [ ] Potatoes or sweet potatoes (1 kg)
- [ ] Whole grain bread or wraps
- [ ] Bananas (bunch)
- [ ] Other fruit (apples, berries, oranges)

### Vegetables
- [ ] Broccoli or green beans (2-3 heads/bags)
- [ ] Spinach or mixed greens (bag)
- [ ] Bell peppers (2-3)
- [ ] Onions (2-3)
- [ ] Garlic (head)
- [ 】 Carrots or sweetcorn (frozen or fresh)
- [ ] Frozen mixed vegetables (backup)

### Fats / Condiments
- [ ] Olive oil
- [ ] Peanut butter or almond butter
- [ ] Mixed nuts or seeds
- [ ] Avocados (2-3)

### Pantry
- [ ] Salt, pepper, spices (cumin, paprika, garlic powder, chilli)
- [ ] Soy sauce or tamari
- [ ] Canned tomatoes
- [ ] Vinegar (balsamic or apple cider)

---

## Portion Guide (No Tracking Version)

| Food Group | Hand Portion | Per Meal |
|------------|-------------|----------|
| **Protein** | 1 palm (hand, palm size) | 1-2 palms |
| **Vegetables** | 1 fist | 1-2 fists |
| **Carbohydrates** | 1 cupped hand | 1-2 cupped hands (more on training days) |
| **Fats** | 1 thumb | 1-2 thumbs |

# Overkill Protocols — Maximum Rate of Progress

*Selected during [[Muscle OS Core Engine]] Phase 4 (Protocol Selection) when recovery capacity is optimal and the goal demands maximum rate.*

**Philosophy:** Optimising every variable simultaneously. For the advanced lifter squeezing out the last 10-20% of genetic potential, or anyone who wants to maximise rate of progress regardless of effort cost.

## Diet Overkill
- Protein: 2.2-2.5g/kg/day, 5-6 meals, minimum 0.5g/kg per meal, leucine 3g+ per meal
- Fasted training: 10g EAAs pre-training, 30g whey + 50g carbs post-training
- Nutrient timing: pre-sleep casein (40-50g), intra-workout carbs (30-60g)
- Calorie cycling: higher on training days, lower on rest days
- Carb backloading: heavier carbs post-training for glycogen resynthesis
- Protein quality: variety of sources for complete amino acid profile

## Training Overkill
- Volume: 15-25 hard sets per muscle group per week
- Frequency: 3-4x per muscle group per week
- Techniques: myo-reps, drop sets, rest-pause, occlusion training
- ROM: maximised on all exercises, stretch-mediated hypertrophy emphasis
- Specialisation: higher volume for weak points, maintenance for strong points
- Periodisation: DUP with daily undulating volume/intensity

## Sleep Overkill
- Duration: 8-10 hours (including strategic napping)
- Temperature manipulation: cool bedroom, warm bath/shower before bed
- Pre-sleep protocol: 40g casein, 5g glycine, 200-400mg magnesium glycinate
- Sleep tracking: Oura Ring or similar, optimise based on deep/REM ratios
- Wake-up protocol: sunlight exposure within 15 minutes of waking

## Recovery Overkill
- HRV tracking: daily morning reading, train based on readiness
- Parasympathetic emphasis: evening routine of breathing, meditation, gratitude journal
- Massage: 2x per week sports massage or percussion gun
- Cold exposure: cold showers/showers post-training for inflammation management
- Contrast therapy: sauna 3-4x per week for heat shock proteins

## Strength Overkill
- Peaking blocks: 4-6 week accumulation → intensification → realisation
- Accommodation cycling: wave loading, block periodisation
- Accessory specialisation: targeted weak point training (sticking points)
- Technique refinement: daily practice with submaximal weight
protocols.Periodization Decision Protocol:
# Periodization Decision Protocol — Structuring Training Over Time

**Purpose:** Provide a framework for organizing training into logical blocks (periodization) to maximize long-term progress, prevent plateaus, and manage fatigue.

---

## Periodization Models

### Linear Periodization (Classic)

| Week | Sets × Reps | Intensity | Volume |
|------|-------------|-----------|--------|
| 1-4 | 3×12 | 65-70% | High |
| 5-8 | 3×8 | 70-75% | Moderate |
| 9-12 | 4×5 | 75-85% | Lower |
| 13 | Deload | — | — |

**Best for:** Beginners (<1 year), athletes with a competition date, simple programming needs.
**Pros:** Easy to understand, works well for raw strength development.
**Cons:** Becomes insufficient as you advance. Does not account for daily fluctuations.

### Daily Undulating Periodization (DUP)

| Day | Focus | Example |
|-----|-------|---------|
| Monday | Strength (heavy) | Squat 4×5 @ RPE 8 |
| Wednesday | Power (explosive) | Squat 6×3 @ 70% |
| Friday | Hypertrophy (volume) | Squat 3×10 @ RPE 7 |

**Best for:** Intermediate lifters, those training 3-4×/week per movement pattern.
**Pros:** Variation keeps CNS fresh. Multiple qualities trained simultaneously. Autoregulation friendly.
**Cons:** Complex to program. Requires discipline to manage RPE across varied loads.

### Block Periodization

| Block | Duration | Focus | Example |
|-------|----------|-------|---------|
| Accumulation | 4-6 weeks | High volume, moderate intensity | 3-4×10-15 @ RPE 7 |
| Intensification | 4-6 weeks | Moderate volume, high intensity | 4×5 @ RPE 9 |
| Realization (peaking) | 2-4 weeks | Low volume, very high intensity | Singles and doubles @ RPE 9.5 |
| Transition (deload) | 1 week | Full recovery | Active recovery |

**Best for:** Advanced lifters, sport athletes, those with specific competition dates.
**Pros:** Systematic fatigue management. Each block has a clear purpose.
**Cons:** Long time horizon. Not suitable for general fitness or body composition goals alone.

### Conjugate / Concurrent (Westside-style)

| Day | Focus | Variation |
|-----|-------|-----------|
| Max effort upper | Heavy + accessory variation | Change main lift every 1-3 weeks |
| Dynamic effort lower | Explosive work | Speed squats/deads at 50-60% |
| Max effort lower | Heavy + accessory variation | Change main lift every 1-3 weeks |
| Dynamic effort upper | Explosive work | Speed bench at 50-60% |

**Best for:** Advanced strength athletes, powerlifters, those with very specific strength goals.
**Pros:** Constant variation prevents accommodation. High skill development.
**Cons:** Very complex. Easy to accumulate junk volume. Not for hypertrophy-focused lifters.

---

## Decision Tree: Which Model to Use

```
Training age:
  <1 year → LINEAR PERIODIZATION or simple weekly progression
  1-3 years → DUP or block periodization
  3+ years → Block periodization or conjugate
  5+ years → Periodization is mandatory. Most advanced models work

Goals:
  General fitness / body composition → DUP or linear
  Strength (no competition) → DUP or block
  Strength (competition) → Block periodization with peaking
  Hypertrophy / bodybuilding → DUP with hypertrophy bias (higher volume, moderate weights)
  Sport performance → Block periodization based on competition calendar

Time available:
  <3 sessions/week → DUP (maximizes stimulus per session)
  3-4 sessions/week → DUP or linear (sweet spot for most)
  5-6 sessions/week → Block periodization or conjugate
```

---

## Mesocycle Design Template

| Week | Block Phase | Volume (% of max) | Intensity (% of max) | RPE Target |
|------|-----------|-------------------|---------------------|------------|
| 1-2 | Base / accumulation | 70-80% | 65-75% | 6-7 |
| 3-4 | Build | 80-90% | 70-80% | 7-8 |
| 5-6 | Overload | 85-95% | 75-85% | 8-9 |
| 7-8 | Peak / realization | 60-70% | 85-95% | 9-9.5 |
| 9 | Deload | 40-50% | 60-70% | 4-5 |

**Progression:** Add 2.5-5 kg per mesocycle on main lifts. If you cannot, either the recovery or the volume was too high.

---

## Microcycle Structure (Weekly)

### 3-Day Full Body (Hypertrophy/General)

| Day | Focus | Volume |
|-----|-------|--------|
| Day 1 | Heavy lower + upper push | Moderate |
| Day 2 | Volume upper + lower pull | High |
| Day 3 | Moderate full body + weak point work | Moderate |

### 4-Day Upper/Lower

| Day | Focus | Volume |
|-----|-------|--------|
| Day 1 | Lower strength | Moderate |
| Day 2 | Upper strength | Moderate |
| Day 3 | Lower hypertrophy | High |
| Day 4 | Upper hypertrophy | High |

### 5-Day PPL (Push/Pull/Legs)

| Day | Focus | Volume |
|-----|-------|--------|
| Day 1 | Push (strength bias) | Moderate |
| Day 2 | Pull (strength bias) | Moderate |
| Day 3 | Legs (strength bias) | Moderate |
| Day 4 | Push (hypertrophy bias) | High |
| Day 5 | Pull + legs (hypertrophy bias) | High |

---

## Autoregulation Within Periodization

| Condition | Adjustment |
|-----------|------------|
| Performance matches expected | Follow the plan |
| Performance exceeds expected (lifts moving faster than programmed) | Accelerate progression. Move to next block early or add weight |
| Performance below expected (RPE higher than programmed) | Stay at current load. Do not force progression. Consider deload |
| Life stress high / sleep poor / illness | Reduce volume 20-40%. Maintain intensity. Do not push PRs |
| 2 consecutive poor sessions (RPE 2+ above target) | Deload immediately |

---

## Common Periodization Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It Fails | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Changing programs too frequently (every 2-4 weeks) | Never accumulate enough stimulus to drive adaptation | Run a program for 8-12 weeks minimum before evaluating |
| No periodization at all (same weight/reps every session) | Accommodation. Progress stops. Boredom | Use ANY periodization model for 8+ weeks |
| Overly complex periodization as a beginner | Simple linear progression works best for the first 6-12 months | Do not periodize as a beginner. Just add weight every session |
| Ignoring autoregulation | Following a rigid program when under-recovered leads to failure | Build autoregulation into your program (RPE, RIR, readiness checks) |
| Skipping deloads | Accumulated fatigue eventually overwhelms any periodization model | Deload every 4-12 weeks depending on phase and training age |

---

protocols.Plant-Based Nutrition Guide:
# Plant-Based Nutrition Guide — Vegan & Vegetarian Protocols

**Purpose:** Provide structured, evidence-based nutrition guidance for vegan and vegetarian users. Plant-based diets can fully support athletic performance and body composition goals — but they require intentional planning around key nutrients that are less bioavailable or absent from plant foods.

---

## Who This Is For

| Diet | Description | Nutrients to Watch |
|------|-------------|--------------------|
| **Lacto-ovo vegetarian** | No meat/fish/poultry. Eggs and dairy included | Iron, zinc, B12 (milder concern), omega-3 |
| **Lacto-vegetarian** | No meat/fish/poultry/eggs. Dairy included | Iron, zinc, B12, omega-3 |
| **Ovo-vegetarian** | No meat/fish/poultry/dairy. Eggs included | Iron, zinc, B12, calcium, omega-3 |
| **Vegan** | No animal products at all | B12, iron, zinc, calcium, omega-3 (DHA/EPA), vitamin D, iodine, protein quality (lysine) |
| **Flexitarian** | Mostly plant-based with occasional animal foods | Same as vegan if animal foods are infrequent |

---

## Protein (The Most Common Concern)

### Protein Quality

Plant proteins are typically lower in one or more essential amino acids. The key limiting amino acid in most plant proteins is **lysine** (low in grains) and **methionine** (low in legumes).

| Source | Protein per 100g | Limiting AA | Leucine per 100g | Complete Protein? |
|--------|-----------------|-------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Tofu (firm)** | 12-18 g | None (soy is complete) | 1.2-1.8 g | Yes |
| **Tempeh** | 19-20 g | None (soy is complete) | 1.5-1.7 g | Yes |
| **Edamame** | 11-12 g | None (soy is complete) | 0.9-1.1 g | Yes |
| **Seitan** | 25-30 g | Lysine | 1.8-2.2 g | No (low lysine) |
| **Lentils (cooked)** | 9 g | Methionine | 0.7 g | No (low methionine) |
| **Chickpeas (cooked)** | 7-9 g | Methionine | 0.6 g | No (low methionine) |
| **Black beans (cooked)** | 8-9 g | Methionine | 0.7 g | No (low methionine) |
| **Quinoa (cooked)** | 4-5 g | None (pseudo-grain, complete) | 0.3 g | Yes (but low total protein) |
| **Pumpkin seeds** | 19 g | Lysine | 1.5 g | No (low lysine) |
| **Hemp seeds** | 30-32 g | None (complete) | 1.4 g | Yes |
| **Chia seeds** | 17 g | None (complete) | 1.3 g | Yes |
| **Pea protein powder** | 80-85 g | Methionine (minor) | 6-8 g | Near-complete |
| **Soy protein isolate** | 85-90 g | None (complete) | 7-8 g | Yes |

### Complementary Proteins (Pairing Strategy)

You do NOT need to combine proteins at every meal (the old "complementary protein" myth has been debunked). As long as your total daily intake includes a variety of plant proteins, amino acid needs are met. However, for convenience:

| Pairing | Completes |
|---------|-----------|
| Grains + legumes | Rice + beans, bread + lentil soup, oats + soy milk |
| Grains + seeds | Oats + hemp seeds, bread + pumpkin seeds |
| Legumes + seeds | Lentils + pumpkin seeds, chickpeas + tahini |
| Soy + anything | Tofu/tempeh with any grain or legume |

### Protein Target Adjustment

| Goal | Standard Target | Plant-Based Adjustment | Why |
|------|----------------|----------------------|-----|
| Maintenance | 1.2-1.6 g/kg | 1.4-1.8 g/kg | Lower digestibility of plant protein (~70-85% vs 90-95% for animal) |
| Muscle gain | 1.6-2.0 g/kg | 1.8-2.4 g/kg | Lower leucine content per gram requires higher total intake |
| Fat loss | 2.0-2.4 g/kg | 2.2-2.6 g/kg | Higher requirement in deficit + lower digestibility |
| Strength | 1.6-2.0 g/kg | 1.8-2.4 g/kg | Same logic as muscle gain |

**80 kg vegan male wanting to gain muscle:**
- Protein target: 1.8-2.4 g/kg = 144-192 g/day
- To hit 160 g: 400 g tofu (60 g) + 100 g lentils (9 g) + 60 g hemp seeds (18 g) + 2 scoops pea protein (50 g) + 100 g quinoa (4 g) + 2 tbsp peanut butter (8 g) + 100 g pumpkin seeds (19 g)

**This requires intentional eating.** Most vegan meal plans fall short on protein. If you are struggling, a plant-based protein powder is not optional — it is necessary.

---

## Critical Micronutrients

### B12 (MANDATORY for vegans)
- **Why:** B12 is not naturally present in plant foods. Deficiency causes irreversible neurological damage.
- **Source:** Fortified foods (nutritional yeast, plant milks, breakfast cereals) or supplement
- **Dose:** Sublingual methylcobalamin 1,000 mcg/day (most reliable)
- **Risks:** Estimated 50%+ of long-term vegans are B12 deficient. Symptoms (fatigue, brain fog, neuropathy) often appear before blood levels drop below "normal."

### Iron
- **Why:** Heme iron (animal) is absorbed at 15-35%. Non-heme iron (plant) is absorbed at 2-20%.
- **Sources:** Lentils (3.3 mg/100g cooked), tofu (2.7 mg/100g), spinach (2.7 mg/100g cooked), pumpkin seeds (8.8 mg/100g), blackstrap molasses
- **Enhancers:** Pair with vitamin C (citrus, bell pepper, tomatoes) at the same meal — increases absorption 2-6x
- **Inhibitors:** Avoid tea/coffee within 1 hour of iron-rich meals (tannins block absorption). Calcium also competes
- **Female athletes:** Bloodwork recommended. Ferritin <30 = supplement

### Zinc
- **Why:** Phyrate in grains and legumes binds zinc, reducing absorption by 35-50%.
- **Sources:** Pumpkin seeds (7.5 mg/100g), hemp seeds (5 mg/30g), tofu (1.5 mg/100g), lentils (1.3 mg/100g cooked)
- **Strategies:** Soak/sprout legumes and grains to reduce phytate. Pair with acid (lemon juice, vinegar). Avoid calcium supplements at same meal
- **Target:** Plant-based athletes should aim for 1.5x the standard RDA (15-20 mg/day)

### Calcium
- **Why:** Vegans typically consume 500-600 mg/day vs 1,000+ mg recommended.
- **Sources:** Fortified plant milks (300 mg per cup), tofu set with calcium sulfate (350 mg per 100g), tahini (120 mg per tbsp), kale (100 mg per cup cooked), blackstrap molasses (180 mg per tbsp)
- **Note:** Calcium from many greens (spinach, chard, beet greens) is poorly absorbed due to oxalates. Do not rely on these as primary sources

### Omega-3 (DHA/EPA)
- **Why:** Plant-based ALA (from flax, chia, walnuts) converts to DHA/EPA at only 5-15%. DHA is critical for brain health, inflammation regulation, and recovery.
- **Source:** Algae-based DHA/EPA supplement (500-1,000 mg/day). Only reliable way to get enough.
- **Note:** Flax and chia are good for ALA but insufficient alone for DHA/EPA status

### Vitamin D
- **Why:** Same as general population but worse — vegan vitamin D3 (lichen-derived) is less common. Most vitamin D3 supplements are lanolin-based (not vegan)
- **Source:** Vegan D3 (lichen-derived) 2,000-4,000 IU/day OR D2 (ergocalciferol) — D2 is less effective but better than nothing

### Iodine
- **Why:** Plant foods grown in iodine-depleted soil contain little iodine. Seaweed is variable and unreliable.
- **Source:** Iodized salt (1/2 tsp = 150 mcg). or iodine supplement (150 mcg/day)
- **Do NOT overdo:** Excess iodine is also harmful. Stick to 150 mcg/day

---

## Sample Vegan Meal Plan (150 g protein, ~2,500 kcal)

| Meal | Food | Protein | Notes |
|------|------|---------|-------|
| **Breakfast** | 50 g oats + 250 ml soy milk + 30 g hemp seeds + 1 banana + 30 g peanut butter | 28 g | Hemp seeds + soy milk boost protein significantly |
| **Lunch** | 200 g firm tofu + 200 g quinoa + 200 g broccoli + 1 tbsp sesame oil | 42 g | Tofu + quinoa = complete protein profile |
| **Snack** | 2 scoops pea protein + 250 ml oat milk + 100 g berries | 48 g | Protein powder bridges the gap |
| **Dinner** | 200 g lentils + 100 g brown rice + 200 g roasted veg + 1 tbsp tahini dressing | 28 g | Lentils + rice. Tahini adds calcium |
| **Evening** | 200 g soy yogurt + 30 g pumpkin seeds | 22 g | Total: ~168 g protein = 2.1 g/kg for 80 kg person |

**Key takeaway:** Every meal has a protein strategy. No meal is carbs-only.

---

## Supplement Stack (Vegan)

| Supplement | Dose | Why | Timing |
|------------|------|-----|--------|
| B12 (methylcobalamin) | 1,000 mcg sublingual | Non-negotiable. Deficiency risk is high | Daily |
| Vitamin D3 (vegan/lichens) | 2,000-4,000 IU | Most vegans are deficient | Daily |
| DHA/EPA (algae oil) | 500-1,000 mg | Conversion from ALA is insufficient | Daily |
| Iron (if ferritin <30) | Ferrous bisglycinate 60 mg | Only after bloodwork confirms deficiency | Every other day, with vitamin C |
| Zinc picolinate | 15-30 mg | Bioavailability concern | With food |
| Creatine monohydrate | 5 g | Vegans have lower baseline creatine stores | Daily |
| Iodine (optional) | 150 mcg | If not using iodized salt | Daily |

---

protocols.Progressive Overload Protocol:
# Progressive Overload Protocol — The Engine of All Progress

**Purpose:** Define the methods, decision rules, and troubleshooting for applying progressive overload — the systematic increase in training stress that drives adaptation.

---

## Overload Variables (Ordered by Priority)

| Priority | Variable | How to Apply | When to Increase |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------------|
| 1 | **Weight on bar** | Add 2.5-5 kg (upper body) or 5-10 kg (lower body) | When target reps are hit with good technique at RPE ≤8 |
| 2 | **Repetitions** | Add 1-2 reps to each set | When weight cannot be increased but reps are below target |
| 3 | **Sets** | Add 1 set per exercise | When volume is the limiting factor (advanced lifters) |
| 4 | **Frequency** | Add 1 session per muscle group per week | When weekly volume exceeds per-session capacity |
| 5 | **Exercise difficulty** | Swap to a harder variation | When technique is mastered and load cannot progress on current variation |
| 6 | **Rest reduction** | Decrease rest by 15-30 sec | Only when time efficiency is the goal. Performance trade-off |

---

## Progression Methods

### Linear Progression (Best for Beginners)

| Method | How It Works | Example |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| **Add weight every session** | Add 2.5 kg per session to main lifts | Session 1: 60 kg. Session 2: 62.5 kg. Session 3: 65 kg |
| **Add reps first, then weight** | Stay at same weight. Add reps until target. Then add weight and drop reps | 3×5 → 3×6 → 3×7 → 3×8 → then 3×5 at 2.5-5 kg heavier |

**Duration:** Works for 4-12 weeks for beginners. When progress stalls 2-3 sessions in a row on the same lift → switch to double progression.

### Double Progression (Best for Intermediates)

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Pick a rep range (e.g., 6-10 reps) |
| 2 | Start at the bottom of the range (6 reps) with a challenging weight |
| 3 | Stay at that weight until you can hit the top of the range (10 reps) across all sets |
| 4 | Add 2.5-5 kg and drop back to the bottom of the range (6 reps) |
| 5 | Repeat |

**Why it works:** Eliminates guesswork. You DO NOT add weight until you have earned it by hitting the rep target.

**Rep range guidelines by goal:**

| Goal | Rep Range | Sets | Rest |
|------|-----------|------|------|
| Strength | 3-6 | 3-5 | 3-5 min |
| Hypertrophy (main lifts) | 6-10 | 3-5 | 2-3 min |
| Hypertrophy (accessories) | 8-15 | 2-4 | 60-90 sec |
| Endurance / pump work | 15-30 | 1-3 | 30-60 sec |

### Wave Loading / Periodized (Best for Advanced)

| Week | Sets × Reps @ RPE | Wave Pattern |
|------|-------------------|-------------|
| Week 1 | 3×8 @ RPE 7 | Build phase |
| Week 2 | 3×7 @ RPE 8 | |
| Week 3 | 3×6 @ RPE 9 | Overload phase |
| Week 4 | 4×5 @ RPE 9 | Peak phase |
| Week 5 | Deload | Recovery |
| Week 6 | Repeat with 2.5-5 kg increase on wave start | |

---

## Stalling Protocol

**When you fail to progress for 3+ sessions in a row on the same lift:**

| Action | Details |
|--------|---------|
| 1. Check recovery | Sleep, calories, stress. If any are poor → fix these FIRST before changing training |
| 2. Reduce volume | Drop 1 set per exercise. See if progress resumes (volume may be exceeding recovery capacity) |
| 3. Reduce frequency | Drop from 2× to 1.5× per week. More frequency != better for everyone |
| 4. Deload | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Deload Protocol.md\|Full deload protocol]] — 40-50% volume reduction for 1 week |
| 5. Change exercise | Swap to a variation (e.g., barbell squat → front squat or safety bar squat) |
| 6. Vary rep range | If stalled at 5 reps → drop to 8 reps with lighter weight for 4-6 weeks. Then return |
| 7. Assess form | Record yourself. Poor technique caps strength. Fix technical errors before chasing numbers |

---

## Rate of Progress Expectations

| Level | Upper Body (per month) | Lower Body (per month) | Notes |
|-------|----------------------|----------------------|-------|
| Beginner (0-6 months) | +5-10% per session | +5-10% per session | Linear progression works. Ride it as long as possible |
| Novice (6-12 months) | +2.5-5 kg | +5-10 kg | Slowing but still session-to-session |
| Intermediate (1-3 years) | +2.5-5 kg per 2-4 weeks | +2.5-5 kg per 2-4 weeks | Need double progression or periodization |
| Advanced (3-5 years) | +2.5-5 kg per 4-8 weeks | +2.5-5 kg per 4-8 weeks | Progress is measured in months per plate PR |
| Elite (5+ years) | +2.5-5 kg per 8-16 weeks | +2.5-5 kg per 8-16 weeks | A 2.5 kg PR is still a PR |

**Critical:** If you are not progressing at these rates → something is wrong with your program, recovery, or effort. Do not accept slow progress at any level without investigating.

---

## Common Overload Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It Fails | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Adding weight too fast | Technique breaks. Injury risk rises. Progress stalls quickly | Use double progression. Earn the weight increase |
| Never adding weight | No stimulus for adaptation. Muscle and strength plateau | Track every session. If reps are all above the target range → add weight |
| Adding volume instead of weight | Accumulates unnecessary fatigue. Most people do not need more than 10-20 sets/week per muscle group | Prioritize weight progression first. Volume is a secondary lever |
| Changing exercises too often | Never accumulate enough volume on one movement to drive adaptation | Run a lift for 6-12 weeks before swapping. Do not program hop |
| Ignoring technique for numbers | Everyone has a max that exceeds their technical capacity. That is not real strength | Back off 10%. Own the technique. Then progress from there |

---

protocols.Recomp Decision Protocol:
# Recomp Decision Protocol — Body Recomposition Guide

**Purpose:** Determine whether body recomposition (building muscle while losing fat) is realistic for a given user, and provide protocols for those who qualify.

---

## What Recomp Is (and Isn't)

| Is | Is Not |
|----|--------|
| Building muscle while losing fat simultaneously | A magic bullet for fast results |
| A slow process (0.25-0.5% body composition change per month visible) | Something that works for everyone |
| Possible only under specific conditions | A replacement for bulking/cutting cycles at advanced levels |
| Best for beginners and returning lifters | Efficient for anyone past the intermediate level |

---

## Recomp Eligibility Decision Tree

```
Q1: What is your training age?
  → <6 months → RECOMP LIKELY. Beginners build muscle and lose fat easily.
  → 6-12 months → RECOMP POSSIBLE. Strong candidate.
  → 1-2 years → RECOMP POSSIBLE but slow. Depends on body fat and consistency.
  → 2+ years → RECOMP UNLIKELY. You need dedicated bulking/cutting phases.
  → Returning after 3+ month break → RECOMP LIKELY (muscle memory effect).

Q2: What is your body fat percentage?
  → Male: >18% / Female: >28% → RECOMP LIKELY. Higher body fat has more energy for muscle building.
  → Male: 12-18% / Female: 22-28% → RECOMP POSSIBLE. Moderate candidate.
  → Male: <12% / Female: <22% → RECOMP UNLIKELY. Body has insufficient energy reserves. Need surplus.

Q3: Are you taking any body composition-altering compounds?
  → Yes (PEDs, GLP-1 agonists, etc.) → RECOMP IS EASIER. Drug-naive applies more to natty.
  → No → See above guidelines.

Q4: What is your primary goal?
  → "I want to lose fat but I'm afraid of losing muscle" → RECOMP is ideal
  → "I want to get bigger and leaner at the same time" → RECOMP is possible but slow
  → "I need to lose 10+ kg of fat" → Pure cut first, then recomp or bulk
  → "I need to gain 10+ kg of muscle" → Pure bulk first

Decision:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RECOMP LIKELY: Beginner (<6 mo) OR returning OR BF >18/28%│
  │  RECOMP POSSIBLE: 6-12 mo OR BF 12-18/22-28%               │
  │  RECOMP UNLIKELY: >2 years OR BF <12/22%                   │
  │  BETTER TO BULK: Underweight or very low BF, wants mass    │
  │  BETTER TO CUT: Overweight/obese, BF >25/35%               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Recomp Nutrition Protocol

### Calorie Setup

| Variable | Setting |
|----------|---------|
| **Starting point** | Maintenance calories (TDEE) |
| **Adjustment** | Small deficit: 100-300 calories below maintenance |
| **Protein** | 2.0-2.4 g/kg (higher end of standard range) |
| **Fat** | 0.8-1.0 g/kg (lower end. Recomp draws from body fat stores) |
| **Carbs** | Remainder of calories. Minimum 3 g/kg |
| **Deficit limit** | Never exceed 300 cal deficit. Larger deficits block muscle building |

**Why only 100-300 cal deficit:** Muscle building requires energy. If the deficit is larger, the body does not have enough energy to build new tissue while also losing fat. The recomp window is narrow.

### Macronutrient Distribution (80 kg male example)

| Macro | g/kg | Grams | Calories |
|-------|------|-------|----------|
| Protein | 2.2 | 176 g | 704 (35%) |
| Fat | 0.8 | 64 g | 576 (29%) |
| Carbs | 3.0-3.5 | 240-280 g | 960-1,120 (36-56%) |
| **Total** | — | — | **2,240-2,400** |

### Protein Distribution (Critical for Recomp)

| Timing | Target | Why |
|--------|--------|-----|
| Per meal | 30-50 g | Maximize MPS stimulation |
| Pre-training | 20-30 g | Provides amino acids during session |
| Post-training | 30-50 g | Maximizes post-training MPS window |
| Pre-bed | 30-40 g (casein ideally) | Sustains MPS through the night |

### Rate of Progress

| Timeframe | Visible Change |
|-----------|---------------|
| 4 weeks | Subtle. Waist may reduce slightly. Strength may increase |
| 8 weeks | Noticeable in progress photos. Clothes fit differently |
| 12 weeks | Clear body composition shift |
| 6 months | Dramatic difference if consistent |

**Warning:** Recomp is slow. If you need faster results, use dedicated cut or bulk phases instead.

---

## Recomp Training Protocol

| Variable | Setting |
|----------|---------|
| **Primary focus** | Hypertrophy (strength gains will be slow in a deficit) |
| **Volume** | 12-18 sets/muscle group/week (moderate-high) |
| **Intensity** | RPE 7-9 (1-3 RIR). Do not push RPE 10 regularly |
| **Frequency** | 2×/muscle group/week |
| **Progressive overload** | Double progression. Progress will be slower than in surplus |
| **Cardio** | 5,000-8,000 steps/day. Minimal added cardio (40 = 8,640 bits, 64B/factor → 576g → 192g fat)
| **Deload frequency** | Every 6-8 weeks (fatigue management in deficit is critical) |

**Key training rule for recomp:** If strength drops on any lift for 2+ consecutive sessions → you are in too deep a deficit. Increase calories by 100-200/day.

---

## When to Switch Out of Recomp

| Signal | Action |
|--------|--------|
| No visible change in 8-12 weeks | You are not in the right phase for recomp. Switch to dedicated bulk or cut |
| Strength drops consistently | Deficit too large OR recovery insufficient. Increase calories or deload |
| Hunger is unmanageable | Recomp requires precision. If hunger is distracting, intentional cut/bulk will feel better |
| Progress resumes after deficit | Consider increasing calories to maintenance or slight surplus for 2-4 weeks (diet break) |
| You have been recomping for 6+ months | Switch to a 8-12 week bulk or cut. Recomp loses efficacy over time |

---

## Who Should NOT Recomp

| Profile | Why | Better Approach |
|---------|-----|----------------|
| Obese (BF >30% male, >40% female) | Recomp is too slow. Larger deficit is safe and effective | Cut at 500-750 calorie deficit |
| Very lean (BF <10% male, <18% female) | Insufficient body fat stores to fuel muscle building | Bulk (surplus of 200-300 cal) |
| Low training age + underweight | Building mass should be primary focus | Bulk (surplus of 300-500 cal) |
| Advanced lifter (>2 years consistent, low BF) | Recomp does not produce noticeable results | Traditional bulk/cut cycles |
| Female with menstrual cycle disruption or HA | Energy restriction must be addressed first | Reverse diet to maintenance or surplus. Re-establish cycle |

---

# RPE RIR & Intensity Management Protocol — Training at the Right Intensity

**Purpose:** Define the RPE (Rate of Perceived Exertion) and RIR (Reps in Reserve) systems, how to use them, and common pitfalls. Intensity management is the difference between productive training and accumulating junk volume.

---

## RPE Scale (Reps in Reserve Based)

| RPE | Meaning | Reps From Failure | How It Should Feel |
|-----|---------|-------------------|---------------------|
| 10 | Maximum effort. Cannot do another rep | 0 reps left | Failed rep or absolute max. Technique breakdown |
| 9.5 | Could maybe do 1 more rep with great difficulty | 0-1 | Grinder. 100% effort. Do not use often |
| 9 | Definitely 1 rep left | 1 rep left | Hard but you know you could do one more |
| 8.5 | 1-2 reps left | 1-2 | Challenging. Could grind out 1 more but not 2 |
| 8 | 2 reps left | 2 | Moves fast. You know you have 2 more in the tank |
| 7 | 3 reps left | 3 | Comfortably challenging. Good speed. |
| 6 | 4+ reps left | 4+ | Light. Technique work. Warm-up territory |
| 5 | Bar moves easily | — | Warm-up only |

**For hypertrophy work:** RPE 7-9 (1-3 RIR) is ideal. Going to failure (RPE 10) is not necessary and accumulates disproportionate fatigue.

**For strength work:** RPE 8-9.5 (0-2 RIR). Occasional RPE 10 on max attempts.

---

## RPE by Rep Range

| Reps | RPE 10 | RPE 9 | RPE 8 | RPE 7 |
|------|--------|-------|-------|-------|
| 1RM | 100% | ~97% | ~95% | ~92% |
| 3RM | ~95% | ~92% | ~90% | ~87% |
| 5RM | ~90% | ~87% | ~85% | ~82% |
| 8RM | ~83% | ~80% | ~77% | ~73% |
| 10RM | ~78% | ~75% | ~72% | ~68% |
| 12RM | ~75% | ~72% | ~68% | ~65% |

**Note:** These are estimates. Individual variation exists (fiber type distribution, fatigue resistance). Use as starting points and calibrate.

---

## How to Estimate RIR During a Set

| Cue | What to Assess |
|-----|---------------|
| Bar speed | The single best indicator. If bar speed slows noticeably → you are closer to failure |
| Rep quality | If technique degrades or reps become uneven → close to failure |
| How the rep feels | If you have to grind/push hard → <2 RIR |
| Breath holding | If you are holding your breath through the concentric → close to failure |
| After the set | Ask: "Could I have done 1 more rep? 2 more?" Be honest. Calibrate each session |

**Practice:** During warm-up sets, estimate RPE/RIR for every set. Compare to your actual bar speed and feel. Within 2-3 weeks, most people are accurate within 1 RPE point.

---

## RPE Drift

As the session progresses, the same absolute weight will feel harder due to accumulated fatigue.

| Set | Example | RPE |
|-----|---------|-----|
| Set 1 | 100 kg × 5 | RPE 7 |
| Set 2 | 100 kg × 5 | RPE 8 |
| Set 3 | 100 kg × 5 | RPE 8.5 |
| Set 4 | 100 kg × 5 | RPE 9 |

**What to do:**
- If RPE stays within 1 point of target → no adjustment needed
- If RPE drifts >1.5 points (e.g., sets 1-2 @ RPE 7, sets 3-4 @ RPE 9+) → weight is too heavy for the prescribed volume
- If all sets are at target RPE → next session add 2.5-5 kg
- If first set is already at or above target RPE → reduce weight 5-10%

---

## Autoregulation Protocols

### Reps in Reserve (RIR-Based)

| Session Goal | RIR Target | Adjust If |
|-------------|------------|-----------|
| Strength | 0-1 RIR across all sets | If you hit 0 RIR on first set → reduce weight 5% |
| Hypertrophy | 1-3 RIR | If you hit 0 RIR on any set → reduce weight or reduce sets |
| Skill / technique | 4+ RIR | Never approach failure. Focus on speed and form |
| Recovery / deload | 4+ RIR | Reduce sets by 40-50% |

### Percentage to RPE Conversion

If you are coming from a percentage-based program:

| Phase | % of 1RM | Equivalent RPE |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Accumulation | 65-75% | RPE 6-8 |
| Intensification | 75-85% | RPE 8-9 |
| Peak / realization | 85-95% | RPE 9-10 |

**RPE is superior to percentages** because it accounts for daily fluctuations in fatigue, recovery, and readiness. A percentage assumes you are always fresh. RPE adapts.

---

## When to Use RPE 10 (and When Not To)

| Use RPE 10 | Do NOT Use RPE 10 |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Testing a new 1RM (once every 8-12 weeks) | Most training sessions |
| Competition | Regular hypertrophy sets |
| Final set of a strength peaking block | Accessory exercises |
| Once every 2-3 weeks on a main lift (optional) | When technique is not dialled in |
| | When fatigued or under-recovered |
| | Every session (leads to CNS burnout) |

**Every set to failure is not better.** RPE 10 disproportionately fatigues the CNS relative to the muscle stimulus. 3 sets at RPE 8 (2 RIR) produce similar or better hypertrophy than 3 sets at RPE 10, with significantly less fatigue.

---

## Common RPE Mistakes

| Mistake | Reality | Fix |
|---------|---------|-----|
| Underestimating RPE (thinking weight is lighter than it is) | Very common, especially in early sessions | Record video. Compare bar speed. Calibrate against an RPE chart |
| Overestimating RPE (thinking weight is harder than it is) | Less common. Associated with fear of failure | Have a coach or training partner call your RPE. Trust the data |
| Using RPE as an excuse to train lighter | RPE is a management tool, not a permission tool | If you typically train at RPE 8 but "feel" RPE 6 → push the weight |
| Not tracking RPE | Without data, autoregulation is guesswork | Log RPE for every set of every exercise |
| Ignoring RPE drift | Sessions 1 and 4 at the same weight are not the same stimulus | Adjust weight down as drift occurs, or accept drift as fatigue management |

---

# Shift Work & Circadian Rhythm Protocol — Sleeping Against the Clock

**Purpose:** Provide structured protocols for shift workers, night owls, early risers, and anyone whose schedule conflicts with natural circadian rhythms. Circadian misalignment is one of the most significant unmeasured stressors on health and performance.

---

## Circadian Biology Brief

| Time (Natural) | Physiological Event | What Happens |
|----------------|-------------------|--------------|
| 6-8 AM | Cortisol rise | Natural wake signal. Body temp begins rising |
| 8-10 AM | Peak alertness | Best time for analytical work |
| 12-2 PM | Post-lunch dip | Core body temperature dips. Alertness drops naturally |
| 2-5 PM | Secondary alertness peak | Good for physical performance (peak strength often here) |
| 9-10 PM | Melatonin rise | Body prepares for sleep. Core temp begins dropping |
| 2-4 AM | Deepest sleep signals | Strongest circadian sleep drive. Lowest core body temp |

**Shift work disrupts all of this.** Your body never fully adapts to night shift because even on days off, natural light pushes your rhythm back toward a diurnal pattern. The goal is not perfect adaptation but minimizing the damage.

---

## Shift Type Protocols

### Night Shift (Overnight, e.g., 10 PM - 6 AM)

This is the most disruptive shift pattern.

**Sleep Schedule Strategy:**

| Option | Schedule | Best For |
|--------|----------|----------|
| **Anchor sleep** (recommended) | Main sleep: 8 AM - 12 PM (4h) after shift. Anchor nap: 4-6 PM (2h) before shift | Splitting sleep into two blocks aligns better with circadian biology |
| **Block sleep** | Sleep 8:30 AM - 3:30 PM (7h) straight | Simpler but harder to maintain. More social disruption |
| **Gradual shift** | Delay bedtime by 2h each day until aligned with night shift schedule | For permanent night shift only |

**Light Management (Critical):**

| Time | Action | Why |
|------|--------|-----|
| After shift ends (6-8 AM) | Wear blue-blocking (amber) glasses on the way home. No direct sunlight | Sunlight signals your brain "morning = wake up." Block it |
| After waking (12-2 PM) | Get 10-15 min of natural light | Resets your circadian rhythm enough for daytime function but signals "afternoon" not "morning" |
| Before shift (9-10 PM) | Bright light (500+ lux). Cool white light if possible | Suppresses melatonin to keep you alert for work |
| During shift (midnight-4 AM) | Moderate lighting. Take breaks in brighter areas if drowsy | Maintain alertness without over-suppressing melatonin (some melatonin is useful for post-shift sleep) |

**Meal Timing:**
- Pre-shift meal (9-10 PM): Protein + moderate carb. Not too heavy
- During shift: Small, protein-rich snacks. Avoid large meals between 1-5 AM (worst metabolic impact)
- Post-shift meal (7-8 AM): Small, easy to digest. Protein + some carbs. Do NOT eat a full meal — this signals wakefulness
- Main meal: Eat after waking (12-2 PM) — largest meal of the day

### Rotating Shifts

| Rotation Direction | Recommendation | Why |
|--------------------|---------------|-----|
| Forward rotation (morning → evening → night) | Better | Shifting later is easier biologically than shifting earlier |
| Backward rotation (night → evening → morning) | Worse if unavoidable | Each shift forces you to go to sleep earlier, which is harder |

**Protocol for Rotating Shifts:**
- Use a 1-2h transition day between shift changes
- On transition day: sleep as much as possible, use bright light when awake to help reset
- If shifting from night → day: stay awake after last night shift until 8-9 PM, then sleep
- If shifting from day → night: take a 2-3h nap in late afternoon before first night shift

### Early Morning Shift (e.g., 4 AM - 12 PM)

| Problem | Protocol |
|---------|----------|
| Waking at 3 AM when natural melatonin is still high | 10,000 lux light box for 20-30 min at wake time. Keep room dark until ready to wake |
| Sleeping early enough | Bedtime 7-8 PM. Blackout curtains. No screens after 6 PM |
| Afternoon crash | Accept that you will be tired by 2-3 PM. Nap 15-20 min if needed. Do NOT nap longer — it will disrupt next night's sleep |
| Evening social events | Difficult. Prioritize sleep over socializing on work nights. Move socializing to days off |

---

## Circadian Alignment for Non-Shift Workers

### Morningness vs Eveningness (Chronotype)

| Chronotype | Natural Peak | Bedtime | Wake Time | Risk |
|------------|-------------|---------|-----------|------|
| **Early chronotype** (lark) | 6 AM - 2 PM | 8-10 PM | 5-6 AM | Forced late nights cause sleep deprivation |
| **Intermediate** | 8 AM - 4 PM | 10-12 PM | 6-8 AM | Most flexible |
| **Late chronotype** (owl) | 12 PM - 8 PM | 12-2 AM+ | 8-10 AM+ | Forced early mornings = chronic sleep debt |

**Protocol for Late Chronotypes Forced Into Early Schedules:**
- 10,000 lux light box: 20-30 min immediately on waking
- Do NOT hit snooze — get up immediately and get light
- Morning caffeine: delay 60-90 min after waking (allows natural cortisol rise, reduces tolerance)
- Evening wind-down: strict 90-min pre-bed routine starting at 9 PM regardless of alertness
- Melatonin 0.3-0.5 mg: 1-2h before desired bedtime (helps phase advance)

### Jet Lag Protocol

| Direction | Strategy |
|-----------|----------|
| **Eastward travel** (earlier time zone) | Harder. Fast 12-16h before arrival. Expose to bright morning light at destination. Melatonin 0.5 mg at destination bedtime for 3 days |
| **Westward travel** (later time zone) | Easier. Stay awake until local bedtime. Morning light exposure. Delay meals gradually |

**General Jet Lag:**
- 1 day per time zone crossed to fully adapt
- Hydrate aggressively during flight. No alcohol. Minimal caffeine
- Set watch to destination time immediately on boarding
- Upon arrival: align light exposure with local time. Seek morning light, avoid evening light

---

## Light Exposure Cheat Sheet

| Goal | Light Type | Timing | Duration |
|------|-----------|--------|----------|
| Wake up / phase advance | Natural sunlight or 10,000 lux cool white | First 30 min after wake | 15-30 min |
| Maintain alertness | Cool white 500+ lux | During work hours | Continuous |
| Prepare for sleep | Warm 2700K or red light | 2h before bed | Until bedtime |
| Sleep (night shift, daytime) | Total darkness + blackout curtains | During sleep period | Full duration |
| Reset from night shift | Blue-blocking glasses + dim light | Last 2h of shift + commute home | Until sleep |
| Seasonal depression | 10,000 lux therapy light | Morning | 20-30 min |

---

## Supplement Support

| Supplement | Dose | Timing | Use Case |
|------------|------|--------|----------|
| Melatonin | 0.3-0.5 mg | 30 min before desired sleep | Phase shifting. Night shift sleep. Jet lag. LOW dose is key |
| Melatonin ER | 1-2 mg | Before sleep | Maintaining sleep. Staying asleep during daytime sleep |
| L-theanine | 100-200 mg | Before sleep | Sleep quality, relaxation without sedation |
| Magnesium glycinate | 200-400 mg | Before sleep | Sleep quality. Muscle relaxation |
| Vitamin D | 2,000-4,000 IU | With largest meal | Shift workers are chronically low. Important for circadian regulation |
| Ashwagandha | 300-600 mg | Morning or before bed | Cortisol regulation in high-stress shift workers |

**Melatonin Warning:** Do NOT use melatonin long-term without circadian assessment. Melatonin is a hormone, not a vitamin. Extended use can suppress endogenous production. Use for specific phase-shifting scenarios only (shift change, jet lag, 7-14 day max).

---

## Measuring Circadian Health

| Signal | Good | Concerning |
|--------|------|------------|
| Sleep onset | Within 15-30 min of getting into bed | >45 min regularly |
| Wake | Feeling refreshed, ± 30 min of alarm | Need alarm to wake, groggy >30 min |
| Energy pattern | Predictable high/low windows | Random crashes, unpredictable energy |
| Digestive regularity | Regular bowel movements, consistent appetite | Erratic hunger, irregular digestion |
| Mood | Stable throughout day | Noticeable shifts, irritability |
| If 3+ concerning signals persist for 4+ weeks despite protocol adherence | Consultant with sleep specialist |

---

# Sleep Hygiene Protocol — Optimize Recovery Through Sleep

**Purpose:** Provide actionable protocols for improving sleep quality and quantity. Sleep is the single most powerful recovery tool — poor sleep sabotages diet, training, and health regardless of how well you execute everything else.

---

## The Sleep Foundation (Non-Negotiables)

| Factor | Target | Why |
|--------|--------|-----|
| Duration | 7-9 hours per night | <6h = significant performance/recovery impairment. >9h may indicate poor quality or health issue |
| Consistency | Same bedtime + wake time ± 30 min | Circadian disruption from inconsistent sleep is as harmful as insufficient sleep |
| Timing | Asleep by midnight ideally | Early sleep (10 PM-12 AM) has higher restorative quality per hour than late sleep (2-4 AM) |

**Note:** If you sleep 6 hours and feel fine, you are not "optimized" — you are adapted to insufficient sleep. Objective performance testing almost always shows impairment at <7h.

---

## Sleep Environment Optimization

### Light

| Action | Specification |
|--------|---------------|
| Darkness | Total darkness. Cover all LED indicators. Use blackout curtains or sleep mask |
| Blue light (pre-bed) | No screens 60-90 min before bed. If unavoidable, use blue-blocking glasses (amber/red lens, 450-550 nm block) + device night mode |
| Evening lighting | Dim, warm lighting (2700K or lower) after sunset. Red or amber bulbs for bathroom/hallway |
| Morning light | 5-15 min of natural light within 30 min of waking. On cloudy days, use 10,000 lux therapy light |

### Temperature

| Area | Target | Method |
|------|--------|--------|
| Room temp | 18-20°C (65-68°F) | Cooler temperatures facilitate core body temperature drop needed for sleep onset |
| Hands/feet warm | Comfortable | Warm extremities help vasodilation and heat dissipation. Wear socks if needed |
| Bedding | Breathable natural fibers | Avoid synthetic sheets that trap heat. Cotton, linen, or bamboo |

### Sound

| Scenario | Strategy |
|----------|----------|
| Quiet environment | Silence is best |
| Noisy environment | White noise, pink noise, or brown noise (better than earplugs alone) |
| Sudden noises | Heavy curtains, door seals, earplugs as backup |
| Partner snoring | Address snoring cause first. Separate sleeping if needed — sleep quality > ego |

### Other

| Factor | Protocol |
|--------|----------|
| Air quality | Ventilate room before bed. CO2 buildup degrades sleep quality |
| Electronics | All charging blocks and electronics at least 1 m from head. WiFi router off or in another room |
| Clock visibility | Turn clock away. Clock-watching increases sleep anxiety |

---

## Wind-Down Protocol (90-Minute Pre-Bed Routine)

| Time Before Bed | Action |
|-----------------|--------|
| T-90 min | Stop work, emails, stressful conversations |
| T-90 min | Dim lights. Switch to warm lighting |
| T-90 min | Last caffeine of the day (if sensitive to caffeine, make this T-10h) |
| T-60 min | Stop screens. Put phone in another room or airplane mode |
| T-60 min | Light reading (fiction, non-stimulating non-fiction) or journaling |
| T-45 min | Evening hygiene routine (shower, skincare, brushing teeth) |
| T-30 min | Light stretching or foam rolling (optional but helpful) |
| T-30 min | Meditation / deep breathing (4-7-8 or box breathing for 5 min) |
| T-15 min | Set room temperature, check darkness, prepare for next morning |
| T-5 min | Get into bed. Read or relax until drowsy |
| T-0 min | Lights out |

**No phone in bed.** The bed is for sleep and sex only. Do not train yourself to associate bed with scrolling.

---

## Sleep Disruption Troubleshooting

| Problem | First-Line Intervention | Second-Line |
|---------|------------------------|-------------|
| Can't fall asleep (>30 min) | Get out of bed. Do something boring in dim light until drowsy. Do NOT stay in bed awake | 0.5-1 mg melatonin (sublingual, immediate release) — take 30 min before desired sleep time |
| Waking up at 3-4 AM and can't fall back | Do NOT look at phone or clock. Stay in dark. Deep breathing. If >30 min, get up briefly | 0.3-0.5 mg melatonin extended release (at bedtime) OR magnesium glycinate 200-300 mg |
| Racing mind / anxiety | Journal: write down everything on your mind. Box breathing (4-4-4-4). Progressive muscle relaxation | Inositol 2 g OR magnesium glycinate 200-400 mg before bed |
| Restless legs | Check iron status (ferritin). Rule out iron deficiency. Magnesium glycinate. Stretching before bed | Iron supplementation only if low ferritin |
| Night sweats | Check room temperature. Lower 1-2°C. Breathable bedding. Hydrate during day, not right before bed | Rule out sleep apnea, hormonal issues |
| Frequent urination (>1x/night) | Stop fluids 1-2h before bed. Rule out excessive evening fluid intake. Reduce caffeine and alcohol | If persistent, check blood glucose (could be early sign of hyperglycemia) |
| Snoring / sleep apnea suspicion | Side sleeping. Nose strips. Reduce alcohol. If BMI >30, weight loss is primary treatment | Sleep study for formal diagnosis |
| Partner disturbance | Separate blankets. If severe, separate beds — sleep divorce is for health, not relationship failure | Discuss and experiment. Do NOT sacrifice sleep for perceived togetherness |

---

## Supplements for Sleep (Use as Tools, Not Crutches)

| Supplement | Dose | Timing | Best For |
|------------|------|--------|----------|
| Magnesium glycinate | 200-400 mg | 30-60 min before bed | General sleep quality, muscle relaxation, restless legs |
| Melatonin | 0.3-1 mg | 30 min before bed | Sleep onset delay. Use lowest effective dose. NOT for long-term use |
| L-theanine | 100-200 mg | 30 min before bed | Racing mind, anxiety. Can also use during the day for focus |
| Glycine | 3 g | 30 min before bed | Falling asleep faster, next-day alertness |
| Apigenin | 50 mg | 30 min before bed | Sleep onset and quality. Often combined with L-theanine |
| Taurine | 500-1,000 mg | 30 min before bed | GABA support, sleep onset |
| Inositol | 2-4 g | Before bed | Racing thoughts, anxiety-driven insomnia |

**Rules:**
- Try one supplement at a time for 1 week before adding another
- Do NOT rely on supplements as primary sleep intervention. Environment + routine come first
- Cycle melatonin: 2-5 days on, 2-3 days off. Tolerance develops quickly
- If sleep is still poor after 4 weeks of consistent protocol → see a sleep specialist

---

## Caffeine & Alcohol Management

### Caffeine
| Factor | Guideline |
|--------|-----------|
| Cutoff time | 10h before bedtime (e.g., if bed at 10 PM, no caffeine after 12 PM) |
| Sensitive individuals | 12h cutoff or eliminate afternoon caffeine entirely |
| Maximum daily | 400 mg (approx 4 cups coffee). Higher doses increase sleep disruption even if you don't notice |
| Note | "I can sleep after coffee" does not mean coffee doesn't impair your sleep quality. It does. |

### Alcohol
| Factor | Guideline |
|--------|-----------|
| Cutoff time | 3-4h before bedtime minimum |
| Effect | Alcohol fragments sleep in second half of night, reduces REM, worsens sleep apnea |
| "Nightcap" myth | Alcohol helps fall asleep faster but degrades sleep quality significantly |
| Trade-off | If you drink, keep to 1-2 standard drinks and stop 3h+ before bed |

---

## Napping Protocol

| Nap Type | Duration | Best Timing | Benefit |
|----------|----------|-------------|---------|
| Power nap | 10-20 min | Before 3 PM | Alertness + cognitive function. No sleep inertia |
| Recovery nap | 60-90 min | Before 3 PM | Full sleep cycle. Includes REM + deep sleep. May cause inertia |
| Caffeine nap | 20 min + coffee | Pre-nap coffee | Drink coffee immediately before 20 min nap. Caffeine kicks in as you wake |

**Rules:**
- No naps after 3 PM (disrupts nighttime sleep)
- If you struggle with nighttime sleep, eliminate naps entirely
- 90-min naps are more restorative than 30-45 min naps (which leave you in deep sleep)

---

## Sleep Tracking (Minimal Approach)

| Metric | How to Track | Useful? |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| Total sleep time | Manual log or wearable | Yes. Best single metric |
| Wake time (consistency) | Manual log | Yes |
| Subjective quality (1-10) | Manual log | Yes. Correlates well with objective recovery |
| HRV trend | Wearable (weekly average) | Yes. Rising HRV trend = good recovery. Falling = accumulating fatigue |
| Sleep stages | Wearable | No. Consumer wearables are poor at stage detection. Ignore this data |
| Sleep score | Wearable composite | No. Mostly marketing. Focus on total time + consistency + subjective |

---

# Strength vs Hypertrophy Decision Protocol — Training for Your Primary Goal

**Purpose:** Help users determine whether to prioritize strength or hypertrophy training, and how to periodize between the two depending on their goals, training age, and current phase.

---

## Goal Decision Tree

```
Q1: What is your primary long-term goal?
  → Build muscle / change body composition → HYPERTROPHY PATH
  → Get stronger at specific lifts → STRENGTH PATH
  → Both equally → CONCURRENT PATH

Q2: What is your training age?
  <1 year → HYPERTROPHY PATH (beginners build strength and muscle simultaneously)
  1-3 years → Choose based on current priority. Can switch every 8-12 weeks
  3+ years → Must periodize. Cannot maximize both simultaneously

Q3: Are you in a calorie surplus, deficit, or maintenance?
  Surplus → Either path works well. Strength path may be optimal
  Deficit → HYPERTROPHY PATH (preserve muscle. Strength gains unlikely in deficit)
  Maintenance → HYPERTROPHY PATH (slow muscle gain possible. Strength gains slow)
```

---

## Path Comparison

| Variable | Hypertrophy Path | Strength Path |
|----------|-----------------|---------------|
| **Primary stimulus** | Metabolic stress + mechanical tension | Neural adaptation + mechanical tension |
| **Rep range** | 5-30 (optimal: 8-15 for most muscles) | 1-6 (optimal: 3-5) |
| **Sets per muscle group/week** | 12-20 | 6-12 (higher intensity means lower volume tolerance) |
| **RPE / RIR** | 7-9 RPE (1-3 RIR) | 8-9.5 RPE (0-2 RIR) |
| **Rest periods** | 60-120 sec | 3-5 min |
| **Exercise selection** | More variation, isolation, angles | Compound-focused, specific to the lift |
| **Training to failure** | Last set of some exercises (optional) | Rarely. Failure on strength work = CNS burnout |
| **Frequency per muscle group** | 2× per week | 1-3× per week (depends on lift) |
| **Progression metric** | More reps or weight in target range | More weight on the bar |
| **Time to see progress** | 4-8 weeks visible | 2-6 weeks on the bar |

---

## Hypertrophy Path (Detailed)

### Principles
- Volume is the primary driver (total weekly sets in appropriate rep ranges)
- Use a variety of exercises to target all regions of a muscle
- Focus on mind-muscle connection and time under tension for isolation work
- Proximity to failure matters less than total volume (RPE 7-9 is sufficient)
- Progressive overload is still important but measured in total work, not just weight

### Rep Range Distribution

| Percentage of Volume | Rep Range | Purpose |
|---------------------|-----------|---------|
| 20% | 1-5 reps | Heavy compound work (neural stimulus, strength carryover) |
| 60% | 6-15 reps | Primary hypertrophy zone |
| 20% | 15-30 reps | Pump work, metabolic stress, blood flow |

### Sample Exercise Selection

| Muscle Group | Compound | Isolation |
|-------------|----------|-----------|
| Chest | Incline dumbbell press, flat barbell press | Cable fly, pec deck |
| Back | Pull-up, barbell row | Lat pulldown, face pull, straight arm pulldown |
| Shoulders | Overhead press, upright row | Lateral raise, reverse fly |
| Quads | Squat, leg press, hack squat | Leg extension |
| Hamstrings | RDL, good morning | Leg curl (lying or seated) |
| Arms | Close-grip press, chin-up | Bicep curl, tricep extension |

---

## Strength Path (Detailed)

### Principles
- Intensity is the primary driver (percentage of 1RM)
- Compound lifts are central. Accessories support the main lifts
- Technique is paramount. Strength is a skill
- Fatigue management is critical. Every rep at high intensity is expensive
- RPE 9 should be the ceiling for most sets. RPE 10 is for testing, not training

### Rep Range Distribution

| Percentage of Volume | Rep Range | Purpose |
|---------------------|-----------|---------|
| 5% | 1-2 reps | Max strength exposure (peaking only) |
| 60% | 3-6 reps | Primary strength zone |
| 20% | 6-10 reps | Volume accumulation, hypertrophy support |
| 15% | 10-20 reps | Accessory work, prehab, technique practice |

### Sample Weekly Structure (Powerlifting Focus)

| Day | Main Lift | Supplemental | Accessories |
|-----|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| Day 1 | Squat (heavy, 3-5 reps) | Front squat or pause squat (5-8 reps) | Leg curl, core |
| Day 2 | Bench (heavy, 3-5 reps) | Incline or close-grip (5-8 reps) | Row, tricep, lateral raise |
| Day 3 | Deadlift (heavy, 3-5 reps) | RDL or deficit deadlift (5-8 reps) | Pull-up, core, grip |
| Day 4 | Bench (volume, 6-10 reps) | Overhead press (5-8 reps) | Face pull, curl, tricep |

---

## Concurrent Path (Mixed)

| Approach | How It Works | Best For |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| **Block periodization** | 6-8 weeks hypertrophy → 6-8 weeks strength → repeat | Lifters who want both, intermediate+ |
| **Concurrent (daily undulating)** | Heavy compound first, hypertrophy accessories after | Most lifters. Best all-round approach |
| **Concurrent (upper/lower split)** | Strength-focused lower body, hypertrophy-focused upper body (or vice versa) | Lifters with imbalanced priorities |
| **Periodized within mesocycle** | Start with hypertrophy, progress to strength as mesocycle advances | Advanced. Requires careful programming |

### Recommended Default: Concurrent

| Day | Focus | Example |
|-----|-------|---------|
| Day 1 | Strength main + hypertrophy supplemental | Squat 4×5 @ RPE 8 → Leg extension 3×12 @ RPE 8 |
| Day 2 | Strength main + hypertrophy supplemental | Bench 4×5 @ RPE 8 → Cable fly 3×15 @ RPE 8 |
| Day 3 | Strength main + hypertrophy supplemental | Deadlift 3×5 @ RPE 8 → RDL 3×10 @ RPE 8 |

**Why this works for most people:** Strength work drives neural adaptation and progressive overload on compounds. Hypertrophy work ensures all muscle fibers are stimulated. Fatigue is managed because heavy work is limited.

---
