protocols.Stress Management Protocol:
# Stress Management Protocol — Regulating Allostatic Load

**Purpose:** Provide active stress management tools that complement the recovery and fatigue management systems. Stress is the most under-diagnosed cause of stalled progress. This protocol gives users actionable techniques to reduce allostatic load without requiring major lifestyle changes.

---

## How Stress Affects Training Outcomes

Chronic stress elevates cortisol, which:
- Suppresses testosterone and IGF-1 (reduced anabolic signalling)
- Increases visceral fat storage (via 11β-HSD1 upregulation in adipose)
- Impairs sleep quality (reduced SWS, fragmented REM)
- Reduces GLUT4 translocation (poorer nutrient partitioning)
- Increases muscle protein breakdown (FOXO-mediated proteolysis)
- Impairs immune function (increased illness risk)

**A user with stress 7+/10 for 2+ weeks will NOT make optimal progress regardless of how perfect their training and nutrition are.**

---

## Stress Assessment

| Level | Description | Impact on Training | Recommended Action |
|-------|-------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| 1-3 | Low — normal daily fluctuations | None. Training helps reduce stress | No intervention needed |
| 4-5 | Moderate — noticeable but manageable | Training may feel harder but still productive | Monitor. Consider one technique below (choose the easiest) |
| 6-7 | High — affecting sleep, appetite, or mood | Performance declining. Recovery impaired | Protocol required. Reduce training volume 20-30%. Implement stress techniques |
| 8-10 | Severe — feeling overwhelmed, chronic | Overtraining risk. Illness risk elevated. Likely mood disorder | Protocol + consider professional support. Training at MEC only (2x/week) |

---

## The Stress Management Toolkit

Choose techniques based on time available and personal preference. Do NOT try all at once — pick ONE, practice for 2 weeks, then assess.

### Tier 1: High-Efficiency (5-10 min/day)

| Technique | Time | When to Do It | How |
|-----------|------|---------------|-----|
| **Box breathing** | 5 min | Before bed, before a stressful event, or any transition | Inhale 4s → Hold 4s → Exhale 4s → Hold 4s. Repeat 5-10 cycles |
| **4-7-8 breathing** | 2 min | Before meals, after waking, when craving a binge | Inhale 4s → Hold 7s → Exhale 8s. Repeat 4-8 cycles |
| **2-min grounding** | 2 min | Any time stress spikes | 5-4-3-2-1: name 5 things you see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste |
| **Walking break** | 5-10 min | Mid-work, after stressful meeting | Walk without phone. Focus on surroundings. Not "exercise" — just walking |
| **Single-task focus** | 10 min | When feeling scattered | Set timer for 10 min. Do ONE thing. No phone, no tabs, no interruptions |

### Tier 2: Moderate Investment (10-20 min/day)

| Technique | Time | When to Do It | How |
|-----------|------|---------------|-----|
| **Meditation / breathwork session** | 10-15 min | Morning or pre-bed | Use app (Headspace, Calm, Waking Up) or guided. Consistency > duration |
| **Journaling** | 10 min | Evening | Write 3 things you're grateful for + 1 thing that went well + 1 thing to improve tomorrow |
| **Progressive muscle relaxation** | 15 min | Pre-bed | Tense each muscle group 5s, release 10s. Feet → calves → quads → glutes → core → hands → arms → shoulders → face |
| **Cold exposure** | 5 min | Post-shower | 30-90s cold at end of shower. Cold activates ventral vagal pathway, increases dopamine baseline |
| **Music / podcast break** | 15 min | During commute, lunch | Active listening (not background). Music with 60-80 BPM synchronizes HRV |

### Tier 3: Lifestyle Changes (Daily / Weekly)

| Practice | Commitment | Why It Works |
|----------|------------|--------------|
| **Consistent sleep timing** | ±30 min bedtime daily | Stabilizes cortisol rhythm. Most powerful stress intervention |
| **Morning light exposure** | 5-10 min outdoor light within 1h of waking | Sets circadian clock, improves sleep onset, reduces evening cortisol |
| **No phone first 30 min** | Daily | Prevents cortisol spike from news/social media/email |
| **Weekly "buffer" day** | 1 day/week with no schedule | Prevents allostatic load accumulation. One unstructured day |
| **Social connection** | 1 meaningful conversation/day | Oxytocin counter-regulates cortisol. Even a 5-min call helps |
| **Reduce news / social media** | Limit to 30 min/day | Continuous negative news exposure elevates baseline cortisol |

---

## Stress — Training Volume Adjustment Table

| Stress Level | Volume (vs normal) | Intensity | Frequency | Notes |
|-------------|-------------------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| 1-3 | 100% | Normal | Normal | No adjustment |
| 4-5 | 90% | Normal | Normal | Reduce accessory sets, keep compounds |
| 6-7 | 70-80% | Maintain (do not reduce load) | 3x/week | Drop accessories. Compounds only. Add stress technique |
| 8-10 | 50% (MEC) | Low (RIR 4) | 2x/week | Bodyweight or light loads. Prioritize stress management. Consider coach escalation |

**Important:** Do NOT reduce training load for stress unless you also add a stress management technique. Volume reduction alone without replacement does not fix the problem — it just reduces the training stimulus.

---

## Integration Points

### When to Add This Protocol

1. **Recovery Failure Decision Tree** — at "High allostatic load" diagnosis (stress >7/10 for 2+ weeks), route to this protocol
2. **Pillar 4 Recovery Maxing** — Allostatic Load Budget section
3. **Pillar 6 Fatigue Management** — Chronic fatigue diagnosis
4. **Constraint Resolution Engine** — When Adherence or Recovery is the binding constraint
5. **Any user with self-reported stress >6/10 on intake or reassessment**
6. **Safety Triage C3** — Anxiety/depression Yellow flag → recommend stress management as complement to professional care

### When to Escalate

| Signal | Action |
|--------|--------|
| Stress >8/10 for 4+ weeks despite protocol | [[05_SYSTEMS/Coach Escalation Rules.md\|Coach Escalation]] Tier 2 — strongly recommend therapist |
| Stress causing missed food or training | Route to [[04_PROTOCOLS/Gentle Entry Protocol.md\|Gentle Entry Protocol]] |
| Stress accompanied by suicidal ideation | Crisis service immediately. Tier 3 mandatory |
| Stress + significant weight change (>5% BW in 4 weeks) | Medical consult |

---

protocols.Tracking & Measurement Protocol:
# Tracking & Measurement Protocol — What to Measure and How to Use the Data

**Purpose:** Define what to track, how often, and — most importantly — how to use the data to make decisions. Tracking without action is just data collection. This protocol ensures every metric you track drives a decision.

---

## Tracking Tiers

| Tier | Effort | Metrics | Best For |
|------|--------|---------|----------|
| **Tier 1 — Minimal** | 2 min/day | Weight (weekly avg), training log (sets/reps/RPE), subjective readiness | Everyone. This is the default |
| **Tier 2 — Standard** | 5 min/day | Tier 1 + waist measurement (weekly), sleep log (daily), step count | Most users after first 4 weeks |
| **Tier 3 — Comprehensive** | 10 min/day | Tier 2 + HRV (daily), progress photos (biweekly), body fat measurement (monthly) | Advanced users, those stalling, data enthusiasts |

**Recommendation:** Start at Tier 1 for 4 weeks. Add Tier 2 elements one at a time. Never jump to Tier 3 unless you have a specific reason (stalling, contest prep, medical monitoring).

---

## What to Track

### Training (Non-Negotiable)

| Metric | What to Record | Frequency | Decision Use |
|--------|---------------|-----------|-------------|
| Exercise | Name of the lift | Every set | — |
| Weight | Load on the bar | Every set | Overload decisions |
| Reps | Reps completed | Every set | Overload decisions |
| RPE / RIR | Perceived exertion | Every set | Intensity management, autoregulation |
| Notes | How the set/session felt | Per session | Context for future review |

**Minimum viable training log:** Exercise + weight + reps + RPE. Without these, you cannot make informed overload decisions.

### Body Composition

| Metric | How to Measure | Frequency | Decision Use |
|--------|---------------|-----------|-------------|
| Scale weight | Same time, same day (morning, post-toilet, pre-food). Weekly average | Daily OR weekly | Calorie adjustment (trend, not single weigh-in) |
| Waist circumference | At navel, relaxed. Use a flexible tape | Weekly | Fat loss progress (more reliable than scale alone) |
| Progress photos | Same lighting, same pose, same time of day | Every 2-4 weeks | Visual trend. Inspect when scale does not move |
| Body fat % (skinfold/DEXA) | By trained professional or consistent self-measure | Every 4-8 weeks | Trend over accuracy. Single readings are unreliable |
| How clothes fit | Subjective feel of your usual clothes | Ongoing | Real-world proxy. If clothes fit better, you are progressing |

**Rule:** Look at the 4-week trend, not the daily number. Bodyweight fluctuates 1-3 kg due to water, food mass, and hormonal factors. A single weigh-in tells you nothing.

### Recovery

| Metric | How | Frequency | Decision Use |
|--------|-----|-----------|-------------|
| Sleep duration | Wearable or manual log | Daily | If <6h → reduce training volume next day |
| Subjective readiness | 1-10 scale (10 = best) | Before each session | If <4/10 two sessions in a row → deload |
| HRV (optional) | Wearable, on waking | Daily | Downward trend >5 days → deload or lifestyle audit |
| DOMS / soreness | 1-10 scale | Before each session | If >6/10 persistent → excessive volume or poor recovery |

---

## How Often to Assess and Adjust

| Timeframe | Assessment | Adjustment |
|-----------|-----------|------------|
| **Session to session** | RPE, readiness, performance | Autoregulate: add weight if reps are easy, back off if RPE is too high |
| **Weekly** | Weight trend, waist measurement, total training volume | Calorie adjustment if weight is moving in the wrong direction for 2 weeks |
| **Monthly** | Progress photos, strength levels (estimated 1RM), adherence rate | Program adjustment: change exercises, rep ranges, or volume |
| **Every 3 months** | Full assessment: photos, measurements, strength test, body composition | Major program change: new mesocycle, new goal, diet phase change |
| **Every 6-12 months** | Bloodwork, health markers | Health optimization. Rule out deficiencies or issues |

---

## Decision Rules Based on Tracking

### Weight / Body Composition

| Scenario | Action |
|----------|--------|
| Weight stable for 2+ weeks in a deficit phase | Reduce calories by 100-200/day OR increase step count by 2,000/day |
| Weight dropping too fast (>1% bodyweight/week) | Increase calories by 100-200/day. Rapid loss risks muscle and metabolic adaptation |
| Weight stable in a surplus phase | Increase calories by 100-200/day |
| Weight gaining too fast (>0.5-1% bodyweight/week while bulking) | Reduce surplus. Excess calories are stored as fat, not muscle |
| Waist circumference increasing faster than scale would suggest | Possible muscle gain + fat gain. If waist is growing rapidly → surplus is too large |
| Waist staying same while weight increases | Likely muscle gain (good sign for surplus phase) |

### Strength / Performance

| Scenario | Action |
|----------|--------|
| RPE decreasing at same weight and reps | Progress. Add weight next session |
| RPE increasing at same weight and reps | Fatigue accumulating or recovery deficit. Deload or reduce volume |
| Weight + reps stagnant for 3+ sessions | Stalling. Check recovery. If recovery is fine → deload + technique review |
| Estimated 1RM drops >5% from peak | Overreaching or undertraining. Review total training stress |
| Performance inconsistent (RPE varies 2+ points session to session) | Recovery inconsistency. Address sleep, nutrition, life stress |

---

## Tracking Tools

| Tool | Best For | Notes |
|------|----------|-------|
| **Notebook + pen** | Training log | Zero friction. No batteries. Recommended for beginners |
| **Simple app (Strong, Hevy, Fitnotes)** | Training log | Digital convenience. Auto-rest timer. History search |
| **Spreadsheet (Excel/Google Sheets)** | Full tracking + analysis | Most customizable. Good for advanced analysis |
| **MacroFactor / MyFitnessPal** | Nutrition tracking | For counting calories and macros. MacroFactor has automatic TDEE adjustments |
| **Wearable (Whoop, Garmin, Apple Watch)** | Recovery + sleep + HRV | Good for trends. Ignore proprietary "scores" and focus on raw data (HRV, RHR) |

**Rule:** Use the simplest tool that captures your minimum viable data. If tracking takes >5 min/day, you will quit.

---

## Common Tracking Mistakes

| Mistake | Why It's a Problem | Fix |
|---------|-------------------|-----|
| Tracking too many metrics | Overwhelm. Tracking becomes the workout | Track only 3-5 metrics. Tier 1 is enough |
| Responding to daily fluctuations | Over-adjusting leads to erratic programming | Never adjust based on a single data point. Look at 7-14 day trends |
| Not tracking at all | No data → no informed decisions | Start with Tier 1. A notebook costs $2 |
| Never reviewing the data | Tracking without review is just collection | Schedule 15 min every Sunday to review the week's data |
| Obsessing over the scale | One of the worst metrics for short-term assessment | Cover the scale. Uncover it once per week. Trust photos + waist measurement more |
| Using different measurement methods inconsistently | The data becomes noise | Same scale, same time, same conditions. Always |

---

protocols.Warm-Up & Cool-Down Protocol:
# Warm-Up & Cool-Down Protocol — General Standards

**Purpose:** Provide a universal warm-up and cool-down framework that applies across all training protocols. Warm-ups prepare the body for the session's demands. Cool-downs initiate recovery and reduce soreness.

---

## Warm-Up Standards

### General Warm-Up (5-7 min)

Every session, regardless of goal or experience level:

| Duration | Activity | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| 2 min | Light cardio (jump rope, brisk walk, stationary bike, rower) | Raise core temperature, increase blood flow |
| 3-5 min | Dynamic mobility — joint-specific movements below | Increase range of motion, activate nervous system |

**Dynamic Mobility Sequence (do all, 30-60s each):**
1. Ankle circles (each direction)
2. Knee circles or leg swings (front-to-back, side-to-side)
3. Hip circles or hip CARs (controlled articular rotations)
4. Torso twists or cat-cow
5. Arm circles (forward, backward)
6. Neck rolls (half circles, not full rotations)

### Movement-Specific Prep (3-5 min)

After the general warm-up, prepare for the specific exercises in today's session:

| For This Movement | Do This | Volume |
|-------------------|---------|--------|
| Squat pattern | Bodyweight squat → goblet squat → bar squat (empty) | 10+5+5 reps |
| Hip hinge | Glute bridge → single-leg RDL (light) → bar hip thrust | 10+5+5 reps |
| Horizontal push | Band pull-apart → wall push-up → incline push-up | 10+10+8 reps |
| Horizontal pull | Band row → cable row (light) → scapular pull-up | 10+8+5 reps |
| Vertical push | Band pull-apart → DB press (very light) | 10+8 reps |
| Vertical pull | Band pull-down → lat pulldown (very light) | 10+8 reps |

**Rule:** For the first working set of each exercise, use 50% of working weight for 5 reps, then 70% for 3 reps, before loading to working weight.

### Warm-Up Adjustments by Context

| Context | Adjustment |
|---------|------------|
| Morning session (<2h after waking) | Extend general warm-up by 3-5 min. Add 2 min of light cardio. Mobilize longer |
| Cold environment | Add 3-5 min light cardio. Wear warm clothing during warm-up |
| Injury recovery / chronic pain | Add 3-5 min of targeted activation for the affected area. Use the rehab protocol's specific warm-up |
| Masters athlete (40+) | Extend general warm-up to 10-12 min. Move through slower, more deliberate ROM |
| Beginner (<3 months) | Focus on movement quality, not speed. Use bodyweight only for prep |
| Session >1h | Re-warm-up after 45 min (2 min light cardio + 1 round of mobility) |
| Second session same day | Reduce warm-up to movement-specific prep only (5 min) |

---

## Cool-Down Standards

### Post-Session Cool-Down (5-7 min)

| Duration | Activity | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| 1-2 min | Low-intensity cardio (walk, easy bike, very light row) | Gradual HR deceleration, venous return |
| 3-5 min | Static stretching or targeted mobility | Maintain ROM, reduce post-exercise muscle tension |

**Static Stretch Sequence (hold each 20-30s, do NOT force into pain):**
1. Standing hamstring stretch (each leg)
2. Quad stretch (each leg, standing)
3. Chest doorway stretch
4. Lat stretch (overhead grab, side bend)
5. Glute stretch (figure-4 seated or standing)
6. Child's pose (if back or hips feel tight)

**Note:** Static stretching post-session is for relaxation and ROM maintenance. It does NOT prevent injury or reduce DOMS significantly (evidence review: Herbert et al., 2011). If time-constrained, skip stretching and just walk 2 min.

### Cool-Down Adjustments by Context

| Context | Adjustment |
|---------|------------|
| Evening session | Extend cool-down to 7-10 min. Add 2 min of diaphragmatic breathing. Promotes parasympathetic activation before sleep |
| High-intensity session | Walk 3-4 min instead of 2. Heart rate takes longer to decelerate after HIIT |
| Lower-body focus | Add hip flexor stretch (half-kneeling), adductor stretch (wide stance), calf stretch |
| Upper-body focus | Add triceps stretch (overhead reach), wrist flexor/extensor stretch |
| Beginner | Keep cool-down simple. Walk 2 min + stretch only the muscles that feel tight |

---

## Warm-Up / Cool-Down Quick Reference

```
WARM-UP (8-12 min total):
  ├── General (5-7 min): Light cardio + dynamic mobility
  └── Specific (3-5 min): Movement patterns for today's exercises

COOL-DOWN (5-7 min total):
  ├── Cardio deceleration (1-2 min): Walk or easy bike
  └── Static stretch (3-5 min): Major muscle groups, 20-30s each
```

# Anterior Pelvic Tilt — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Hyperlordosis, lumbar lordosis, "duck butt" posture, lower cross tightness*

---

## What It Is

The pelvis tilts forward (anteriorly), increasing the lumbar curve. The hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris) and lumbar erectors are short/tight. The glutes, hamstrings, and deep abdominals are long/weak.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes for lifters:** Prolonged sitting (hip flexors adaptively shortened), heavy squatting without adequate glute activation, deadlifting with excessive lumbar extension, weak core, poor bracing technique.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Wall test:** Stand against wall. Low back gap is >1 hand thickness (approximately >2 inches)
- **Thomas test:** Lie on back, pull one knee to chest. If the other thigh lifts off the table, you have tight hip flexors (contributing to APT)
- **Standing test:** Stand normally. Place one hand on ASIS (front hip bone) and one on PSIS (back hip bone). If ASIS is lower than PSIS (front tilts down, back tilts up), you have APT
- **Supine leg test:** Lie flat on floor. Can you keep your low back flat against the floor without effort? If your lower back arches off the floor, you have APT

---

## Red Flags

- Sharp low back pain that radiates into the legs (rule out disc involvement)
- Pain that worsens when extending the spine (bending backward)
- Numbness/tingling in legs or feet
- Bilateral leg weakness

→ Any of these → see physical therapist. APT with these symptoms may be masking a disc issue.

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Iliopsoas (hip flexor) | Gluteus maximus |
| Rectus femoris | Gluteus medius |
| Tensor fasciae latae (TFL) | Hamstrings |
| Lumbar erector spinae | Transversus abdominis (deep core) |
| Quadratus lumborum (can contribute) | Internal/external obliques |
| Thoracolumbar fascia (tight) | Pelvic floor muscles |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (3-5 min)

1. **Kneeling hip flexor stretch** — Half-kneeling, squeeze glute on the back leg, gently push hips forward (tuck tailbone slightly). 45s each side. **Key:** Do not let ribcage flare — keep ribs down
2. **Psoas release (lacrosse ball)** — Lie face down, ball slightly medial and inferior to ASIS. Breathe. Let weight settle. 60-90s each side. Deep, uncomfortable — this is normal
3. **Quad stretch (side-lying)** — Lie on side, pull heel toward glute. Keep hips stacked. 30s each side
4. **Child's pose (lat stretch)** — Knees wide, arms forward, sit back onto heels. 45s. If underactive low back muscles are actually tight, this helps
5. **Lacrosse ball into glute** — Sitting on ball, find tender spots in glute. 60s each side. Tight glutes inhibit glute function paradoxically

---

## Activation (5-7 min)

1. **Prone hip extension (bird dog variation)** — On hands and knees, extend one leg behind, keeping hips level. Squeeze glute at extension. Do NOT let pelvis rotate. 3×10 each. **Key:** Glute squeeze must happen BEFORE leg lifts
2. **Dead bug** — Lie on back, arms up, knees at 90°. Slowly extend opposite arm and leg while keeping low back flat. 3×8 each side. Low back stays pressed into floor
3. **Supine bridge with posterior tilt** — Lie on back, knees bent. Squeeze glutes, tuck pelvis under (posterior tilt), lift hips. Hold 2s at top. 3×12. Do NOT use hamstrings to lift — use glutes
4. **McGill curl-up** — Lie on back, one knee bent, arms under low back. Lift head and shoulders slightly. Do NOT use hip flexors. 3×8 each side
5. **Bodyweight squat (tempo)** — 3s descent, hold at bottom, 3s ascent. Focus on keeping pelvis neutral (not tucking under at bottom, not arching at top). 3×8

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Squat:** Maintain pelvic neutral. Do NOT let the pelvis tuck into posterior tilt at the bottom (butt wink) OR hyperextend at the top (anterior tilt). Brace before each rep
- **Deadlift:** Set your back BEFORE pulling. Cue: "show the wall your belt buckle" — slight posterior tilt of pelvis. Do NOT hyperextend at lockout
- **Hip thrust:** Emphasize glute squeeze at the top. Do NOT hyperextend the low back
- **Core:** Breathe into the 360° belt (expand ribcage, back, and sides) before bracing. Do NOT brace by sucking in or arching back

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Low bar back squat | Reduce weight. Use front squat or goblet squat | Low bar position encourages lumbar extension |
| Conventional deadlift (heavy) | Use trap bar or sumo temporarily | Same hip hinge, less lumbar extension demand |
| Hyperextension (back extension) | Avoid end-range extension. Stop at neutral | Full extension = reinforcing lumbar overactivity |
| Reverse hyper | Use light weight. Stop at parallel | Same as above — end-range extension reinforces APT |
| Standing OHP | Brace core hard before pressing | OHP load on a hyperextended lumbar spine = high injury risk |
| Hanging leg raises | AVOID during correction. Use dead bugs | Hanging leg raise = hip flexor dominant, reinforces APT |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Sitting:** Do not sit with pelvis tucked forward. Sit on the "sit bones" (ischial tuberosities), not on the tailbone. Use a lumbar roll if needed
- **Standing:** Gentle posterior pelvic tilt (tuck tailbone slightly). Practice while waiting for the kettle to boil
- **Walking:** Squeeze glutes slightly during each stride. This is the "glute walk" — glutes should fire during every step, not just at the gym
- **Sleeping:** On back: pillow under knees to reduce hip flexor tension. On side: pillow between knees, slight curl (not fetal position)
- **Stretching:** Stretch hip flexors AFTER training (they're cold before — risk of strain)

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Low back flat on floor in supine test | 2-4 weeks | Lie on back — feel if arch reduces |
| Thomas test — thigh lowers toward floor | 4-8 weeks | Re-test Thomas test |
| Wall test gap decreases (1.5 → 1 hand thickness) | 4-8 weeks | Re-measure low back gap on wall |
| No hyperextension at squat lockout | 4-8 weeks | Video your squat from side |
| Full correction (hand thickness gap on wall) | 8-12 weeks | Wall test — lumbar gap |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Glute bridge with posterior tilt** — 2×/week as a warm-up segment
- **Dead bugs** — 2×/week, 3×8 each side
- **Mid-thigh pull trap bar deadlift** — replaces conventional deadlift permanently if APT is recurrent
- **Early warning sign:** Feeling tightness in the front of the hip after long sitting + squat session → do 1 min of hip flexor stretching before next squat session

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Lower Crossed Syndrome.md|Lower Crossed Syndrome]] (if combined with weak glutes/core)*
protocols.Posture/Flat Back Posture:
# Flat Back Posture — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Posterior pelvic tilt, decreased lumbar lordosis, "flat butt" posture, hypolordosis*

---

## What It Is

The lumbar curve is reduced or flattened. The pelvis is tucked under (posterior tilt). The hamstrings and rectus abdominis are short/tight. The hip flexors, lumbar erectors, and deep core stabilizers are long/weak.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes:** Excessive sitting with tucked pelvis, overemphasis on "tuck the tailbone" cues in squatting/deadlifting, tight hamstrings pulling the pelvis into posterior tilt, poor core bracing (sucking in instead of 360° expansion).

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Wall test:** Stand against wall. Low back gap is LESS than hand thickness or no gap at all
- **Standing test:** Place one hand on ASIS (front hip bone) and one on PSIS (back hip bone). If PSIS is higher than ASIS (front tilts up, back tilts down), you have posterior pelvic tilt
- **Supine test:** Lie flat on floor. Can you slide your hand under your lower back? If no, your lumbar spine is flattened against the floor
- **Visual:** From the side, the butt appears flattened, the torso may lean slightly forward, and the hamstrings appear prominent

---

## Red Flags

- Low back pain that worsens with prolonged standing or walking (loading a flat lumbar spine)
- Hip pain with extension (tight hamstrings + compressed posterior joint)
- Numbness/tingling in legs — rule out disc involvement (rare with flat back but possible)
- Difficulty standing up straight without "locking back" the knees

→ See physical therapist if any of these persist

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Hamstrings (long head) | Iliopsoas (hip flexor) |
| Rectus abdominis (upper) | Lumbar erector spinae |
| Gluteus maximus (clenched, not functional) | Quadratus lumborum |
| Adductors (can contribute) | Transversus abdominis |
| Tensor fasciae latae | Deep core stabilizers |
| | Thoracolumbar extensors |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (3-5 min)

1. **Hamstring stretch (seated)** — Sitting with one leg extended, lean forward from hips, not waist. 45s each side
2. **Rectus abdominis release (lacrosse ball)** — Lie face down, ball in upper abdomen near ribcage. Breathe. 60s
3. **Adductor stretch** — Standing, wide stance, shift weight to one side. 30s each side
4. **Glute release** — Sitting on lacrosse ball, find tender spots. 60s each side
5. **Cat-camel (lumbar focus)** — Emphasize extension (cow pose) on hands and knees. 10 reps

---

## Activation (5-7 min)

1. **Prone lumbar extension (cobra)** — Lie face down, hands near shoulders. Gently extend upper back, keeping hips on floor. Hold 3s. 3×8. Do NOT use arms to push — use back extensors
2. **Quadruped hip flexor stretch with contraction** — Half-kneeling, squeeze glute on back leg, gently push hips forward. This is lengthening under activation. 3×20s each side
3. **Dead bug with low back neutral** — Lie on back, arms up, knees at 90°. Externally rotate arms (palms up). Keep LOW BACK OFF THE FLOOR (maintain neutral, don't flatten). Slowly extend opposite arm/leg. 3×8 each
4. **Supine arch (gentle)** — Lie on back, place hands under low back. Gently press low back into hands, then release to create a small arch (do NOT push into full extension). 3×10
5. **Bird dog with extension emphasis** — On hands and knees, extend opposite arm and leg. Focus on the leg extending BACK slightly higher than parallel (hip extension). 3×8 each

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Squat:** Maintain a neutral pelvis. Do NOT cue "tuck your tailbone." Instead cue "screw your feet into the floor" (external rotation torque) to naturally engage glutes without tucking
- **Deadlift:** Set up with a neutral spine. Do NOT flatten the back. Let the lumbar curve exist naturally. Use the cue "proud chest"
- **Standing:** Practice standing with weight evenly distributed, soft knees (not locked), and a relaxed pelvis. Do NOT squeeze glutes in standing (that tucks the pelvis)
- **Walking:** Allow the hips to extend naturally behind you with each stride — this creates lumbar extension naturally

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Heavy RDL or SLDL | Switch to trap bar deadlift or hip thrust | Full ROM RDL can reinforce hamstring overactivity + posterior tilt |
| Crunches / sit-ups | Eliminate temporarily | Rectus abdominis overactivity reinforces posterior tilt |
| Hamstring curls (seated) | Reduce weight, focus on eccentric control | Heavy hamstring curls reinforce the tight-hamstring pattern |
| Deadlift (conventional, heavy) | Use trap bar or sumo temporarily | Conventional deadlift at lockout encourages posterior tilt cue |
| Glute bridge (clam-shell) | Focus on glute squeeze without tucking pelvis | Many people posterior-tilt during bridges — keep neutral |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Standing:** Avoid locking knees back (genu recurvatum). Stand with soft knees, weight slightly forward on balls of feet
- **Sitting:** Use a lumbar roll. Do NOT sit with pelvis tucked under. Sit on sit bones, not tailbone
- **Walking:** Allow natural hip extension — don't constrict the stride
- **Sleeping:** On side with knees slightly bent and a pillow between knees. Avoid sleeping in a tight fetal position (can reinforce posterior tilt)
- **Posture cue:** "Show your belly" (not literally — but relax the abdominal tension slightly to allow natural lumbar curve)

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can create a small lumbar arch on demand | 1-2 weeks | Lie on back, create arch — should feel like a natural curve |
| Wall test shows finger-thickness gap | 4-6 weeks | Re-measure lumbar gap |
| Hamstring flexibility improves | 4-8 weeks | Seated forward fold — can reach closer to toes |
| Standing posture feels more relaxed (not locked) | 4-8 weeks | Subjective: standing doesn't feel like effort |
| Normal lumbar curve restored (hand gap) | 8-16 weeks | Wall test passes |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Prone cobra** — 2×/week, 8 reps, in warm-up
- **Avoid** chronic posterior tucking during lifts — let the lumbar curve exist
- **Early warning:** If you catch yourself standing with locked knees + tucked pelvis → 5 standing hip flexor stretches + walk with exaggerated hip extension for 2 min

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Swayback Posture.md|Swayback Posture]] (differential)*
protocols.Posture/Flexibility Continuum:
# Flexibility Continuum (NASM Framework)

*Four types of flexibility work — when to use each, why, and how*

---

## Overview

NASM's flexibility training framework organizes flexibility work into 4 types, progressing from mechanical release to full-range dynamic movement. Each type uses a different mechanism and is appropriate at different times.

```
SMR (Foam Roll) → Static Stretch → Active Stretch → Dynamic Stretch
   Inhibit            Lengthen         Activate          Integrate
```

**The ILAI framework:** Each flexibility type corresponds to one step in the corrective exercise progression (Inhibit → Lengthen → Activate → Integrate).

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## 1. Self-Myofascial Release (SMR)

| Detail | Prescription |
|--------|-------------|
| **Mechanism** | Autogenic inhibition — sustained pressure on a trigger point causes the muscle spindle to reduce its firing rate, allowing the muscle to relax |
| **When to use** | BEFORE training. **Never do SMR after training** — you want muscles primed, not inhibited, for performance |
| **Duration** | 30-90s per tender spot, 1-3 sets |
| **Tools** | Foam roller, lacrosse ball, massage stick, percussive gun |
| **Pressure** | Moderate — enough to feel release, not so much that you're bracing against it |
| **Key rule** | Breathe through the discomfort. If you hold your breath, you're too tight or too aggressive |
| **Source** | NASM Ch.14: Flexibility Training Concepts |

**When NOT to use SMR:** Acute injury (first 48h), varicose veins, fractures, open wounds, areas of numbness/tingling.

---

## 2. Static Stretching

| Detail | Prescription |
|--------|-------------|
| **Mechanism** | Decreased muscle spindle activity + increased stretch tolerance over time. Does NOT permanently lengthen the muscle — it increases your tolerance to the stretch position |
| **When to use** | AFTER training or as a standalone session. NOT before training (reduces force output for up to 1 hour) |
| **Duration** | 30s per stretch, 1-3 sets |
| **Sensation** | Mild tension, NOT sharp or burning pain |
| **Breathing** | Inhale before the stretch, exhale into it |
| **Source** | NASM Ch.14 |

**When to use in corrective context:** After SMR, before activation. For overactive/tight muscles identified in the postural assessment (e.g., pecs for rounded shoulders, hip flexors for APT).

---

## 3. Active Stretching

| Detail | Prescription |
|--------|-------------|
| **Mechanism** | Reciprocal inhibition — contracting the agonist causes the antagonist (the muscle you're stretching) to relax |
| **When to use** | During warm-up, between sets, or as part of activation work |
| **Duration** | Hold 1-2s, 5-10 reps per set, 1-3 sets |
| **Example** | Lying on back, pull one knee to chest (active: hip flexor stretches while glute contracts) |
| **Key difference from static** | You hold the stretch position by contracting the OPPOSITE muscle, not by using your hands or gravity |
| **Source** | NASM Ch.14 |

**When to use in corrective context:** After SMR and static stretching, before activation exercises. Bridges the gap between releasing a tight muscle and activating its antagonist.

---

## 4. Dynamic Stretching

| Detail | Prescription |
|--------|-------------|
| **Mechanism** | Reciprocal inhibition + momentum. Uses the force production of muscles + body momentum to take joints through full ROM |
| **When to use** | During warm-up, immediately before the working sets |
| **Duration** | 1 set, 10-15 reps, 3-10 exercises |
| **Examples** | Leg swings (forward/lateral), torso twists, cat-camel, walking lunges with rotation |
| **Key rule** | Controlled momentum. Do not use ballistic bouncing — this triggers the stretch reflex (muscle spindle) and increases injury risk |
| **Source** | NASM Ch.14 |

**When to use in corrective context:** After activation exercises, before compound lifts. Integrates the corrected movement pattern into functional ROM.

---

## Practical Application: The Flexibility Sequence

```
BEFORE TRAINING:
  1. SMR (foam roll) — 30-90s on tight areas
  2. No static stretching
  3. Active stretching — 5-10 reps on target areas
  4. Dynamic stretching — 10-15 reps per movement
  5. → Begin warm-up sets

AFTER TRAINING (or as standalone session):
  1. SMR if needed (less priority post-training)
  2. Static stretching — 30s × 2-3 sets on tight muscles
  3. No active or dynamic needed post-training
```

---

## NASM Flexibility Continuum in Corrective Context

| ILAI Step | Flexibility Type | Example (Rounded Shoulders) |
|-----------|----------------|-----------------------------|
| **Inhibit** | SMR | Lacrosse ball on pec minor, 60s |
| **Lengthen** | Static stretch | Doorway pec stretch, 30s × 2 |
| **Activate** | Active stretch | Band pull-apart (holds at end-range) |
| **Integrate** | Dynamic stretch | Arm circles progressing to wall slides |

---

## Controversial Stretches (NASM Caution)

These stretches are flagged by NASM as potentially dangerous when performed incorrectly:

| Stretch | Risk | Safe Alternative |
|---------|------|------------------|
| Standing toe touch (straight legs) | Lumbar disc stress, hamstring strain | Seated hamstring stretch with back supported |
| Hurdler's stretch | Medial knee ligament stress | Side-lying quad stretch |
| Plow pose (yoga) | Cervical spine compression | Supine knee-to-chest |
| Head circles (full neck circles) | Cervical joint stress | Chin tucks, neck CARs |

---

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Injury Management Protocol.md|Injury Management Protocol]]*
protocols.Posture/Forward Head Posture:
# Forward Head Posture — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Text neck, anterior head carriage, upper cervical extension*

---

## What It Is

The head sits forward of the shoulders (>1 inch from wall in wall test). The deep neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis) are weak and lengthened. The suboccipitals, upper traps, and levator scapulae are short and tight.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes for lifters:** Heavy deadlifts with cervical extension (looking up), prolonged desk work between sessions, poor mirror-checking posture, excessive upper trap training (shrugs, upright rows) without adequate neck flexor work.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Wall test:** Stand against wall. Can you touch the back of your head to the wall without lifting your chin? If no, you have forward head
- **Photo:** Ear is >1 inch in front of the acromion (shoulder) in side view
- **Neck flexion test:** Lying on back, try to lift head 1-2 inches with chin tucked. If you lead with your chin (SCC fires first instead of deep flexors), you have forward head compensation

---

## Red Flags

- Headache originating at the base of the skull (cervicogenic headache) that worsens
- Numbness/tingling in hands or arms — may indicate cervical nerve root compression, not just posture
- Dizziness when looking up — may be cervicogenic vertigo or vertebral artery issue
- Jaw pain or clicking (TMJ involvement may coexist with forward head)

→ Any of these → see physical therapist or sports medicine

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Suboccipitals (deep upper neck) | Deep cervical flexors (longus colli, longus capitis) |
| Upper trapezius | Lower trapezius |
| Levator scapulae | Rhomboids |
| Sternocleidomastoid (SCM) | Hyoid muscles (suprahyoid/infrahyoid) |
| Temporalis/masseter (jaw) | |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (2-3 min)

**Do these before training, daily:**

1. **Suboccipital release** — 2 lacrosse balls taped together (or one) at base of skull, lying on back, gentle nod chin toward chest, hold 60s
2. **Upper trap stretch** — Sit tall, one hand behind back, opposite ear toward shoulder, hold 30s each side
3. **Chin tuck with overpressure** — Sitting against wall, tuck chin using fingertips for added pressure, hold 5s, 5 reps
4. **SCM stretch** — Lie on back, turn head gently away from tight side, extend slightly, hold 20s each side

---

## Activation (5-7 min)

**Do these as daily corrective work (can be done anywhere, not just at gym):**

1. **Chin tucks (supine)** — Lie on back, gently tuck chin (as if making double chin), hold 5s, do NOT lift head. 3×10. **Key:** Eyes stay on ceiling, head stays on floor. Source: McGill
2. **Chin tucks (standing)** — Against wall, same movement, 3×10
3. **Dead bug (cervical)** — Lie on back, knees bent, gently press back of head into floor while keeping chin tucked, hold 10s, 3 reps
4. **Isometric neck flexor** — Lie on back, lift head 1-2 inches keeping chin tucked (neck fully flexed), hold 10s, 5 reps. Only do this after mastering chin tucks
5. **Neck CARs (controlled articular rotations)** — Slow, deliberate head rotation through full pain-free ROM, 3 circles each direction. Source: Knees Over Toes

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Deadlift:** Keep cervical spine neutral — look at a spot on the floor 6-8 ft in front of you, NOT in the mirror on the wall
- **Squat:** Same — neutral neck. Do not look up
- **Overhead press:** Brace core, keep chin tucked, do NOT jut head forward to clear the bar
- **Throughout the day:** Set a timer every 20 min → check: is your head forward? Tuck chin, align ears over shoulders. Takes 2-4 weeks of conscious reminders before it becomes automatic

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Deadlift (heavy) | Reduce weight until you can maintain neutral neck throughout | Heavy pulls encourage cervical extension |
| Shrugs (barbell) | Use dumbbells, keep chin tucked, do not look up | Barbell shrugs trigger upper trap + neck extension |
| Standing OHP | Lower the weight. Press from rack (not clean from floor) | Cleaning creates neck snapping reflex |
| Programming | Avoid all neck extension exercises temporarily | Face pulls from low pulley (keep cervical neutral) |
| Face pulls | Do NOT let head extend. Keep chin tucked throughout. | Most people extend head at end-range of face pulls |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Desk setup:** Top of monitor at eye level or slightly below. Do NOT look down at laptop screen — use a stand
- **Phone use:** Bring phone to face level. Do NOT lower head to phone. Known as "text neck" — look down with your eyes, not your neck
- **Sleeping:** Side sleepers: use a pillow that fills the gap between head and mattress without tilting the neck up. Back sleepers: thin pillow or cervical roll. Stomach sleepers: switch to side — stomach sleeping exaggerates forward head
- **Driving:** Adjust headrest so the middle of the headrest is at ear level, 2-4 inches behind head. Do not drive with head forward

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can do chin tucks without jaw compensation | 1-2 weeks | Lie on back, chin tuck — jaw should not jut forward |
| Wall test gap decreases by 0.5 inch | 4-6 weeks | Re-measure head-to-wall gap |
| Head stays neutral during deadlift | 4-8 weeks | Have someone video your deadlift from side |
| Natural standing head position improves | 8-12 weeks | Side photo — ear is closer to shoulder |
| Full correction (≤1 inch gap on wall test) | 8-16 weeks | Depends on severity and consistency |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Once corrected:** 2×/week chin tucks (supine) + neck CARs. 3 min total
- **Monthly wall test re-check**
- **Early warning sign:** Feeling like you need to look up during deadlifts → reset neck position. This is the first sign of regression

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Upper Crossed Syndrome.md|Upper Crossed Syndrome]] (if combined with rounded shoulders)*
protocols.Posture/Forward Shoulder Posture:
# Forward Shoulder Posture — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Scapular protraction, scapular winging, serratus anterior dysfunction, scapular dyskinesis*

---

## What It Is

The scapulae sit forward (protracted) and the medial borders may lift off the ribcage (winging). The pec minor is tight. The serratus anterior, middle/lower traps, and rhomboids are weak. Unlike pure "rounded shoulders" where the humerus internally rotates, this involves scapular position and control.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes:** Excessive pushing (bench press, push-ups) without adequate scapular retraction work, poor push-up form (elbows flared, scapulae not retracted), heavy backpacks, desk work, weak serratus anterior from disuse.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Scapular winging test:** Stand facing away from mirror. Can you see the medial (inner) border of your shoulder blades lifting off your ribcage? If yes, you have winging
- **Wall push-up test:** Stand facing wall, hands on wall, lean in. Do the shoulder blades wing? If yes → serratus anterior weakness
- **Posterior view:** From behind, do the shoulder blades sit outward (protracted) rather than flat against the ribcage?
- **Reach test:** Lift arms overhead. Do the scapulae rotate upward smoothly, or does the shoulder blade wing/hitch up?

---

## Red Flags

- Sharp pain under the shoulder blade during reaching — may be snapping scapula syndrome
- Numbness/tingling running down the arm — rule out thoracic outlet syndrome (pec minor tightness compressing brachial plexus)
- Shoulder pain during overhead movements — may be subacromial impingement related to scapular dyskinesis
- Scapular winging after a traumatic injury — may be long thoracic nerve injury (PT referral, do not self-treat)

→ Any of these → see physical therapist

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Pectoralis minor | Serratus anterior |
| Upper trapezius | Middle trapezius |
| Levator scapulae | Lower trapezius |
| Rhomboids (may be overactive in winging, paradoxically) | Rhomboids (in protracted position — lengthened) |
| Latissimus dorsi (can contribute to internal rotation) | Posterior deltoid |
| Anterior deltoid | Infraspinatus/teres minor |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (3-5 min)

1. **Pec minor release (lacrosse ball)** — Ball just below clavicle, between pec and shoulder. Lean into wall. 60s each side. **Key:** Breathe deeply — pec minor is an accessory breathing muscle and tightness here correlates with shallow breathing
2. **Doorway pec stretch** — Focus on the upper fibers of pec major (arm at shoulder height, slightly above). 45s each side
3. **Upper trap stretch** — Ear to shoulder, hand behind back. 30s each side
4. **Levator scapulae stretch** — Ear to shoulder, then rotate chin toward armpit of same side (gaze toward armpit). 30s each side

---

## Activation (5-7 min)

1. **Serratus anterior punch** — Lie on back holding a light dumbbell (2-5 lb) in one hand. Punch the weight straight up toward the ceiling while keeping the shoulder blade on the ribcage. At the top, protract the scapula (reach further). 3×10 each side. **Key:** The scapula should move — the arm is just along for the ride. **Source:** NASM CEX framework
2. **Wall slide with protraction emphasis** — Stand against wall, arms in goal post. Slide arms up while pressing them into the wall. At top, push hands slightly forward off the wall (scapular protraction). 2×8
3. **Prone Y-T-W-L** — On floor or incline bench. Emphasize scapular retraction AND depression (shoulder blades go back AND down). 8 reps each position
4. **Band pull-apart with pause** — At chest height, pull band apart, squeeze shoulder blades, hold 3s. 3×10
5. **Four-point serratus punch** — On hands and knees, push the floor away from you (protract scapulae) without moving the spine. Hold 2s. 3×10

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Push-ups:** Focus on protracting the scapulae at the top (push the floor away). Do NOT let the scapulae wing during the movement. If you can't control scapular position, do incline push-ups until you can
- **Bench press:** Before each rep, retract shoulder blades and pull them DOWN. Touch lower on sternum. At lockout, do NOT protract excessively — keep scapulae stable
- **Rows:** Emphasize scapular retraction and depression. Drive elbows back, squeeze blades together
- **Overhead work:** Before any overhead press, practice "packing the shoulder" — pull the shoulder blade down and back. If scapular control overhead is poor, do presses in the scapular plane (slightly in front of the body, not pure lateral raise or OHP)

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Heavy bench press (flat) | Reduce weight, add pause at bottom, maintain scapular retraction | Heavy bench with forward shoulders = shoulder pathology risk |
| Dips | Use assisted or reduce depth | Deep dips at end-range with winging = extreme stress on AC joint |
| Upright rows | Eliminate | High impingement risk with forward scapulae |
| Overhead press (barbell) | Switch to dumbbell or landmine press | Allows natural scapular movement, doesn't force a fixed bar path |
| Lateral raises (dumbbell) | Cable lateral raise (better tension curve) | Dumbbell lateral raises often done with shrugged scapulae — reinforces upper trap dominance |
| Push-ups (full ROM, flared elbows) | Incline push-ups with elbows at 45° | Full push-ups with forward shoulders = scapular winging at top |

**Programming note:** Increase pulling volume to 2-3× pressing volume during active correction. Add serratus anterior work to EVERY session.

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Desk posture:** Set shoulders back and DOWN. Imagine holding a pencil between your shoulder blades. Check every 20 min
- **Walking:** Arms should swing with palms facing thighs, not backward. Keep shoulders relaxed (not shrugged)
- **Carrying:** When carrying bags (groceries, backpack), consciously pull shoulders back. Unilateral carrying (suitcase) can increase scapular asymmetry — alternate sides
- **Phone:** Bring to face level, not down. Forward shoulder + forward head = scapular winging worsens

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can protract scapulae on command without winging | 1-2 weeks | Serratus punch test — scapula stays on ribcage |
| Wall push-up test — no winging | 4-6 weeks | Hands on wall, lean in — scapulae stay flat |
| Scapulae sit flat against ribcage at rest | 4-8 weeks | Posterior photo check — are medial borders visible? |
| Overhead press without hitching | 8-12 weeks | Video from behind — scapulae should move smoothly |
| Full correction (flat scapulae at rest + no winging) | 8-16 weeks | Posterior view + wall push-up test both pass |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Serratus punches** — 2×/week as warm-up, 3×10 each side (forever for overhead athletes)
- **Band pull-aparts** — 2×/week, 3×10 in warm-up
- **Monthly posterior photo check** — if scapular winging re-appears, add 1 week of daily serratus activation
- **Early warning:** First sign of regression is scapular elevation during pressing (shoulders shrug up toward ears) → regress to wall slides + serratus punches for 1-2 sessions

---

protocols.Posture/Kyphosis:
# Kyphosis — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Hyperkyphosis, thoracic hyperkyphosis, "hunchback" posture, upper cross kyphotic component*

---

## What It Is

An excessive thoracic curve, creating a hunched upper back. The thoracic erectors are lengthened/weak; the pectorals, anterior chain, and suboccipitals are tight. Kyphosis involves the SPINE (thoracic vertebrae), not just scapular position.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes:** Prolonged sitting without upper back support, excessive pressing without thoracic mobility work, poor overhead position in squats and presses, age-related changes.

**Relation:** Often coexists with forward head and rounded shoulders (full UCS triad).

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Thoracic extension test:** Stand against wall, butt and shoulders touching. Hands behind head. Try to touch elbows to the wall. Elbows stay forward = limited extension
- **Wall test (upper back):** Stand against wall — does your mid-upper back touch the wall?
- **Photo:** Side view — increased upper spine curvature
- **Flexibility test:** Lie on back on the floor without pillows. Does your head touch the floor?

---

## Red Flags

- Sharp mid-back pain with deep breathing (costovertebral joint dysfunction)
- Difficulty swallowing (severe kyphosis can compress esophagus)
- Rapid onset (>20° increase in <6 months) — may be Scheuermann's or compression fracture

→ Any of these → physical therapist or orthopedic specialist

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Pectoralis major/minor | Thoracic erector spinae |
| Upper trapezius | Lower trapezius |
| Levator scapulae | Rhomboids |
| Suboccipitals | Serratus anterior |
| Anterior deltoid | Scapular retractors |
| Anterior intercostals | Posterior intercostals |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (5-8 min)

1. **Thoracic extension over foam roller** — Roller perpendicular at mid-thoracic (between shoulder blades). Arms behind head, extend backward over roller. 10 reps. **Source:** McGill
2. **Doorway pec stretch** — 45s each side, ribs down
3. **Thoracic rotation (open book)** — Lie on side, arms out. Rotate top arm behind you. 8 reps each
4. **Supine breathing into back** — Towel roll under thoracic spine, breathe into the restriction. 10 breaths

---

## Activation (7-10 min)

1. **Prone cobra / upper back extension** — Face down, arms at sides, thumbs up. Lift chest slightly, squeeze shoulder blades DOWN and together. Hold 3s. 3×8. No neck extension
2. **Prone Y-T-W-L** — 8 reps each, 2-3 lb DBs
3. **Band pull-aparts (chest height, pause 3s)** — 3×10
4. **Wall slides (overhead)** — Arms against wall, slide into partial squat while maintaining contact. 2×8
5. **Cat-camel (thoracic focus)** — One vertebra at a time. 10 reps
6. **Supine elbow prop** — Lie on back, prop on elbows, let thoracic extend. 30-60s

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Squat:** Use front squat grip (clean or crossed arms) — forces thoracic extension. Back squat with narrow grip also helps
- **Overhead press:** Dumbbell press with neutral grip allows better thoracic position than barbell. File away the cue "proud chest, ribs down"
- **Rows:** Chest-supported rows prevent thoracic rounding better than bent-over rows. If doing bent-over rows, keep chest up
- **Deadlift:** Set the lats before pulling. "Put your shoulder blades in your back pockets." Keep chest up

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Barbell row (bent-over) | Chest-supported row, seated cable row | Bent-over row reinforces kyphotic position |
| Barbell back squat (low bar) | Front squat, goblet squat | Front squat forces upright torso |
| Standing OHP (barbell) | Seated dumbbell press (neutral grip) | Allows better thoracic position |
| Good mornings | RDL variations | Good mornings load the thoracic spine in flexion |
| Heavy deadlift (conventional) | Trap bar deadlift (reduces thoracic demand) | Trap bar allows more upright torso |
| Behind-the-neck press | Landmine press, incline press | Behind-neck press at kyphotic end-range = risk |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Desk:** Monitor at eye level. Set chair back angle to 100-110° (slightly reclined) — reduces the tendency to round forward. Every 20 min: roll shoulders back and squeeze blades together
- **Phone:** Bring to face level
- **Sleeping:** Back sleepers — thin pillow or cervical roll. Side sleepers — pillow thickness should fill the ear-shoulder gap without tilting the head
- **Standing:** "Proud chest" position — imagine a string pulling your sternum up and forward
- **Breathing:** Practice 3D breathing (ribcage expands 360°) throughout the day. Kyphosis restricts posterior rib expansion

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Elbows closer to wall in extension test | 4-6 weeks | Re-test thoracic extension |
| Can do wall slides with full contact | 4-8 weeks | Arms stay on wall |
| Mid-back touches wall in wall test | 8-12 weeks | Upper back contact |
| Head touches floor lying supine without pillow | 8-16 weeks | Supine head test |
| Visible curve reduction in side photo | 12+ weeks | Photo comparison |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Thoracic extension (foam roller)** — 2×/week, 10 reps
- **Band pull-aparts** — 2×/week, 3×10 (in warm-up, forever)
- **Open book rotations** — 2×/week, 8 each side
- **Monthly thoracic extension test re-check**
- **Early warning:** If you catch yourself hunching over your phone more than 3 days in a row → 5 min of thoracic extension work the next morning

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Upper Crossed Syndrome.md|Upper Crossed Syndrome]] (if combined with FHP + rounded shoulders)*
protocols.Posture/Lower Crossed Syndrome:
# Lower Crossed Syndrome — Correction Protocol

*Combined protocol for anterior pelvic tilt + weak glutes + weak core + tight hip flexors*

---

## What It Is

Lower Crossed Syndrome (Janda) is a common postural dysfunction in lifters and sedentary individuals. It combines:
- Anterior pelvic tilt (tight hip flexors, tight lumbar erectors)
- Weak/long gluteus maximus and medius
- Weak/long deep abdominals (transversus abdominis, internal obliques)
- Often: hamstring tightness (as a compensation for weak glutes)

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes:** Prolonged sitting shortens hip flexors. Inadequate glute activation in training (quad-dominant programs). Poor bracing technique (belly breathing instead of 360° bracing). Deadlifting with lumbar hyperextension.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

You have LCS if **both** of these are true:
1. **APT:** Wall test — low back gap >hand thickness
2. **Weak glutes:** You cannot perform a glute bridge with full glute squeeze (hamstrings take over), OR glutes feel "asleep" during squats/deadlifts

Additionally check:
- **Belly protrudes forward** even when standing relaxed (poor core tension)
- **Thomas test positive** (hip flexor tightness)
- **Trendelenburg sign:** Standing on one leg, the opposite hip drops — indicates glute med weakness

---

## Red Flags

- Same as [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Anterior Pelvic Tilt.md#red-flags\|APT red flags]]
- Knee pain (patellofemoral) that doesn't resolve — LCS causes quad dominance, which loads the patellofemoral joint
- SI joint pain that persists through this protocol — may require professional manual therapy

→ Any of these → see physical therapist

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Iliopsoas | Gluteus maximus |
| Rectus femoris | Gluteus medius |
| TFL | Transversus abdominis |
| Lumbar erectors | Internal obliques |
| Thoracolumbar fascia | Hamstrings (often inhibited, may present as tight) |
| Adductors (can be tight) | Pelvic floor |
| Quadratus lumborum (can contribute) | Multifidus |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (5-8 min)

1. **Kneeling hip flexor stretch** — 45s each side. Squeeze glute on the back leg. Keep ribs down
2. **Psoas release (lacrosse ball)** — Lying face down, ball in hip flexor area. 60-90s each side
3. **Lateral hip/TFL release (foam roller or ball)** — Side of hip, just below the iliac crest. Roll slowly. 60s each side
4. **Quad stretch (side-lying)** — 30s each side
5. **Glute release (lacrosse ball)** — Any tender spots in glutes. 60s each side
6. **Child's pose** — 45s. Breathe into the back of the ribcage

---

## Activation (7-10 min)

**Daily corrective sequence (do in this order):**

1. **Glute bridge with posterior tilt** — Lie on back, squeeze glutes FIRST, then tuck pelvis, then lift. Hold 2s at top. 3×15. **Key:** If you can't feel glutes, add a band above the knees
2. **Prone hip extension (glute focus)** — Lying face down, squeeze glute, raise leg 4-6 inches off floor, hold 2s. Do NOT arch back. 3×10 each side
3. **Dead bug** — Hold low back flat. Slowly extend opposite arm/leg. 3×8 each side
4. **Side-lying clamshell** — Band above knees, keep feet together, lift top knee. 3×15 each side
5. **Side plank (from knees, progress to feet)** — Hold side plank with hips stacked. No sagging. 3×20-30s each side
6. **Single-leg balance** — Stand on one leg, maintain level hips for 30s. Progress to eyes closed. 3 reps each side

**Total time:** 7-10 min. Do as part of warm-up.

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Squat:** Focus on "spread the floor" (glute activation cue) on the ascent. Do not let knees cave in. Use a moderate stance (not too wide)
- **Deadlift:** Set the back by "showing the wall your belt buckle" — subtle posterior tilt. Do not hyperextend at lockout
- **Hip thrust:** Primary glute builder. Emphasize squeeze at top. Do not hyperextend lumbar
- **Walking lunges:** Keep torso upright. Do not let front knee travel past toe excessively
- **Core bracing:** 360° expansion into the belt, not sucking in. Brace each rep

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Heavy back squat (low bar) | Front squat or goblet squat | Front squat forces upright torso, less lumbar extension demand |
| Conventional deadlift (heavy) | Trap bar deadlift (mid-thigh pull) | Trap bar reduces lumbar lever arm |
| Leg press (high foot position) | Hip thrust, Bulgarian split squat | Leg press doesn't load glutes in the way a hip hinge does |
| Back extension (hyperextension) | 45° back extension, stop at neutral | Full extension reinforces lumbar overactivity |
| Ab exercises (sit-ups, crunches) | Dead bugs, Pallof press | Sit-ups are hip flexor dominant, reinforce APT |
| Standing calf raises | Seated calf raises | Standing calf raise requires core stability (harder with weak core) |

**Training volume adjustment:** During active correction, consider reducing total squat/deadlift volume by 30% and replacing it with hip-dominant work (hip thrust, RDL, glute bridge). Do this until glute activation becomes automatic.

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Standing:** Practice glute squeeze while waiting in line or standing. 10s holds, multiple times per day
- **Sitting:** Sit on sit bones (ischial tuberosities), not tailbone. Do not let pelvis roll into APT while sitting
- **Stairs:** Take stairs two at a time — forces hip extension and glute activation
- **Walking:** Squeeze glute at the end of each push-off. Walk as if you're showing someone your glutes work
- **Posture cue:** "Zip up the front" (imagine zipping from pubic bone to sternum — posterior tilt + tall spine)

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can feel glutes during bridges (not hamstrings) | 1-2 weeks | Place hands on glutes during bridge — should feel contraction before hamstrings |
| Low back flat on floor in supine test | 2-4 weeks | Lie on back — no arch |
| Thomas test — thigh drops toward floor | 4-6 weeks | Re-test Thomas test |
| Wall test gap decreases by 0.5 hand | 4-8 weeks | Re-measure lumbar gap |
| Squat feels "glute-dominant" | 6-12 weeks | You feel glutes on every rep without thinking about it |
| Full correction (hand gap) | 8-16 weeks | Wall test — lumbar gap |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Glute bridge** — 2×/week as warm-up (always after sitting for long periods)
- **Dead bug** — 2×/week, 3×8 each side
- **Side-lying clamshell** — 2×/week, 3×15 each side
- **Trap bar deadlift** — consider this your primary hinge variation permanently if LCS is recurrent
- **Early warning sign:** When you sit for 60+ min and stand up, if your glutes feel "asleep" → 10 glute bridges. If they still feel asleep after 10 → do the full activation sequence next warm-up

---
