protocols.Posture/Posture Correction Hub:
# Posture Correction Hub

*Central reference for all posture correction protocols*

---

## Why It Matters

Posture directly affects lifting performance:

- **Breathing:** Forward head and kyphosis restrict the diaphragm → weaker Valsalva → less core stability under heavy loads
- **Shoulder health:** Rounded shoulders narrow the subacromial space → impingement risk during any overhead or pressing movement
- **Hip mechanics:** APT lengthens the glutes and shortens the hip flexors → reduced hip drive in squats and deadlifts
- **Force transfer:** Every postural deviation creates compensation somewhere in the kinetic chain — force leaks that reduce your working weight

**Bottom line:** Correcting posture is not a separate program. It is prehab for your main lifts. You can (and should) do both simultaneously.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## The Corrective Hierarchy (NASM ILAI Framework)

Every protocol follows the NASM ILAI progression: **Inhibit → Lengthen → Activate → Integrate**

```
Step 1: INHIBIT (reduce overactive tissue)
   └─ Self-myofascial release (foam rolling, lacrosse ball)
   └─ 30-90s per area, before training
   └─ Mechanism: autogenic inhibition (Golgi tendon organ response)
   │
Step 2: LENGTHEN (increase ROM of tight tissue)
   └─ Static stretching of overactive muscles
   └─ 30s × 2-3 sets, after SMR but before activation
   └─ Mechanism: increased stretch tolerance via muscle spindle adaptation
   │
Step 3: ACTIVATE (wake up underactive tissue)
   └─ Isolation exercises, isometrics, low-load corrective work
   └─ Part of warm-up (5-7 min)
   └─ Mechanism: reciprocal inhibition + neuromuscular re-education
   │
Step 4: INTEGRATE (use during compound lifts)
   └─ Maintain corrected posture during squats, presses, rows
   └─ Reduce load if you cannot maintain position
   │
MAINTENANCE (prehab)
   └─ 2×/week corrective drills once posture is normal
   └─ Re-test monthly
```

**Do not skip steps.** Inhibiting (foam rolling) without lengthening (stretching) leaves the muscle short — it will tighten back between sessions. Lengthening without activating creates temporary ROM gain that the nervous system won't use. Activating without integrating creates "gym-only posture."

For detailed flexibility protocols, see: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Flexibility Continuum.md|Flexibility Continuum]]

---

## Timeline Expectations

| Phase | Duration | What Changes |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Conscious correction | 2-4 weeks | You remember to fix posture when you think about it. Gap measurements may not change yet. |
| Motor pattern change | 4-8 weeks | Posture holds naturally during daily activities. First measurable gap changes appear. |
| Structural adaptation | 8-12+ weeks | Tissue length begins to change. Gap measurements decrease. Muscle balance shifts. |
| Maintenance | Ongoing | 2×/week drills prevent regression. Monthly photo check. |

**Do not test daily.** Posture fluctuates with hydration, fatigue, and time of day. Re-photo every 4 weeks. Look for trends, not single measurements.

---

## When to Prioritize Posture vs. Training

| Situation | Priority | Action |
|-----------|----------|--------|
| Posture causes pain during lifts | Posture FIRST | Use [[03_ASSESSMENTS/Posture Assessment System.md\|Assessment]] to identify cause. Reduce load on painful exercises. Follow corrective protocol. |
| Posture deviates but no pain | Training continues | Add corrective work to warm-up. Continue training. Re-check in 4 weeks. |
| Posture deviates + limiting ROM (can't squat depth, can't press overhead) | Posture FIRST | The deviation is reducing training effectiveness. Correct it before adding more load. |
| Posture improving, no complaints | Training focus | 2×/week maintenance only. Focus on performance. |

---

## Your Posture Plan

**How to choose what to fix when:**

1. [[03_ASSESSMENTS/Posture Assessment System.md\|Assess yourself]] → identify primary deviation
2. [[04_TOOLS/Decision Trees/Posture Diagnostic Tree.md\|Diagnose]] → which protocol(s)
3. **Pick ONE deviation** → focus corrective work there for 4-6 weeks
4. Add 10-15 min of corrective work to your daily warm-up
5. Re-photo + re-measure at 4-week mark
6. If progress visible → continue. If not → re-check technique on your corrective exercises
7. When deviation moves from Moderate → Mild, switch focus to next deviation

**Multiple deviations?** Fix pelvis first, then thoracic, then shoulders, then head — in that order. Lower Crossed Syndrome and Upper Crossed Syndrome protocols already structure this for you.

---

## Protocol Index

| Deviation | Protocol | Corrective Focus | Typical Duration |
|-----------|----------|-----------------|------------------|
| **Pelvis Level** | | | |
| Anterior Pelvic Tilt | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Anterior Pelvic Tilt.md\|APT]]| Hip flexor release + glute/core activation | 4-8 weeks |
| Lower Crossed Syndrome | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Lower Crossed Syndrome.md\|LCS]] | Hip flexor release + glute/core + deep ab activation | 6-12 weeks |
| Flat Back Posture | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Flat Back Posture.md\|Flat Back]] | Hamstring release + hip flexor activation + lumbar mobility | 6-10 weeks |
| Swayback Posture | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Swayback Posture.md\|Swayback]] | Hip flexor release + core stabilization + hip shift correction | 6-10 weeks |
| **Thoracic Level** | | | |
| Kyphosis | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Kyphosis.md\|Kyphosis]] | Pec release + thoracic extension + deep neck flexor activation | 8-12+ weeks |
| **Shoulder + Head Level** | | | |
| Upper Crossed Syndrome | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Upper Crossed Syndrome.md\|UCS]] | Pec/upper trap release + rhomboid/lower trap + DNF activation | 6-12 weeks |
| Rounded Shoulders | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Rounded Shoulders.md\|Rounded Shoulders]] | Pec release + mid-trap/rhomboid activation | 4-8 weeks |
| Forward Shoulder Posture | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Forward Shoulder Posture.md\|Forward Shoulder]] | Pec minor release + serratus anterior activation + scapular control | 4-8 weeks |
| Forward Head Posture | [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Forward Head Posture.md\|Forward Head]] | Upper trap/suboccipital release + DNF activation + chin tucks | 4-8 weeks |

---

## Nutrition Note

Posture correction requires tissue adaptation (muscle length change, tendon remodeling, fascia hydration). These factors support it:

- **Protein:** 1.6-2.2 g/kg — muscles need substrate to adapt
- **Hydration:** Connective tissue hydration affects tissue pliability. Adequate water intake (3-4L/day) supports stretching effectiveness
- **Sleep:** Tissue adaptation happens during sleep. Poor sleep = slower postural changes
- **Magnesium:** Supports muscle relaxation. Deficiency can increase resting muscle tone (tightness)

These are supportive, not primary. The corrective exercises do the work — nutrition just enables it to happen faster.

---

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

protocols.Posture/Rounded Shoulders:
# Rounded Shoulders — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Forward shoulders (mild), internally rotated shoulders, upper cross tightness (isolated)*

---

## What It Is

The shoulders sit forward of the mid-ribcage. The pectoralis major/minor and anterior deltoid are short/tight. The rhomboids, mid/lower traps, and posterior deltoid are long/weak. This reduces subacromial space during pressing and increases impingement risk.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes for lifters:** Excessive bench pressing relative to pulling, low row volume, desk work with shoulders rolled forward, poor scapular control during pushing.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Wall test:** Stand against wall. Can you touch the back of your shoulders to the wall? If no, you have rounded shoulders
- **Photo:** Side view — does the shoulder sit in front of the ribcage?
- **Arm hang test:** Stand relaxed. Palms should face your thighs (neutral). If palms face backward (internal rotation), your shoulders are rounded
- **Supine test:** Lie on back, arms at sides. Do your thumbs point up (supination) or toward each other (neutral)? Neutral = normal. Thumbs pointing toward ceiling = internal rotation

---

## Red Flags

- Sharp shoulder pain during pressing — may be impingement or rotator cuff, not just posture
- Clicking/pain with arm overhead — rule out subacromial impingement or labral pathology
- Numbness down the arm into the pinky/ring finger — may be ulnar nerve entrapment at thoracic outlet, not just posture

→ Any of these → see physical therapist first, then return to this protocol

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Pectoralis major (clavicular and sternal) | Rhomboids (major and minor) |
| Pectoralis minor | Middle trapezius |
| Anterior deltoid | Lower trapezius |
| Upper trapezius | Posterior deltoid |
| Biceps brachii (long head) | Serratus anterior |
| Latissimus dorsi (can contribute) | Infraspinatus/teres minor (external rotators) |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (3-5 min)

1. **Pec major stretch (doorway)** — Forearm on door frame, gently rotate body away. Keep ribs down (don't let ribcage flare). 30-45s each side
2. **Pec minor release (lacrosse ball)** — Ball just below clavicle, between pec and shoulder. Lean into wall, small circles. 60s each side. **Key:** Breathe — pec minor tightness often correlates with shallow breathing
3. **Anterior delt stretch** — Arm behind back, gentle extension. Keep chest down. 30s each side
4. **Lat stretch** — Kneeling, arms overhead, lean to one side. 30s each side (if lat is contributing)

---

## Activation (5-7 min)

1. **Wall slides** — Stand against wall, arms in "goal post" position (elbows 90°, upper arms against wall). Slide arms up overhead while maintaining contact with wall — elbows, wrists, and back of hands stay against wall. 2×8. **Key:** If your lower back arches during this, you're compensating with lumbar extension. Keep ribs down
2. **Prone Y-T-W-L** — Lying face down on floor or incline bench, thumbs up:
   - Y (arms overhead at 30° angle): squeeze shoulder blades together. 8 reps
   - T (arms out to sides at 90°): squeeze shoulder blades. 8 reps
   - W (elbows bent, arms at sides at 45°): squeeze shoulder blades DOWN. 8 reps
   - L (elbows bent 90°, arms at sides, rotate forearms up): 8 reps **Source:** Elite Sports Medicine
3. **Band pull-aparts** — Hold band in front of chest at shoulder height, arms straight. Pull band apart, squeeze shoulder blades together. Pause 2s. 3×12
4. **External rotation (side-lying)** — Lie on side, elbow bent 90° at ribs. Rotate forearm up to ceiling. 3×12 each. Use light band or dumbbell (2-5 lb)

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Pressing:** Focus on "bending the bar" (external rotation torque) during bench press. Touch lower on sternum (not high on chest). On every press, feel the shoulder blades stay packed
- **Rows:** Emphasize rowing to the hip (low row) rather than face pulls only. Drive elbows back, squeeze at end-range. 2:1 pulling-to-pressing ratio during correction
- **Lateral raises:** Do NOT let the shoulders roll forward at the top. Keep shoulder blades slightly retracted
- **Standing posture:** Rotate palms forward (supination) to externally rotate shoulders. This is the "proud chest" position — hold it during standing rest, not just during sets

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Barbell bench press (flat) | Reduce weight, add 2-second pause at bottom, focus on scapular retraction | Wide grip + heavy press = maximum internal rotation demand |
| Incline press (barbell) | Switch to dumbbell incline press | Dumbbells allow neutral grip and natural shoulder arc |
| Upright rows | Eliminate entirely during correction | Upright rows = worst for internally rotated shoulders |
| Dips (deep) | Reduce depth or use assisted. Keep elbows in (not flared) | Deep dips at full internal rotation compress the supraspinatus |
| Front raises | Minimize or use cable (low pulley) with palms up | Front raises with internal grip reinforce the pattern |

**Pulling-to-pressing ratio:** Increase to 2:1 or 3:1 during correction (more pulling than pressing). This is temporary until posture normalizes.

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Desk posture:** Sit with shoulders back. Set a visual cue (sticky note: "shoulders back"). Every time you read it, roll shoulders back and squeeze blades together for 3s
- **Car:** Hands at 9-and-3 on the steering wheel (not top). Keep shoulders back against the seat. Palms up on thighs when resting
- **Sleeping:** Side sleepers: avoid curling into a fetal position — this rolls the shoulders forward. Use a pillow between arms to keep shoulders stacked
- **Walking:** Palms facing forward (thumb toward front), not backward. Eliminates the "ape walk" that reinforces internal rotation

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Palms face thighs (not backward) at rest | 2-4 weeks | Relaxed standing arm hang check |
| Shoulders touch wall in wall test | 4-8 weeks | Wall test for shoulder contact |
| Wall slides with full arm contact | 4-8 weeks | Arms should stay on wall during entire slide |
| No internal rotation compensation during pressing | 4-8 weeks | Video your bench from front — elbows shouldn't flare excessively |
| Full correction (shoulders touch wall, palms neutral) | 8-12 weeks | Wall test + arm hang test both pass |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Once corrected:** Keep pulling-to-pressing ratio at 1.5:1 permanently
- **Band pull-aparts** 2×/week (3×10-15) in warm-up for life — high compliance, high effect
- **Wall slides** — 1×/week as a form check. If you can't do them with full arm contact anymore, you're regressing
- **Monthly wall test** — 30s check

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Upper Crossed Syndrome.md|Upper Crossed Syndrome]] (if combined with forward head), [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Forward Shoulder Posture.md|Forward Shoulder Posture]] (if scapular winging)*
protocols.Posture/Swayback Posture:
# Swayback Posture — Correction Protocol

*Also applies to: Hip-forward posture, "slouch" posture, pelvic sway, sway stance*

---

## What It Is

The hips shift forward of the ankles (greater trochanter is anterior to lateral malleolus). The upper torso leans backward to compensate. The result is a C-shaped curve: head forward → upper back flat → pelvis forward → lower back appears flat or slightly flexed.

Swayback is distinct from APT. In APT the pelvis is tilted anteriorly. In swayback the pelvis is shifted forward and may be in neutral or even posterior tilt. The key feature is the forward hip position relative to the ankles.

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes for lifters:** Standing with weight shifted onto one leg (habituated "relaxed stance"), tight hip flexors pulling the pelvis forward, weak core unable to stabilize neutral pelvis, poor standing posture habits, prolonged standing on hard surfaces without micro-movement.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

- **Side photo:** Draw a vertical line from the lateral malleolus (ankle bone). The greater trochanter (hip bone) should be directly above or slightly behind this line. In swayback, the hip is clearly forward of the ankle
- **Plumb line:** From the ear — the line should pass through the shoulder, through the hip, slightly behind the patella, and in front of the lateral malleolus. In swayback, the ear is forward, the hip is forward, and the line hits behind the knee
- **Standing feel:** You feel like you're "sitting into your hips" while standing
- **Check:** Stand with your back against a wall. Your heels should be 4-6 inches from the wall. In swayback, you may need to move your heels closer to the wall to feel stable

---

## Red Flags

- Low back pain that worsens with prolonged standing (typical of swayback — the lumbar spine is in flexion, which loads the discs asymmetrically)
- SI joint pain — common with swayback due to the forward-shifted pelvis
- Pain that improves when you sit down or lean against a wall

→ Persistent pain → see physical therapist. Swayback responds well to manual therapy + activation correction, but self-correction may be slow if structural.

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Iliopsoas (hip flexors) — short and pulling pelvis forward | Core stabilizers (transversus abdominis, obliques) |
| Thoracic erectors (upper back works to pull the torso back) | Hip extensors (glute max, hamstrings) — long and weak |
| Upper trapezius / levator (head forward compensation) | Lower trapezius |
| Hamstrings (may be short if pelvis is in posterior tilt) | Anterior tibialis (can be weak, leading to poor balance) |
| Quadratus lumborum (may be tight on one side) | Deep neck flexors |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

**Key distinction from APT:** In APT the pelvis is tilted forward. In swayback the pelvis is shifted forward but may be neutral or posterior-tilted. The hamstrings are often tight in swayback (they're pulling the pelvis posteriorly against the forward shift).

---

## Release (5-8 min)

1. **Kneeling hip flexor stretch** — 45s each side. Squeeze glute on the back leg. This is crucial for swayback
2. **Quadratus lumborum release (lacrosse ball)** — Side-lying, ball between hip bone and lowest rib. Find the tender spot, breathe. 60s each side
3. **Hamstring stretch (gentle)** — Lying on back, belt or strap around foot. Straight leg raise to mild tension. 30s each side. Do NOT overstretch — hamstrings are already under tension in swayback
4. **Thoracic extension (foam roller)** — Roller at mid-thoracic, arms behind head, extend backward. 10 reps. The upper back is working too hard in swayback — release it
5. **Standing hip circles** — Hands on hips, slow circles, find the range. 10 circles each direction

---

## Activation (7-10 min)

1. **Forward weight shift with core brace** — Standing, shift weight forward onto balls of feet, engage core (brace like you're about to be punched), then shift back to center while keeping core engaged. Do NOT let hips slide forward. 3×10
2. **Supine marching with core brace** — Lie on back, knees bent, low back flat. Lift one knee to 90° while keeping low back pressed into floor. 3×10 each side. If low back arches, regress
3. **Glute bridge with posterior tilt** — Squeeze glutes, tuck pelvis, lift. Hold 2s. 3×15. **Key:** The glute squeeze is the most important cue — swayback patients often have glute amnesia
4. **Single-leg balance (ankle focus)** — Stand on one leg, keep hips level, feel the weight on the WHOLE foot (not just heels). 30s each, 3 reps
5. **Heel-elevated squat (cosack squat variation)** — Stand with heels on a small plate, squat to depth, knees track over toes. 3×8. The heel elevation shifts weight forward, training the body out of the swayback position
6. **Walking with intentional hip extension** — Walk slowly, exaggerating the hip extension at the end of each stride. "Push off from the big toe." 20 steps

---

## Integration (during training)

- **Squat:** Focus on keeping the shins relatively vertical and the hips back (like sitting into a chair). Do NOT let the knees travel excessively forward — this reinforces the forward-hip pattern
- **Deadlift:** In swayback, the deadlift start position is challenging. Use trap bar deadlift to allow more upright torso. Cue: "sit back into your hips, feel the hamstrings load"
- **Standing:** Practice the "tripod foot" (weight on heel, big toe, and pinky toe). Most people with swayback carry weight on their heels. Shift weight forward
- **Overhead press:** Brace core before pressing. Swayback causes a "false core" (lax core, the upper back compensates). Fix the core engagement first

---

## Training Modifications

| Exercise | Modification During Correction | Reason |
|----------|-------------------------------|--------|
| Conventional deadlift | Trap bar deadlift, RDL | Trap bar allows upright torso position |
| Back squat (low bar) | Front squat, goblet squat | Front squat forces weight shift toward mid-foot |
| Standing OHP (heavy) | Seated dumbbell press | Reduces core demand while you're rebuilding core stability |
| Walking lunges (stationary) | Reverse lunges (controlled) | Reverse lunge trains hip extension without forward drift |
| Calf raises (standing) | Seated calf raises | Swayback patients tend to be heel-heavy. Standing calf raises may be hard due to balance |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Standing posture:** Practice the "tripod" foot (heel, big toe, pinky toe all grounded). Slight forward weight shift. Knees soft, not locked. Core braced 10-20% — not relaxed
- **Walking:** Push off from the big toe. The hip extension phase of walking is weak in swayback — exaggerate it
- **Sitting:** Sit on sit bones, not tailbone. Avoid crossing legs (reinforces pelvic asymmetry). Do NOT sit in a slouched C-curve
- **Desk:** Reclined chair position (100-110°) helps. Use lumbar roll. Avoid leaning forward to see the screen — move the screen closer instead
- **Posture cue:** "Stand tall. Forward hips. No — bring hips back under you. Feel weight on the whole foot."

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can feel weight on whole foot (not just heels) | 1-2 weeks | Stand with eyes closed — can you feel forefoot contact? |
| Glutes fire during walking (you feel the push-off) | 2-4 weeks | Walk slowly and pay attention to hip extension |
| Hips closer to ankle in side photo | 4-8 weeks | Re-photo from side. Measure hip-to-ankle horizontal distance |
| Standing feels stable without "sitting into hips" | 4-8 weeks | Self-reported standing comfort |
| Better upright posture without conscious effort | 8-12 weeks | 10 min of standing conversation — check at end |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Daily 1 min "tripod foot" check** — stand on both feet, feel three points, shift weight slightly forward. Do this every time you brush your teeth
- **Glute bridge** — 2×/week, 3×15
- **Forward weight shift drill** — 2×/week, 3×10
- **Early warning sign:** You catch yourself standing with weight on one hip, the other knee locked → reset tripod foot and shift weight forward

---

*Links to: [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Posture Correction Hub.md|Posture Correction Hub]], [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Anterior Pelvic Tilt.md|Anterior Pelvic Tilt]] (differential), [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Flat Back Posture.md|Flat Back Posture]] (differential)*
protocols.Posture/Upper Crossed Syndrome:
# Upper Crossed Syndrome — Correction Protocol

*Combined protocol for forward head posture + rounded shoulders + upper back tightness*

---

## What It Is

Upper Crossed Syndrome (Janda) is the most common postural dysfunction in lifters. It combines:
- Forward head posture (weak deep cervical flexors)
- Rounded shoulders / internally rotated shoulders (tight pecs, weak rhomboids)
- Thoracic kyphosis (tight upper back, weak lower traps)
- Sometimes: scapular winging (weak serratus anterior)

See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]] for joint subtype details.

**Common causes:** Excessive pressing, insufficient pulling, desk work, phone use, looking up during deadlifts, poor thoracic mobility.

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 6-7]] (bone markings) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 10]] (muscle origin/insertion/action) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] (exercise technique, movement correction) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/ACE - Personal Trainer Manual/04 Decision Rules.md\|ACE BC-01, COM-02]] (behavior change, habit formation)

---

## Self-Check

You have UCS if **both** of these are true:
1. **Forward head:** Ear >1 inch in front of acromion (wall test gap >1 inch)
2. **Rounded shoulders:** Shoulders don't touch wall in wall test, OR palms face backward at rest

Additionally check:
- Thoracic extension test: stand against wall, hands behind head, try to touch elbows to wall. If elbows stay forward → kyphosis component
- Scapular winging: from behind, do the medial borders of your shoulder blades lift off the ribcage?

---

## Red Flags

- Same as individual protocols. See [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Forward Head Posture.md#red-flags\|Forward Head red flags]] and [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Rounded Shoulders.md#red-flags\|Rounded Shoulders red flags]]
- Additionally: bilateral arm numbness/tingling — thoracic outlet syndrome may require professional evaluation

---

## Muscle Balance

| Overactive/Tight | Underactive/Weak |
|-----------------|------------------|
| Upper trapezius | Deep cervical flexors (longus colli, longus capitis) |
| Levator scapulae | Lower trapezius |
| Sternocleidomastoid | Middle trapezius |
| Pectoralis major (clavicular and sternal) | Rhomboids |
| Pectoralis minor | Serratus anterior |
| Suboccipitals | Posterior deltoid |
| Scalenes (anterior/middle) | External rotators (infraspinatus, teres minor) |

*Muscle origin/insertion/action data from Seeley Ch 10.*

---

## Release (5-8 min)

**Do these BEFORE training or as a standalone session:**

1. **Suboccipital release** — Lying on back, lacrosse ball(s) at base of skull. Gentle chin nod. 60-90s
2. **Pec doorway stretch** — Both sides, 45s each, focus on keeping ribs down
3. **Upper trap/levator stretch** — Ear to shoulder, hand behind back. 30s each side. Add gentle rotation of head toward armpit for levator
4. **Chin tuck with overpressure** — Against wall, 5 reps, 5s hold each
5. **Thoracic extension over foam roller** — Roller at mid-thoracic (between shoulder blades). Arms behind head, extend backward. 10 reps. **Source:** McGill

---

## Activation (7-10 min)

**Daily corrective sequence (do in this order):**

1. **Chin tucks (supine)** — Lie on back, tuck chin, hold 5s. 3×10. Do not lift head
2. **Prone Y-T-W-L** — Face down on floor or incline bench, thumbs up. 8 reps each position
3. **Band pull-aparts** — Shoulder height, squeeze shoulder blades. 3×12
4. **Wall slides** — Against wall, slide arms up keeping contact. 2×8
5. **Supine 90-90 external rotation** — Elbows 90°, arms at 90° angle from torso. Rotate forearms up. Band or light DB. 3×10 each side
6. **Deep neck flexor endurance** — Lying on back, lift head 1-2 inches keeping chin tucked. Hold 10-20s. 3 reps. Only if chin tucks are pain-free

**Total time:** 7-10 min. Can be done as warm-up or separate session.

---

## Integration (during training)

**The 2:1 pulling-to-pressing rule:** For the first 4-6 weeks of correction, do TWO pulling exercises for every ONE pressing exercise. This is temporary.

- **Pressing:** Touch lower on sternum during bench. Keep scapulae retracted. Use dumbbells where possible
- **Pulling:** Row to hips (low row), not to chin. Emphasize elbow drive and scapular squeeze
- **Deadlift:** Neutral cervical spine throughout. Do NOT look up
- **Overhead press:** Bar path should stay over mid-foot. Do NOT let head jut forward to clear the bar
- **Rear delt work:** Prioritize. Every session should include band pull-aparts or prone reverse flies

---

## Training Modifications

| Avoid During Correction | Prefer | Reason |
|-------------------------|--------|--------|
| Upright rows | Band pull-aparts, face pulls (low pulley, cervical neutral) | Upright rows reinforce upper trap dominance |
| Behind-the-neck press | Dumbbell press, landmine press | Behind-neck press at end-range = impingement risk |
| Barbell bench (heavy, wide grip) | Dumbbell bench, close-grip bench (temporarily) | Wide grip = maximum internal rotation demand |
| Front raises (palm-down) | Cable front raises (palms-up) | Palm-down reinforces internal rotation |
| Shrugs (heavy barbell) | Dumbbell shrugs (maintain neutral neck) | Barbell shrugs trigger neck extension + upper trap overactivity |
| Any exercise with cervical extension | Maintain cervical neutral throughout | Reinforces forward head pattern |

**Technique standards:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/NSCA - Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning/04 Decision Rules.md\|NSCA Ch 11-12]] provide the exercise technique and spotting standards that underpin these modifications.

---

## Daily Habits

- **Phone:** Bring to face level. See [[04_PROTOCOLS/Posture/Forward Head Posture.md#daily-habits\|Forward Head daily habits]]
- **Desk:** Monitor at eye level. Lumbar support. Shoulders back against chair
- **Walking:** Palms facing forward. Chin tucked. Chest proud (not puffed)
- **Sleeping:** Side sleepers — pillow thickness that maintains cervical neutral. Avoid stomach sleeping
- **Posture reminder:** Set phone to chime every 30 min. On chime: chin tuck + roll shoulders back. 3s. That's it

**Applied context:** For exercise technique and movement correction standards, see NSCA Ch 11-12. For habit formation and adherence strategies, see ACE BC-01 (stage-of-change model).

---

## Progress Markers

| Milestone | Timeframe | How to Check |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| Can do chin tucks without jaw jutting | 1-2 weeks | Supine chin tuck test |
| Shoulders start touching wall | 4-6 weeks | Wall test — shoulder contact |
| Head gap decreases by 0.5" | 4-8 weeks | Wall test — head gap re-measure |
| Palms face thighs (not back) at rest | 6-8 weeks | Arm hang test |
| Wall slides with full contact | 8-12 weeks | Arms stay on wall during entire slide |
| Head gap ≤1 inch | 8-16 weeks | Wall test — full correction |

---

## Prehab / Maintenance

- **Permanent 1.5:1 pulling-to-pressing ratio** in all future programming
- **2×/week corrective mini-session:** Chin tucks (10 reps) + band pull-aparts (15 reps) + wall slides (8 reps) = 3 min, do it forever
- **Monthly wall test:** If you fail, add 1 week of daily corrective work
- **Early warning signs:** Desk posture regresses first. Catching it after 3 days of bad desk posture = 1 day of extra corrective work. Catching it after 3 months = starting over

protocols.Rehab/Achilles Tendinopathy:
# Achilles Tendinopathy — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Mid-portion and insertional Achilles tendinopathy, Achilles tendinitis*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Pain/stiffness in the **Achilles tendon** (back of heel/lower calf)
- Worse in the **morning** (first steps), eases after a few minutes of walking
- Stiffness after prolonged sitting or driving
- Gradual onset, associated with increased running/walking/ jumping volume
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Sudden pop/tear + inability to push off (possible rupture), severe swelling + warmth + redness, antalgic gait >48 hours, palpable gap in tendon
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 3 (tendon, poorly vascularized, months-years) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Ankle (hinge, mono-axial) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-5)

- **Modify but DON'T rest completely** — complete rest worsens tendon capacity **Source: E3 Rehab**
- **Reduce high-impact loading:** Switch from running/jumping to cycling, swimming, elliptical (pain-free)
- **Pain management:** Ice after activity if reactive. Paracetamol if needed. NSAIDs not recommended for long-term. **Source: E3 Rehab**
- **Heel lift** in shoes (2-3mm) to reduce tendon load during walking
- **Continued:** Upper body training, non-impact lower body (pain-free)

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-12+)

**Key insight:** Recovery takes 3-6+ months. Focus on function trend, not daily pain. **Source: E3 Rehab**

### Stage 1: Isometric Loading (Week 1-2)
- **Isometric calf raise hold** against wall — hold at end range 30-45s, 3-5 reps. **Source: E3 Rehab** (high irritability isometrics reduce pain)
- **Seated calf raise** (bent knee = targets soleus) — 3×15
- **Pain rule:** ≤3/10 during. No increase in next-day symptoms. Test next-day response with a heel raise. **Source: E3 Rehab** (next-day symptom assessment)

### Stage 2: Heavy Slow Resistance (Week 3-8)
- **Standing calf raise** (straight leg, full ROM, 3s up, 3s down) — 3×10-15. Add load via vest, dumbbell, or leg press
- **Seated calf raise** — 3×10-15 (targets soleus, important for Achilles)
- **Frequency:** Every other day
- **Load:** Work up to heavy (6-8 RM). Heavy loading is superior to stretching for tendon stiffness. **Source: E3 Rehab, Willy & Paquette**
- **Pain rule:** Safe to push into mild discomfort during exercise. Key is next-day response. If symptoms worsen next day → reduce volume 20%. **Source: E3 Rehab** (you didn't do harm, you just did more than you could recover from)

### Stage 3: Energy Storage + Return (Week 8-12+)
- **Pogo hops** (small, stiff hops on both legs) — 3×20
- **Skip rope** — 3×1 min
- **Single-leg calf raise** — 3×10-15 (build to it)
- **Running return:** Start walk-jog. Pain <3/10 during, must not worsen next day

## Return to Running

- **Criteria:**
  - Single-leg calf raise 20+ reps without pain
  - Hop test: 10 single-leg hops without significant pain increase
  - No morning stiffness increase from baseline
- **Graduated return:**
  1. Walk 30 min pain-free → walk-jog 3:1 min (total 20 min) × 1 week
  2. Walk-jog 2:2 min (total 20 min) × 1 week
  3. Run 15 min continuous, flat surface × 1 week
  4. Run 20 min × 1 week, then 30 min
  5. Add gentle hills and speed gradually over 2-3 weeks

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Sprinting early | Gradual run program | High-speed loading spikes tendon stress |
| Heavy plyometrics | Pogo hops, skipping | Progress energy storage slowly |
| Long stretching | Loading (calf raises) | Stretching no better than eccentrics for outcomes |
| Running on camber | Flat routes | Uneven surface increases side-to-side load |
| Minimalist shoes | Supportive shoes with heel drop | Heel drop reduces tendon load |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Calf raises 2×/week (heavy) — continue indefinitely
- Avoid sudden jumps in running volume (>10% per week)
- **Early warning signs:** Morning stiffness returning after period of being symptom-free → reduce running volume 20% for 1 week. Tendon reactive phase = transient, catch it early

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Achilles Tendinopathy / Tendinitis / Tendinosis | Heel Pain Rehab:** https://youtu.be/DnxahqgsAEw — Full guide covering anatomy, myths, isometric loading, eccentric progression, return to running
- **E3 Rehab Podcast — Achilles Tendinopathy w/ Silbernagel & Chimenti:** https://www.youtube.com/@E3Rehab — Research-to-practice translation
- **Squat University — Achilles Pain & Calf Tightness:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Assessment and exercise demo

**Sources:** E3 Rehab (Achilles Tendinopathy guide, podcast with Silbernagel and Chimenti), [P]rehab Achilles guide, Clinical Practice Guidelines (Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy, 2024)

protocols.Rehab/Calf Strain:
# Calf Strain — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Tennis leg (medial gastrocnemius strain), soleus strain*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- **Sudden sharp pain in back of lower leg**, often during sprinting, jumping, or acceleration
- Pain when pointing toe or stretching calf
- Swelling, bruising possible (depending on severity)
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Pop + inability to push off (possible Achilles rupture), severe swelling + warmth + unilateral leg (rule out DVT), numbness/tingling in foot, palpable gap in muscle
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 2 (skeletal muscle, weeks-months) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Ankle/knee (hinge) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-3)

- **Protection:** Avoid walking that causes sharp pain. Crutches if needed for first 1-2 days. **Source: NHS Wales**
- **Pain management:** Ice 15 min every 2-3 hours. Compression sleeve or elastic bandage. Elevate.
- **What to do:** Gentle ankle and knee ROM (without stretching calf) — 10 reps every hour while awake. **Source: Boston Sports Medicine**
- **What to avoid:** Stretching the calf (endanger healing tissue), massage on injured area, running, HARMD protocol (Heat, Alcohol, Running, Massage, Driving) for first 72h. **Source: NHS Wales**
- **Heel lift in shoe** — reduces calf tension during walking

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-6+)

### Stage 1: Isometric Loading (Days 3-7)
- **Standing bilateral calf isometric** (hold at neutral, pain-free angle) — 30s hold, 3 reps, multiple ×/day
- **Seated calf isometric** (bent knee, targets soleus) — 30s hold, 3 reps
- **Ankle ROM** (alphabet, circles) — without stretching
- **Pain rule:** ≤3/10, no worsening next day

### Stage 2: Heavy Slow Resistance (Week 1-4)
- **Standing bilateral calf raise** (slow, controlled, 3s up, 3s down) — 3×10. Progress to single leg when pain-free
- **Seated calf raise** — 3×10-15
- **Straight leg walking** then progress to walking normally
- **Frequency:** Every other day
- **Load:** Build to heavy (6-8 RM). Heavy slow resistance improves tendon stiffness + muscle capacity. **Source: Physio Network**

### Stage 3: Energy Storage + Return (Week 4-6+)
- **Pogo hops** (small, stiff both legs) — 3×15
- **Skip rope** — 3×1 min
- **Single-leg calf raise** — 3×10-15 (both height and control)
- **Return to running** — see below

## Return to Running

- **Criteria:**
  - Pain-free walking for 30+ min
  - Single-leg calf raise 25× pain-free
  - Hop on single leg 10× with minimal pain
- **Graduated:**
  1. Walk → walk-jog (1:3) × 15 min, flat surface — 3×/week
  2. Progress ratio over 2 weeks to continuous jog 15 min
  3. Build to 30 min continuous over 2-3 weeks
  4. Add speed work and jumps after >30 min continuous is pain-free
- **Grade-based timeline:**
  - Grade 1: 1-2 weeks to return
  - Grade 2: 2-4 weeks to return
  - Grade 3: 4-6+ weeks to return
  - **Source: Physio Network (calf strain in runners)**

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Sprinting early | Gradual run program | High-speed ACS = high calf load |
| Stretching | Isometrics, slow loading | Stretching may disrupt healing in early phase |
| Deep squatting | Partial ROM | End-range DF stretches calf |
| Hopping/pogo early | Isometrics, slow raises | Energy storage before capacity = re-injury risk |
| Heavy deadlift (if painful on toes) | Trap bar with higher handles | Heel elevation reduces calf demand |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Heavy calf raises 2×/week — eccentric control important
- Gradual return to sprinting/jumping (increase volume 10% per week max)
- **Early warning signs:** Twinge during sprint finish → stop immediately, 3-day rest, then reintroduce gradually
- **High-risk:** Prior calf strain → higher re-injury risk. Maintain calf strength year-round

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Calf Muscle Strain Injury (Best Exercises for Rehab and Return to Running):** https://youtu.be/Q8egrbpRO2U — Covers anatomy, acute management, isometric → isotonic progression, return to sport criteria
- **Squat University — Calf Pain When Running?:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Assessment and differential diagnosis
- **[P]rehab — Calf Strain Exercises & Treatment:** https://www.youtube.com/@PrehabGuys — Exercise demos with progression guidelines

**Sources:** E3 Rehab (Calf Strain guide), Physio Network (calf strain in runners), Boston Sports Medicine (calf protocol), NHS Wales calf strain advice

protocols.Rehab/Elbow Tendinopathy:
# Elbow Tendinopathy — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow), triceps tendinopathy*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Pain on **outside of elbow** (tennis elbow) — worse with gripping, lifting with palm down, typing, or shaking hands
- Pain on **inside of elbow** (golfer's elbow) — worse with gripping, lifting with palm up, golf, climbing
- Pain **back of elbow** (triceps tendinopathy) — worse with pushing, dips, overhead extension
- Gradual onset from repetitive loading
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Elbow locking/catching, numbness/tingling in ring/pinky finger (ulnar nerve), loss of grip strength, swelling + redness + fever
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 3 (tendon, poorly vascularized, months-years) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Elbow (hinge, mono-axial) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-7)

- **Reduce aggravating loads:** Painful gripping (reduce intensity, use straps/hooks temporarily), repetitive wrist movements, heavy pushing/pulling
- **Pain management:** Ice massage on tendon area for 10 min after activity. Paracetamol if needed. **Source: E3 Rehab** (inflammation not primary driver, limit NSAIDs)
- **What to continue:** Lower body training, core, shoulder + upper back work (pain-free)
- **Counterforce brace** — may reduce symptom during activity by changing load distribution. **Source: NHS, E3 Rehab**

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-12+)

**Key insight:** Recovery takes 3+ months. This is a tendon capacity issue, not inflammation. **Source: E3 Rehab**

### Stage 1: Isometric Grip (Week 1-3)
- **Tennis elbow:** Wrist extension isometric (palm down on table, push hand UP against resistance, hold 30-45s) — 3-5 reps. **Source: E3 Rehab** (isometrics reduce pain + maintain load)
- **Golfer's elbow:** Wrist flexion isometric (palm up on table, push hand UP against resistance, hold 30-45s) — 3-5 reps
- **Triceps:** Against wall, isometric extension hold 30-45s
- **Frequency:** 2-3×/day
- **Pain rule:** ≤3/10 during, no worsening next day

### Stage 2: Eccentric + Concentric Loading (Week 3-8)
- **Tennis elbow:** Eccentric wrist extension (use other hand to lift weight up, lower with injured side over 3s) — 3×10-12. Progress to dumbbell
- **Golfer's elbow:** Eccentric wrist flexion — 3×10-12
- **Triceps:** Push-downs with band, slow eccentrics — 3×10
- **Grip strengthening:** Rice bucket, towel twists, or hand gripper — 3×15
- **Supination/pronation** (forearm rotation with light hammer or dowel) — 3×12 each direction
- **Frequency:** Every other day
- **Load:** Work up to moderate weight (8-12 RM range)

### Stage 3: Sport-Specific (Week 8-12+)
- **Chin-ups/pull-ups** (if pain-free)
- **Dumbbell press** (neutral grip if possible)
- **Return to throwing/racket sports:** Gradual volume increase (50% → 75% → 100% over 3 weeks)
- **Pain rule:** Expect mild discomfort during activity. Monitor next-day response.

## Return to Training

- **Criteria:**
  - Full pain-free grip strength (squeeze hand gripper or shake hands without pain)
  - Pain-free during daily activities
  - Cozen's test (resisted wrist extension) pain-free or <2/10
- **Reintroduction:**
  1. Start with lower volume, longer rest between sets
  2. Avoid supinated grip (palms-up) pulling for first 2 weeks if golfer's elbow
  3. Use neutral grip where possible
  4. Add volume by 10-20% per week, guided by next-day response

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Heavy pull-ups (pronated) | Neutral grip pull-ups, lat pulldown | Reduces medial elbow stress |
| Heavy bench press (wide) | Close-grip bench, push-ups on fists | Narrower grip = less wrist extension |
| Deadlifts (heavy, mixed grip) | Trap bar deadlift, straps | Mixed grip stresses medial elbow |
| Barbell curls | EZ bar curls, dumbbell curls (neutral) | Reduces wrist extension/flexion demand |
| Dips | Push-ups, floor press | Dips = high triceps tendon load |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Wrist extensor/flexor conditioning 2×/week
- Progress grip training slowly (don't jump to heavy farmer's carries without base)
- **Early warning signs:** Dull ache the day after grip-intensive training → reduce grip volume 50% for 1 week. Persistent >2 weeks → earlier stage rehab
- **Ergonomics:** Check desk setup if typing-intensive work

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Lateral Elbow Tendinopathy (Tennis Elbow) Rehab:** https://youtu.be/aOueY1l_X0U — Covers anatomy, myths, isometric → isotonic loading, grip strengthening
- **E3 Rehab — Medial Elbow Tendinopathy (Golfer's Elbow) Rehab:** https://youtu.be/3CJMz0HoGXk — Specific protocol for medial elbow pain
- **E3 Rehab — Elbow & Wrist Rehab Playlist:** https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLK514QIbc_RgR4RHzMWB5yeu5sMQu5W_d — Comprehensive collection
- **Squat University — Tennis Elbow Fix:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Quick assessment and exercise demo

**Sources:** E3 Rehab (Tennis Elbow Rehab, Golfer's Elbow Rehab), NHS clinical guidelines, Cleveland Clinic management guidance

protocols.Rehab/Groin Strain:
# Groin Strain — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Adductor strain, pulled groin, adductor-related groin pain*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Pain in **inner thigh / groin**, especially when squeezing legs together or moving sideways
- Pain with resisted adduction (squeezing a ball between knees)
- May occur with sprinting, cutting, kicking, or sudden direction changes
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Inguinal hernia suspicion (lump in groin), testicular pain, inability to bear weight, hip joint pain (deep in front of hip — FAI/labral tear), numbness/tingling down leg
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 2 (skeletal muscle, weeks-months) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Hip (ball-and-socket, multi-axial) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-5)

- **Protection:** Avoid lunges, wide stance, side-to-side movements, sprinting
- **Pain management:** Ice on inner thigh 15 min, 4-5×/day
- **Crutches** if walking is painful
- **What to continue:** Upper body, core, non-injured leg
- **Gentle isometric adduction:** Squeeze a pillow between knees (supine, knees bent, hold 10s) — no pain. **Source: [P]rehab**

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-6+)

### Stage 1: Isometric Loading (Days 3-10)
- **Supine adductor isometric** (pillow/ball between bent knees, squeeze + hold 10s) — 3×10
- **Side-lying adductor isometric** (top leg on low table, bottom leg lift 2-3 inches, hold 10s) — 3×10
- **Standing adductor isometric** (gym ball between feet + inner thighs, squeeze) — 3×15s
- **Pain rule:** ≤3/10. Ramp up intensity but stay below pain threshold. **Source: E3 Rehab, [P]rehab**
- **Frequency:** 3-4×/day

### Stage 2: Concentric Loading (Week 2-4)
- **Side-lying hip adduction** (slow raise, controlled lower, no weight) — 3×12
- **Standing band adduction** (band on ankle, bring leg across body) — 3×12
- **Sumo squat** (bodyweight, partial ROM) — 3×10
- **Copenhagen adductor hold** (side plank position with top leg on a bench, lower leg suspended, hold) — start with isometric holds, 3×15-30s
- **Frequency:** Every other day

### Stage 3: Sport-Specific + Return (Week 4-6+)
- **Lunges** (forward + lateral, controlled) — 3×8 each direction
- **Lateral shuffle** (pain-free speed and distance) — 3×30s
- **Return to sprinting:** Gradual acceleration protocol over 1-2 weeks
- **Return to sport-specific** (kicking, cutting, direction changes)

## Return to Running

- **Criteria:**
  - Pain-free during walking and daily activities
  - Resisted adduction test pain-free (manual resistance)
  - 15 Copenhagen adductor holds (10s each) pain-free
- **Graduated:** Walk → jog (straight line) → run (gradual acceleration) → direction changes → sport-specific

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Wide-stance squats | Narrow stance, sumo partial ROM | Wide stance loads adductors more |
| Heavy lunges | Bodyweight lunges, limited range | Deep lunges stress adductors at end range |
| Side-to-side drills early | Straight-line running | Cutting loads adductors eccentrically |
| Kicking sports | Non-impact cardio | Kicking = explosive adductor loading |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Copenhagen adductor holds 2-3×/week — single best prevention exercise. **Source: E3 Rehab**
- Adductor strengthening (band adductions) 1-2×/week
- **Early warning signs:** Tightness during cutting drills → reduce intensity 20% and add adductor prehab
- **High-risk:** Prior groin strain = 21% re-injury rate. Stay consistent with maintenance work. **Source: UEFA injury analysis**

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Groin Pain Rehab | Adductor Strain / Pull (Education | Myths | Exercises):** https://www.youtube.com/@E3Rehab — Search "Groin Pain Rehab E3 Rehab" for full video covering 4-level progression
- **E3 Rehab — Adductor Strain Rehab Article with Embedded Video:** https://e3rehab.com/adductorstrainrehab/ — Written guide with video demonstrations of each exercise
- **Squat University — How to Fix A Groin Pull:** https://youtu.be/T0udy4rQwwU — Assessment and exercise demo for adductor strain
- **[P]rehab — Prehab Your Groin:** https://www.youtube.com/@PrehabGuys — Management strategies and exercise progressions

**Sources:** E3 Rehab (Adductor Strain Rehab), [P]rehab (Prehab Your Groin), Aspetar Clinical Guidelines for Adductor Injuries, Mass General Brigham Athletic Pubalgia Protocol

protocols.Rehab/Hamstring Strain:
# Hamstring Strain — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Pulled hamstring, proximal hamstring tendinopathy*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Acute or gradual pain in **back of thigh**, often during sprinting, jumping, or high-speed running
- Pain with bending forward (stretching hamstring)
- Tenderness to touch
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Complete inability to bear weight (possible grade 3 tear), palpable gap in muscle, bruising spreading significantly, numbness in posterior thigh/calf (sciatic nerve involvement). If pain is at the **sitting bone (ischial tuberosity)** and persistent >6 weeks, consider proximal hamstring avulsion → medical eval.
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 2 (skeletal muscle, weeks-months) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Knee (modified hinge) + hip (ball-and-socket) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-3)

- **Protection:** Avoid stretching the hamstring. Do not bend forward with straight legs. **Source: University of Delaware protocol**
- **Pain management:** Ice in lengthened position (long sitting with leg straight, ice on posterior thigh) — 15 min, 4-5×/day **Source: Sanford Health hamstring guideline**
- **Crutches** if walking is painful (antalgic gait)
- **What to continue:** Upper body, core, and non-injured leg training. Avoid any position that lengthens the injured hamstring.
- **Isometrics:** Gentle hamstring isometrics in neutral position (heel digs into floor while seated) — 5×10s holds, no pain. **Source: UDel protocol** (pain up to 5/10 allowed, must return to baseline next day)

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-6+)

### Stage 1: Isometric + Low-Load (Days 3-7)
- **Isometric hamstring slides** (lying on back, heels on floor, dig heels into floor, hold 5s) — 3×10
- **Bridge** (bilateral, focus on glute + hamstring co-contraction) — 3×12
- **Nerve gliding** (sciatic flossing) if neural tension present — gentle, 2×10. **Source: Mass General Brigham protocol**

### Stage 2: Progressive Strengthening (Week 2-4)
- **Nordic curl negatives** (eccentric only, controlled 3s lower) — 3×5
- **Single-leg bridge** — 3×10
- **Prone hamstring curl** (light band, pain-free ROM) — 3×12
- **Dumbbell RDL** (light, short ROM, maintain neutral spine) — 3×10
- **Pain rule:** Up to 5/10 during exercise is acceptable. Must return to baseline by next morning. **Source: UDel pain monitoring model**

### Stage 3: Sport-Specific (Week 4-6+)
- **Fast eccentrics** (Nordic curl with faster descent, catch yourself) — 3×6
- **Single-leg RDL** (loaded) — 3×8
- **Lunges** — 3×8 each leg
- **Return-to-running protocol** (see below)

## Return to Running

**Criteria to start:**
- Pain-free walking
- Full pain-free ROM (ankle to chest with knee straight, compare to other side)
- Bridge test: 30 single-leg bridges without pain

**Graduated running protocol:**
1. Walk 5 min → jog 50% speed 100m × 5 → walk 5 min (2×/week)
2. Walk 5 min → jog 75% speed 100m × 5 → walk 5 min (2×/week)
3. Walk 5 min → run 50% speed 200m × 5 → walk 5 min (2-3×/week)
4. Run continuous 15 min at easy pace (3×/week)
5. Run 20 min + 2×100m strides (3×/week)
6. Full training + gradual sprint reintroduction

**If pain returns at any step:** Rest 2 days, drop back one step. **Source: UDel, Boston Sports Medicine protocols**

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Stiff-leg deadlifts (full ROM) | RDL (partial ROM, knees bent) | Reduces hamstring end-range stretch |
| Heavy RDLs early | Isometrics, bridges | Progressive loading prevents re-tear |
| Sprinting early | Gradual run program (above) | High-speed running = highest re-injury risk |
| Deep forward folds | Standing with bent knees | End-range lengthening slows healing |
| Kettlebell swings | Hip thrusts | Ballistic loading too early |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Nordic curls 2-3×/week (4×6) — single most evidence-supported hamstring injury prevention exercise. **Source: Petersen et al, systematic review**
- RDLs 1-2×/week (3×8-10)
- **Early warning signs:** Tightness during sprinting + not progressing → reduce speed by 20% and add an extra prehab day
- **High-risk periods:** Start of season, after long breaks, after achieving new sprint PR — increase prevention work

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Proximal Hamstring Tendinopathy Rehab (4 Stages):** https://youtu.be/8KI2XL2vg2Q — Covers isometric → eccentric → sport-specific progression
- **Squat University — How to Rehab a Hamstring Strain:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Assessment, exercises, and return to running protocol
- **E3 Rehab — How to Set Up and Program Nordic Hamstring Curls:** https://youtu.be/963K — Progressive regression/progression for nordic curls (search "E3 Rehab Nordic Hamstring Curls")
- **[P]rehab — Hamstring Strain Rehab:** https://www.youtube.com/@PrehabGuys — Exercise demos with progression guidelines

**Sources:** University of Delaware Hamstring Protocol (Schmitt et al), Mass General Brigham Non-Op Hamstring Protocol, Sanford Health Hamstring Guideline, E3 Rehab adductor/calf articles (overlap principles)

protocols.Rehab/Hip Flexor Strain:
# Hip Flexor Strain — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Iliopsoas strain, hip bursitis (mild)*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Pain in **front of hip/groin**, worse with lifting knee up, running uphill, or sitting with hips flexed
- Pain when stretching hip into extension (knee-back position)
- Gradual onset from running, kicking, or core work (hanging leg raises, sit-ups)
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Deep groin pain + restricted hip rotation (possible FAI/labral tear — different protocol), fever + redness, inability to bear weight, snapping sensation that reproduces sharp pain
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 2 (skeletal muscle, weeks-months) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Hip (ball-and-socket, multi-axial) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-5)

- **Reduce aggravating loads:** High knee running, hanging leg raises, sit-ups, deep squat
- **Pain management:** Ice on front of hip 15 min post-activity
- **What to continue:** Upper body, upper back training, glute-dominant lower body (bridges, hip thrusts)
- **Sitting modification:** Take standing breaks every 20-30 min (prolonged hip flexion aggravates)

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-6+)

### Stage 1: Isometric + Pain-Free ROM (Week 1-2)
- **Supine hip flexor isometric** (lying on back, lift knee 6 inches, hold 30s against manual resistance) — 3 reps
- **Standing hip flexor isometric** (lift knee to 90°, hold 30s) — 3 reps
- **Pain-free hip ROM** (flexion, extension, rotation — no stretching)
- **Frequency:** 2-3×/day
- **Pain rule:** ≤3/10, must settle within 30 min

### Stage 2: Eccentric Loading (Week 2-4)
- **Eccentric hip flexor** (stand, slowly lower straight leg behind you, control through full range) — 3×8
- **Leg lowers** (lying on back, lower one straight leg slowly, stop at pain threshold) — 3×8
- **Supine marching** (lie flat, alternately lift knees to 90°, slow, controlled) — 3×12
- **Side-lying leg raises** — 3×12 each side

### Stage 3: Sport-Specific + Return (Week 4-6+)
- **Lunges** (forward, controlled, short stride) — 3×8 each
- **Walking lunges** — progressive
- **Running return** (flat, gradual pace increase)
- **Uphill running** reintroduced last (highest hip flexor demand)

## Return to Training

- **Criteria:**
  - Pain-free during daily activities (walking, sitting, standing up)
  - Full pain-free hip extension (Thomas test)
  - Resisted hip flexion test pain-free
- **Reintroduction:**
  1. Flat running first, add hills last
  2. Avoid high-knee drills and sprinting for first 2 weeks back
  3. Core work: avoid hanging leg raises initially — use dead bugs and planks

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Hanging leg raises | Dead bug, plank on elbows | Hanging leg raise = high hip flexor eccentric load |
| Running uphill early | Flat running | Uphill = increased hip flexor demand |
| Deep squatting | Partial squat to 90° | Deep squat = hip flexor compressed at end range |
| Sit-ups (full ROM) | Crunches (partial), dead bugs | Full sit-up = hip flexor dominant |
| High-knee running drills | Straight-leg jog, shuffle | High knees = explosive concentric hip flexor work |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Hip flexor conditioning (slow leg lowers) 2×/week
- Stretch hip flexors AFTER training (not before) — lunges with tall posture, 60s each side
- **Early warning signs:** Dull ache in front of hip after uphill running → reduce hill work 50% for 1 week

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — Hip Flexor Pain | Strain | Tendinitis Rehab (Iliopsoas Strength & Mobility Exercises):** https://youtu.be/Ujf2h0WWryw — Covers anatomy, isometric loading, stretching, and strengthening progression
- **E3 Rehab — Tight Hip Flexors? (Self-Assessment | Stretches | Exercises):** https://www.youtube.com/@E3Rehab — Assessment and mobility exercises for hip flexor tightness (search "Tight Hip Flexors E3 Rehab")
- **Squat University — Hip Flexor Pain When Squatting?:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Technique and mobility fixes

**Sources:** Mass General Brigham (groin pain protocol), E3 Rehab (hip resilience principles), Sports Medicine guidelines for hip pain

protocols.Rehab/IT Band Syndrome:
# IT Band Syndrome — Self-Managed Rehab

*Also applies to: Iliotibial band friction syndrome, lateral knee pain in runners*

---

**Evidence sources:** [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Junqueira's Basic Histology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Junqueira Ch 5,7,10]] (tissue healing hierarchy, collagen types) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Seeley's Anatomy and Physiology 2019/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Seeley Ch 8]] (joint classification, anatomy) | [[08_EXTERNAL_KNOWLEDGE/Books/Guyton and Hall - Textbook of Medical Physiology 14ed/03 Extracted Concepts.md\|Guyton Ch 72,85]] (metabolic adaptation, energy systems)

## When This Protocol Applies

- Pain on **outside of the knee**, sharp or burning sensation
- Worse with **running** (especially downhill), cycling, walking long distances
- Pain appears after a certain distance/mileage, not at the start
- May also feel tightness along outside of thigh/hip
- **Red flags → do NOT self-treat:** Knee locking/catching, swelling inside the knee, sharp pain with twisting (possible meniscus), inability to bear weight
- **Tissue healing tier:** Tier 3 (ligament/tendon, poorly vascularized) — Junqueira Ch 5,7,10. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Tissue Healing Hierarchy]]
- **Joint classification:** Knee (modified hinge) + hip (ball-and-socket) — Seeley Ch 8. See [[02_PILLARS/Pillar 4 - Recovery Maxing.md\|P4 Recovery — Joint Classification Reference]]

---

## Acute Phase (Days 1-5)

- **Reduce mileage** to below the pain threshold. If pain starts at mile 3, run 2 miles. **Source: Sports Injury Physio, E3 Rehab**
- **Avoid:** Downhill running, cambered surfaces (run on flat or track, switch directions)
- **Pain management:** Ice massage on lateral knee after running — 10 min
- **What to continue:** Upper body, core, cycling (if pain-free), swimming
- **Foam roll** glutes, TFL, and quads. Do NOT foam roll directly over IT band at knee (it's not a muscle, rolling it may increase irritation). **Source: E3 Rehab, Harvard Health**

## Rehab Phase (Week 1-8+)

### Stage 1: Hip Abductor Loading (Week 1-3)
- **Clamshells** (band above knee) — 3×15 each side
- **Side-lying leg raises** (30° lift only — higher angles use TFL, not glute med) — 3×15
- **Lateral band walks** (band at ankles, keep feet forward) — 3×10 steps each direction
- **Glute bridge** (single leg when ready) — 3×12
- **Frequency:** Daily
- **Key insight:** Hip abductor weakness is the PRIMARY risk factor for ITBS. Fix the hip, fix the knee. **Source: Physios Unit, Sports Injury Physio**

### Stage 2: Movement Control (Week 3-6)
- **Step-downs** (small box, controlled descent, knee tracking over 2nd toe) — 3×10
- **Single-leg squat** (to 45°, focus on hip/knee alignment) — 3×8
- **Lunges** (forward and lateral, controlled) — 3×8
- **Deadlift** (single-leg RDL) — 3×8
- **Monitor:** Knee valgus/collapse during any exercise = glute not firing correctly

### Stage 3: Return to Running (Week 4-8+)
- **Start walk-run** at 1:3 ratio on flat surface
- **If pain returns:** Drop back one stage, check hip strength
- **Camber management:** Run on flat, alternate direction on track

## Return to Running

- **Criteria:**
  - 30 single-leg bridges pain-free
  - Single-leg squat with good control (no valgus)
  - Pain-free during daily activities
- **Graduated return:**
  1. Walk-run 1:3 (1 min run, 3 min walk) × 15 min total, flat surface — 3×/week
  2. Walk-run 2:2 × 20 min — 3×/week
  3. Run 15 min continuous — 3×/week
  4. Add 5 min/week, stop at pain threshold. Over 4 weeks build to 30 min
  5. Gentle hills and speed in week 5+

## Exercise Modifications

| Avoid | Substitute | Why |
|-------|-----------|-----|
| Downhill running | Flat or slight uphill | Downhill = higher eccentric load = more compression |
| Running on camber | Track (alternating direction), flat loop | Banked surface compresses IT band at knee |
| Deep squats (>90°) | Half squats (to 60°) | Deep flexion = more IT band compression |
| Heavy deadlifts | RDL (controlled) | If painful at end range |
| Crossover stretching | Leg lowers | Traditional ITB stretch may compress painfully |

## Prehab / Prevention

- Glute med work (clamshells, band walks) 2-3×/week — this is the #1 prevention
- Avoid sudden mileage increases (>10% per week)
- Replace running shoes every 300-500 miles
- **Early warning signs:** Dull ache on outer knee at fixed mileage → reduce by 20% and add glute med work
- **Vary training surfaces** — don't always run on cambered roads

---

### Video Resources

- **E3 Rehab — IT Band Syndrome Rehab | Iliotibial Band Pain (Education | Myths | Exercises):** https://youtu.be/l3SaCH3p9do — Covers anatomy, friction vs compression theories, 4-stage rehab progression
- **Squat University — IT Band Pain When Running?:** https://www.youtube.com/@SquatUniversity — Assessment, hip weakness contribution, and corrective exercises
- **[P]rehab — Prehab Your IT Band:** https://www.youtube.com/@PrehabGuys — Management strategies and exercise progressions

**Sources:** E3 Rehab (IT Band Rehab), Sports Injury Physio (exercises for ITBS), Harvard Health (prevention + treatment), UPMC (management guide), Physios Unit (12% of running injuries)
